content: As the US Congress prepares to usher in a Democratic majority, Musk director Alex Gibney wants to know if there will be renewed interest in government investigations into Elon Musk’s business practices. “Is our political system capable—assuming the Democrats win the House and the Senate—of ignoring the power of money … to hold really tough investigations?” Gibney asked WIRED contributing editor Zoë Schiffer following a screening of Musk at the WIRED World Fair just before many of the major congressional races were called for Democrats. Gibney’s sweeping documentary highlights United States government agencies’ multiple investigations into Musk, positing that these actions partially motivated Musk’s support for Donald Trump and other Republican candidates in recent years. On Tuesday, Gibney pointed to the more than $474 million Musk has donated to Republican political groups this election cycle, adding that, “Last I looked, things weren’t going Elon’s way, particularly in Texas.” Not long after those remarks, James Talrico was declared the winner of his Senate race and Gina Hinojosa was elected the state’s governor, some of the first Democrats to win a Texas statewide election in more than three decades. Musk, who has enjoyed close relationships with Texas bigwigs for years, donated at least $158 million to super PACs supporting Talrico’s opponent, Texas attorney general Ken Paxton. Musk “now has such an extraordinary amount of money that dropping $500 million on an election means nothing to him,” Gibney says. However, much of that money is tied up in his companies’ stock. “The question is: What if that stock begins to fall?” While making Musk, Gibney spoke with tech entrepreneurs, former employees, and, in two particularly damning interviews, Musk’s exes—his first wife, Justine Wilson, and ex-girlfriend, Ashley St. Clair. Musk also features interviews with Schiffer and WIRED global editorial director Katie Drummond. Musk declined to be interviewed for the film. Instead, Gibney’s team used Musk’s past public comments to create a simulated version, pairing actual quotes with a tanned, chiseled avatar wearing a leather jacket. On X, Musk has decried the documentary as a “hit piece.” In September, Alex Spiro, an attorney for Musk, sent Gibney’s Jigsaw Productions a letter threatening to file a defamation lawsuit ahead of the film’s release. The rollout for Musk has been complex. In early October, independent film distributor Bleecker Street—which owns Musk’s domestic theatrical rights—moved up the release date by a week, following strong festival reviews. According to The Hollywood Reporter, YouTube, TikTok, and Meta all initially declined to advertise the trailer for Musk leading up to the film’s debut; X did not advertise the trailer at all. Musk will be available to rent or buy starting November 6, at which point it will no longer play in theaters. Author of the CMO Insider newsletter Cybersecurity startup Abnormal AI wants its marketing to be anything but ordinary. Abnormal AI exclusively told CMO Insider on Wednesday that it has appointed Don Jeter as its chief marketing officer. In an interview, Jeter said he has big ambitions to use unconventional marketing techniques as part of a plan to build Abnormal AI into a "household name" brand. "I want my nephew, who is 14, and my parents to know Abnormal," Jeter said. "I want to be the most talked-about cybersecurity company in 2027." Jeter said that's why he intends to throw out the traditional business-to-business marketing playbook, which often focuses on features and functions, and instead plans to create "cultural moments" that will capture the attention of all kinds of consumers beyond its CISO target audience. Founded in 2018, Abnormal made its name using behavioral AI to detect email security threats. It has since expanded the technology to help companies spot unusual activity in employees' digital accounts and logins, and is increasingly applying the same approach to securing organizations' use of AI tools. The company was valued at $5.1 billion after a $250 million Series D funding round in 2024. One of Jeter's near-term challenges is resetting the narrative that Abnormal is only an email security company. He'll be attempting to do so in a noisy market, competing for mindshare against the marketing heft of trillion-dollar tech giants and buzzy frontier AI companies, as well as the cybersecurity vendors jostling for chief information security officers' budgets. "Right now, in this market, you've got to build trust and awareness before the sales conversation starts," Jeter said. "If you do brand marketing correctly, everything else gets easier; it signals to the market you are winning." While he wanted to keep his specific plans under wraps for now, Jeter said out-of-home advertising and other IRL activations are likely to play key roles in Abnormal AI's marketing mix. "We want to create stuff that people naturally want to share and participate in," Jeter said. "With great marketing, you never have to ask your employees to 'please share and retweet.'" B2B brands are increasingly taking a more business-to-consumer marketing approach. Salesforce and Adobe hold their glitzy Dreamforce and MAX conferences. Autodesk has a string of major sports team partnerships and splurged to advertise on the Las Vegas Sphere. Elsewhere, Ramp enlisted former pro skater Tony Hawk for a comedic campaign that culminated with him dropping in and skating on a ramp during a live event outside the New York Stock Exchange and around the trading floor. "A B2B buyer is still a person who remembers a great story, and in a category where nearly every company is promising smarter AI, tighter security, or faster results, IRL connection gives people a reason to remember one brand over another," said Steve Nottingham, CEO of the commerce experience agency RSM&, about Jeter's plans for Abnormal AI. Nottingham said CMOs who want to execute these kinds of activations need to start with a clear objective, an idea that could only come from their brand, a defined audience, a parallel content strategy that allows for amplification, and measurement that clearly connects the buzz to brand awareness and the sales pipeline. "Done thoughtfully, a real-world moment can work harder than almost any other line in the budget, because the conversation it starts keeps going well beyond the day itself," Nottingham said. Jeter has experience in this area. As CMO of cybersecurity startup Torq, he built the brand through deliberately offbeat marketing campaigns. Torq sponsored Monster Jam's nationwide tour for its "Torq, not torque" campaign, then brought a 20-foot inflatable skeleton and an on-site tattoo bus to the 2026 RSAC cybersecurity conference. "B2B marketing, in general, has played it safe for a very long time, and what we are seeing is that's no longer working in today's culture and scarce attention economy," Jeter said. "Safe is boring, and boring is invisible." Jump to

Ross Bowdey was trying to be reasonable. Residents of his hometown of Boulder had been dreaming big for months: The Sundance Film Festival was slated to make its Colorado debut there in January, and many homeowners figured they could make a killing by renting their places to the regular crowd of celebrities and cinephiles. But Bowdey, a longtime property manager, cringed at the lofty dollar figures being floated — in some cases, nearly $10,000 a night for homes that had no business asking that much. He recently met with owners who were interested in renting out their three-bedroom condo in downtown Boulder during the festival. What the home lacked in size it made up for in location, right off the town's main strip. Bowdey thought he could get them about $2,500 a night. "Their response to me was, 'You're not even close,'" Bowdey tells me. Sundance's decision to ditch its longtime home of Park City, Utah, in favor of Boulder marked a coup for the city — and a conundrum. Among the biggest questions: Where to put everybody? The city sees brief swells of visitors for University of Colorado-related celebrations such as family weekend or graduation day, but it has never hosted an event on the scale of Sundance, which tends to draw about 100,000 people over 11 days. The hotel squeeze was exacerbated by a long-standing ban on investor-owned Airbnbs, leaving Boulder well short of the rentals needed to accommodate the festival. Boulder officials' response has been to open the floodgates, inviting practically anyone to apply for a special license to list their home as a short-term rental during Sundance. Investors, longtime Boulderites, part-time residents, even renters — all are welcome to help shore up the city's stock of Airbnbs and Vrbos. The city has approved more than 1,300 short-term rentals since opening up the process and receives about 40 more applications each week. Businesses are popping up to connect luxury homeowners with studios, sponsors, and A-listers in need of places to stay, while some residents are orchestrating renovations to lure premium-paying guests. Not everyone is pleased. Some festival-goers are balking at the high nightly rates and biding their time until owners slash prices. First-time hosts are realizing their hauls may be smaller than originally hoped. Even the city's tourism organization is asking rate-happy hosts to exercise restraint. "I think people need to get over that idea that they're going to just make their retirement on the first year of Sundance coming to Boulder," says Juli Kovats, a longtime real estate agent there. "It's not gonna happen." The Sundance festival was once synonymous with Park City. For more than 40 years, film buffs and movie stars descended upon the snowy resort town each January in their best approximations of alpine chic. Two years ago, though, the Sundance Institute invited other cities to bid for the hosting gig as the Park City contract neared its 2026 expiration date. Boulder officials were eager to throw their hat in the ring: The local arts scene, nearby mountains, and small-town feel seemed like a natural landing spot for the storied festival. Boulder boosters touted the city's connection to nearby communities, including Denver, and sweetened the deal with tens of millions of dollars' worth of incentives. By the time Sundance and Boulder sealed the deal in the spring of 2025, city officials and leaders at Visit Boulder, the local tourism organization, had already spent months gaming out the lodging situation. They could count on nearly 3,000 hotel rooms but fewer than 700 short-term rentals, thanks to a decade-old city ordinance. In Boulder, you had to actually live in a house if you wanted to rent it out for anything short of 30 days — investors or absentee owners were barred from operating the types of full-time Airbnbs or Vrbos that had proliferated in other markets. Sure, Sundance attendees could retreat each evening to the ample housing options in nearby Denver or its other suburbs, but event organizers wanted as many people as possible to stay near the festivities. They estimated the city would need about 1,500 new short-term rentals to fill the gap. The city's solution was to spin up an exception to Boulder's strict rental rules. In October 2025, the City Council approved a special kind of short-term rental permit, known as a Festival Lodging Rental License, that will allow any owner or tenant to rent out their home from January 11 to February 9, 2027, providing a 10-day cushion on either side of the Sundance dates. Once-banned Airbnbs would be welcomed with open arms. Since then, the potential paydays have captivated Boulder locals. "The hype around it has been crazy," says Zori Levine, a local real estate agent. January is typically Boulder's quietest tourism month, since the place isn't a ski destination like Aspen, Breckenridge, or Park City. Airbnb has already seen a 1,000% year-over-year increase in searches for Boulder rentals during the festival dates, and nearby areas will also get a boost. Denver searches are up nearly 40%, the company says. Kovats, another local real estate agent, hosted a happy hour this summer for the landlord-curious, inviting Bowdey and other real estate insiders to share tips on managing short-term rentals. Usually she'll get about a dozen people at her events, she tells me. This time, nearly 60 people showed up. "I think everybody kind of wants a piece of the pie," Kovats says. Airbnb, in an effort to gin up more intrigue, has offered $200 to first-time hosts during the festival. That amount pales in comparison to some of the nightly rates trotted out by new license holders testing the waters. Charlene Hoffman, the chief executive of Visit Boulder, tells me she's seen listings ranging from $50,000 to $70,000 for the duration of the festival, which she broadly characterizes as "unrealistic." A quick search on Airbnb confirms there are plenty of high-dollar options: a five-bedroom with "breathtaking Rocky Mountain views" can be yours the length of the fest for a whopping $42,380; a four-bedroom near the popular Pearl Street Mall for $42,340; or a six-bedroom with a private, second-floor hot tub for $60,540. "I mean, if it's a six- or seven-bedroom house that has a screening room and a hot tub and a full kitchen and whatever, some of those may demand a higher price," Hoffman tells me. "I just don't think there's many people that will rent them." The majority of Sundance attendees last year — roughly two-thirds — hailed from the state of Utah, an analysis by Y² Analytics found. Generally speaking, these aren't the high rollers who can stomach a five-figure lodging bill. Hoffman tells me she expects next year's festival to draw a similar crowd of Colorado locals, and she's working to ensure they'll find places in the city that fit their budgets. Visit Boulder's "Host with Heart" initiative included educational sessions with Airbnb reps and homeowners, along with suggested pricing: $250 to $300 per night for a one-bedroom condo and $1,100 to $1,400 per night for a four-bedroom house. An Airbnb spokesperson said in an emailed statement that the company is "committed to supporting Boulder in increasing available accommodations." While pricing is left up to individual hosts, the spokesperson said, "we always encourage fair and transparent pricing practices." Some Boulder residents are trying the more modest tack, aiming for hospitality rather than top dollar. Kovats plans to rent out her home's small basement apartment but hasn't yet settled on pricing. She guesses she'll fall somewhere in Visit Boulder's suggested range, maybe $1,000 for five nights: not "outrageous," she tells me, since she considers anyone willing to travel for a film festival "my kind of people." "The market is all over the place from a pricing standpoint," Bowdey tells me. The first year in Boulder was always going to be a learning process, says Paula DuPré Pesmen, a longtime film producer, Boulder resident, and Sundance's managing director of festival and institute operations. She, too, has been working to temper expectations around rental pricing and the typical clientele. "I've often said, George Clooney is probably not going to be booking your home," she tells me. "Most of the people coming are going to be independent artists and their communities." While plenty of pie-in-the-sky prices can be found on Airbnb and Vrbo, the true moonshots may never even reach public platforms. VelareLX, founded in 2025, is working with more than 100 property owners looking to rent out their places for Sundance and other marquee Boulder events. The firm connects hosts and guests based on their requirements, with many of its clients coming from the film industry, says Pete Dawson, VelareLX's managing director. Some are waiting to book until they find out whether their films have made the festival's cut. (The full programming slate will be unveiled in the first half of December). Cris Jones, the Boulder official in charge of coordinating Sundance logistics, acknowledges that some owners are asking for "significantly higher prices than what the Sundance folks were used to." But he's been encouraged to see prices trend downward as more places come up for grabs, and he considers the new license a resounding success, given that it's on track to deliver enough new rentals to surpass the city's goal. The city has received 1,421 applications for the Festival Lodging Rental License and nearly 600 applications for its traditional short-term rental license since December 2025. The bigger challenge on the lodging front, Jones tells me, has been "matching expectations to reality." Boulderites may lack a local precedent for this kind of influx, but similarly short-lived frenzies happen all the time. Hundreds of thousands descend upon Austin for South By Southwest each spring. Some Augusta, Georgia, homeowners collect a year's worth of mortgage payments during the polo-clad Masters pilgrimage. When the World Cup brought soccer's marquee event to nearly a dozen US cities this summer, new short-term rental hosts rushed to turn game day into payday. Yet year one of Sundance in Boulder marks a unique experiment — for the festival and its new host city, sure, but also for the rental rules that have clamped down on Airbnbs and the like around the country. Some places, like Boulder, have taken a restrictive stance toward short-term rentals, limiting licenses to actual residents or outlawing them in certain zones. Others have adopted a looser approach, leaving the number of rentals up to the laws of supply and demand. Many fall somewhere in the messy middle. In the span of a few weeks this winter, Boulder will speed-run both ends of the spectrum. Hoffman says her contacts at Airbnb have reassured her that the aspirational prices will come down as the festival dates near, just as they tend to when a big event like the World Cup or Super Bowl touches down in a new city. "Everybody tests the market in the beginning, and they always shoot very high," Hoffman tells me. Good news for festival-goers — maybe not so much for the hosts dreaming of their five-figure checks. Then again, Sundance has agreed to call Boulder home for at least the next decade. In Park City, many regular attendees returned to the same accommodations each year. Hosts in Colorado may be wise to play the long game. "If you price too high," Bowdey tells me, "it doesn't start off on the right foot." One of the interesting things about the slow-moving AI apocalypse we seem to be trapped in is watching the knock-on effects reverberate through communities and economies. We’ve seen how — and lamented that — the LLM-driven datacenter build up has increased demand for GPUs, RAM and SSDs directly, and we watched that in turn increase demand for traditional, spinning rust hard drives. Perhaps it was only a matter of time before demand came for the tapes, too. Yes, tapes: good old fashioned “sticky tape and rust”. With AI increasing demand for archival material, Fujifilm has announced they’ll be increasing production by 5x through 2028. This production increase is specifically targeting about the latest and greatest 10th generation of Linear Tape, Open (LTO) which Fujifilm has produced since its inception. Indeed, Fujifilm has been in the tape storage business for almost as long as we’ve been storing data on magnetic tape, with their first forays into the field dating to the 1950s. The Ultrium10 tapes are available in 30 TB and 40 TB standard sizes, which are advertised as 75 TB and 100 TB based on a perhaps-optimistic 2.5:1 compression ratio. Given it’s already a linear standard and not exactly blazing fast at 400 uncompressed MB/s, there’s no reason not to compress the heck out of data being sent to cold-storage on tape. While not great by modern SSD or HDD standards, those are dizzying numbers if the last tape drive you used was a Datasette. Still, it shows that the industry is reacting to the same trends that have hackers bringing surplus tape drives into their homelabs. This isn’t a small bet by Fujifilm, with 10 billion yen (about $63 million) at stake. While some of us have been making more use of optical media these days, it looks like Sony isn’t reversing course on getting out of the Blu-ray business, so don’t expect to see giant disk changers coming to a server room near you. Tape bots are apparently a different story. Header image: Fujifilm. Maybe Fuji should restart those chinese factories making Fuji DR-II audio cassettes, while at it. Toshiba, get ready to resume making analog boomboxes (Akai already did, though, unsure if those are true Akai, but good enough, sell reasonably well) : ] Who knows. Physical media deserves its come-back. This is really no more of a physical media than a hard drive. What are some examples of non-physical media? “Physical media” just means “local media”    no reason not to compress the heck out of data being sent to cold-storage on tape   There’s one – bitrot. A bitflip on uncompressed data means that one bit flipped and might not even matter for the whole file. A bitflip on a compressed archive might render the whole archive unusable.  I feel like it’s standard to backup multiple copies across tapes. Also I’m not sure the built in compression that it does would be resistant to that issue either. LTO-10 goes a very long way to protect the data with error correction, data spreading over the tape and read after write. The bit error rate is better than 1 error per 10¹⁹ bits transferred or around 1 error per 100 exabytes transferred. Not error free, obviously, but really, really good. And by organising data in blocks, the effect of any errors can be minimised. Anyone storing data to tape should be doing their own erasure coding or mirroring or backing up anyway on top of whatever the tape is doing, after whatever compression you might personally choose to use. In reality there’s no reason not to write it all uncompressed multiple times to enable data reconstruction later. It’s tape. It’s extremely cheap per bit, no need to be stingy. Er, 100TB compressed down to 40TB, is that not a compression ratio of 2.5:1 instead of 1.5:1? I pity the fool who made that typo, but ’tis fixed now. Now if only they could get the price down to something reasonable for consumers. I’d love if it was cheap to backup everything to a few tapes that I could store in a few places for resiliency. Last, I checked it’s still incredibly expensive unless you get something absolutely ancient. Big too. Maybe now would be the right time to try cheap optical tape archive again? On the roll, not those silly squares trying to compete with thumbdrives like last time. Many years ago they said that they had massive storage in 3D ‘holographic’ cubes as good as done, and they showed samples too. So where are they? It’s not like there is no market at the moment. nor is there a problem with those being expensive to produce right now, you can ask insane amounts for storage, especially if it’s fast. Every time I’ve done the math on an LTO5 or LTO6 installation the total cost (including drive, tapes, library, etc) has always come out very close to that of just building the same storage out of used hard drives. Maybe with the current doubling/tripling of hard drive prices that would become viable, but it’s probably easier and more cost effective to just wait for hard drive prices to come down. Especially if tape prices go up too in reaction. Depends how much data you want to store. Once you’re over the hump, it becomes cheaper. PS5SonyTrade-InXbox  In normal times, console makers regularly cut the price of their latest hardware in order to boost sales and increase revenue. As the cost of manufacturing a new console comes down, they’d drop the price to reach consumers who might not have previously considered buying one. They certainly weren’t begging existing players to trade in their machines for big refunds. But that’s basically what Sony was doing in a recent alert that went out to some current PS5 owners. The alert, titled “Trade in your PS5 console for up to $400,” went out on November 2, and a screenshot of it was shared on the gaming forum ResetEra. “Enjoy simple, hassle-free service if you choose to trade in with Back Market,” the announcement read. “If you’re ready to sell your console, you could soon receive a cash payment into your nominated bank account. Find out how much you could get today.” The deal seemed surprisingly good, even if getting the full $400 did require sending in two DualSense controllers rather than just one. That’s the price the all-digital PS5 launched at in 2020. Instead of going down, the official price tag has ratcheted up to $600. Used PS5s sold on places like eBay are currently going for around $435. Rarely do you see third-party refurbishment offers get anywhere close to lone seller price. Xbox has been similarly aggressive, pinging players who haven’t turned on their Xbox Series X/S consoles in a while with offers of up to $375 to trade them in. That’s one strategy for getting around dwindling supplies and getting existing hardware into the hands of people who will actually buy and play new games on it. In the lead-up to Grand Theft Auto 6, both companies have every incentive to bolster inventory and limit the number of consoles sitting out there in the wild that are just collecting dust. And if you happen to be in the market to get rid of your PS5 Pro, well, you’re in luck. They’ve become so hard to get that GameStop is currently selling used ones for up to $1,400. Boulder is finally embracing short-term rentals … on a short-term basis. The city is lifting its long-standing ban on most Airbnbs, allowing permanent residents to rent out their homes during four weeks spanning January and February. It's a potential model for other cities looking to dabble with the short-term rental market again. Boulder's shift is due to the arrival of The Sundance Film Festival. The college town is replacing Park City as the host of the iconic independent film festival for the next decade. But with roughly 100,000 expected visitors and only 3,000 hotel rooms, the local government needed to get creative. Now residents are hoping to lure film enthusiasts into their homes, erasing some mortgage payments in the process. BI's James Rodriguez has the full rundown on the Boulder community's crash course on the short-term rental business. Some residents are already having an Instagram-vs-reality moment when it comes to pricing their abodes. They're eyeing five-figure stays despite their homes not necessarily fitting the bill. "I think people need to get over that idea that they're going to just make their retirement on the first year of Sundance coming to Boulder," Juli Kovats, a longtime real estate agent there, told James Boulder's success would show how a city can allow residents to benefit from Airbnb without swallowing up housing supply. Short-term rentals have been a hotly debated topic for years, especially as the housing market has worsened. Many cities have banned or enacted strict regulations to prevent investment properties from sitting dormant while hopeful homebuyers struggle with limited inventory. Vacation homes, once viewed as almost a fool-proof play in real estate, have proven to be a nightmare to sell, James previously reported. Rentals based around specific events come with their own issues. Owning a rental property near a big stadium is great when the team is crushing it. The appeal drops if it's a losing team that struggles to fill the stadium, making it harder for you to book guests. Boulder's approach could be a happy medium. Permanent residents have the chance to cash in on specific events without turning the community into a bunch of rental properties that risk sitting empty most of the time Jump to

It's looking like the election might become even more expensive for Elon Musk. Shares in Tesla and SpaceX fell around 5% at market open on Wednesday after the Democrats won a string of midterm victories in Texas, where both companies are based. Both Tesla and SpaceX pared back heavier overnight losses, with Musk's two public companies down as much as 6% and 7% premarket. The Texas results, which saw James Talarico beat Republican nominee Ken Paxton to the Senate seat and Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa unseat longtime governor Greg Abbott, will be especially painful for Musk. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO spent roughly $224 million backing Republican candidates in Texas, according to The New York Times, including $158 million in September alone. SpaceX and Tesla's share price drops at market open mean Musk's companies have shed more than $100 billion in combined market value. Musk, who moved SpaceX's HQ from California in 2024 after criticizing the state's lawmakers, now faces the prospect of his two public companies once again being regulated by Democratic officials. Texas is the home of Tesla's Austin gigafactory, and the company's robotaxi service operates in multiple cities across the state. SpaceX, meanwhile, launches its Starship rocket from its Starbase facility in Boca Chica, near the Mexican border. Dan Ives, a Wedbush analyst who is bullish on SpaceX and Tesla, said in a Wednesday note that Musk "needs to find the path forward with Texas now with a Democratic win on both the Senate and Governor race." According to Counterpoint Research, Apple and Samsung were the only major smartphone chip vendors to gain market share in Q3 2026, as global shipments declined 21% year-over-year. Here are the details. At this point, most 9to5Mac readers are probably familiar with the challenges that smartphone vendors have been facing due to rising memory costs, and how Apple has managed to weather the impact better than many of its competitors. Over the past few months, many reports have noted that while most smartphone vendors raised prices more than once throughout the year, Apple held off on increasing iPhone prices until September, with the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro series. Those same reports have been showing the iPhone outperforming the broader market in smartphone, even as the industry experiences a sharp downturn. That said, Counterpoint Research recently published a report (via MacMagazine) examining how rising memory costs and slowing smartphone demand have affected the global smartphone chip market. According to the report, Apple remained in third place among smartphone chip vendors in the third quarter, with its market share increasing from 17% in Q3 2025 to 21%. MediaTek still led the global smartphone SoC market with a 28% share (down 6 percentage points year-over-year), followed by Qualcomm with 22% (down from 25%). After Apple, UNISOC ranked fourth with 13% (down from 14%), while Samsung remained in fifth with an 8% share, up from 6% in Q3 2025. Other manufacturers went from a 4% share to 8%. Overall, the market saw a 21% decline year-over-year, though the report didn’t disclose how many chips were shipped during the quarter. Commenting on the numbers, Counterpoint Research Senior Analyst Shivani Parashar said: “We saw three notable flagship chipset launches in September 2026, based on TSMC’s 2nm process node: Apple’s A20 series, MediaTek’s Dimensity 9600 Pro and Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 series. These launches are expected to boost premium smartphone SoC shipments in Q4 2026, although volumes are still likely to remain below Q4 2025 levels.” Looking ahead, Counterpoint expects global smartphone chip shipments to decline 20% year-over-year in 2026, followed by another 3% to 4% drop in 2027. The research firm also expects memory prices to continue rising next year. During its fiscal Q4 2026 earnings call, Apple described the current memory pricing situation as “unprecedented,” warning that further increases would continue to put pressure on its profit margins in the coming quarters. Publisher tinyBuild celebrates turnaround after very underwhelming demo numbers  Space station trading game Probably Stolen – Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim has been doing rather well on Steam, attracting over 162,000 concurrent players last night. I've been feeling the urge to fire it up again myself, after my brief launch-day trawl through its quagmire of black market economics and factional rivalries. The game's big numbers come as a shock given that it began life as another, non-cyberpunk kiosk job sim called Deepspace Emporium, which still has a Steam page as of writing. Deepspace Emporium seemed doomed to fizzle out in obscurity. But publisher tinyBuild got behind it regardless, working with developers Questing Goose to overhaul the art direction and lay on extra brainchips. The gamble paid off.   "Probably Stolen was initially a game under a different name with a released demo," summarises tinyBuild CEO Alex Nichiporchik on Twitter. "That demo peaked at 28 concurrent players. We loved the concept and gameplay, and worked with the dev to reinvent the visuals and focus on what works design wise. This is the result."   The original Deepspace Emporium seems very similar to Probably Stolen in broad strokes. The core of the game is haggling with strung-out ne'er-do-wells, buying or selling goods of varying quality and legality in order to surf a fluctuating market and pay the rent. It's Papers, Please, but you're searching for fake watermarks on cigarette packets, and wondering whether you dare stock contraband weaponry. You also have to appease or outmanouevre factions with competing interests, from station security to underworld barons.   From what I've played, Probably Stolen essentially takes all that and pumps up the Netrunner parallels with posher visuals. Not having played the now-unavailable Deepspace demo, I can't say how much intrigue it adds to all the shady transactions going on beneath the hood. I'm not blown away by Probably Stolen's pixelart – I find it quite flavourless, as depictions of cyberpunk space stations go – but it has pleasing texture. I am disproportionately fond of the rolled-up sleeping mat beneath my counter. Looks nicely padded! Still, the meat of this game is undoubtedly the vast collection of items you can get your greasy fingers on, with a choice of retail lines and vocational pathways such as gunsmith and chemist. You can sell rat corpses, tins of caviar, robotic hands, scavenged shotguns, and purple tubers of uncertain origin. I am Commander Silverhand, and this is my favourite store on the Citadel.   It's lovely to think of a developer transforming a probable write-off into a chart-topper by means of some canny plumping and reorganising. The situation is almost certainly more complicated than Nichiporchik makes it sound. Still, let's take the opportunity to reminisce moist-eyed about a few other games that underwent a dramatic visual transformation during development. The obvious one is Team Fortress 2, which once upon a time looked like a prototype Silent Hill environment with some khaki toy soldiers. Gearbox worked similar sorcery upon Borderlands, which once looked like a hungover Fallout 3. The prevailing wisdom is that piping in some colour and whimsy propelled these games to greatness, but who knows, perhaps if they'd clung to the old "football stadium toilet bowl" vibe, they'd have made an extra billion apiece. Any other precedents come to your mind?   Probably Stolen - Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim           PC               Rock Paper Shotgun is better when you sign in                 Sign in and join us on our journey to discover strange and compelling PC games.        © 2026 Rock Paper Shotgun, an IGN Entertainment, Inc. brand. 60 Whitechapel High Street, London, E1 7PE, United Kingdom. Voters delivered a stunning rebuke of Republicans and everything they stand for Tuesday night, taking control of both the House and the Senate in a wave of wins that just kept coming. Democrats kept winning, again and again, wave after wave. A bluekkake, if you will. And while that's great news for the stock market, the Middle East, healthcare, trans kids' safety, and so many other hugely important issues, voters also rejected Elon Musk and his billionaire meddling. We won't be able to get rid of him overnight, but at least Musk's dreams of a Tesla-SpaceX-Twitter-xAI merger are probably dead. If you remember, Musk has long been reported to want his companies all under one roof to complete Tesla's tranformation into an AI/robotics company (or stop making cars without crashing the stock price). xAI already merged with Twitter and stuck Musk's antisemitism-spewing, CSAM-generating chatbot in Teslas, then merged with Spacex ahead of its IPO. As previously reported, Musk had then ordered Tesla to look at spinning off its China business to help his main division merge with SpaceX more easily. Musk also floated the possibility with investors, and one of the Trump administration's lasting legacies will be its love of corporate mergers, so it sounded plausible.  With Democrats winning control of both the House and the Senate, likely finishing with 258 Representatives and 55 (or 56!) Senators, the left doesn't just have power, it has a mandate from the voters to put a stop to everything the Trump administration is doing. Raskin will chair the House Judiciary Committee, Garcia will chair the House Oversight Committee, and both have promised investigations into any criminal activity that's taken place. That's not exactly fertile ground for a major corporate merger, especially after Musk attempted to inflame a race riot in Ireland, campaigned for Germany's Nazi-adjacent AfD party, and blew hundreds of millions of dollars trying to elect Republicans.  Yes, our friends over at the Tesla Takedown kept a running thread going last night, highlighting every race Musk lost and how much money he wasted. Nearly two dozen races, all won by Dems, even though a Republican billionaire tried to buy their elections. Per Vanity Fair, Musk dumped an eye-watering $474 million into this election, and he still got kicked in the nards. He could have given $50,000 to 9,400 people and still wasted less of his money.  Democrats who haven't been bought off by the crypto and AI lobbies have been sounding the alarm in recent months about the dangers of any one person having as much power as Elon does. The man has the power to slow down Ukraine's military's internet, and the prospect of combining SpaceXAI with the most valuable car company in the world makes a lot of regulators nervous. Expect it to be a fight with the centrists in the party, but Dems are more likely to try to weaken Musk's power, not hand him a win. Because our election system is weird, Republicans won't lose power until January and could theoretically rush the merger through. But even the Motley Fool — a website that published "Prediction: SpaceX Stock Will Go Parabolic After Nov. 6" the day both Tesla and SpaceX shares plunged — doesn't think that's likely. In an article foolishly calling the merger "inevitable," the MFers timeline is still "within the next 12 months" not "before January." They also admit many factors, including antitrust enforcement could be a problem for the merger.  With Dems winning a huge mandate to govern, Republican politicians should be less willing to stick their necks out for that eternally sticky loser, too, so calling it "inevitable" is certainly a take. More importantly, Republicans have a much more important activity on their agenda than facilitating this merger. With Trump humiliated and unable to run for a third term anyway, Republicans are leaderless. When they move from depression to anger, they're going to start pointing fingers. Infighting and power struggles are inevitable unless Republicans just give up completely.  With Tucker Carlson and Marjorie Taylor-Greene-whatever waiting in the wings, the far-right giving up isn't likely either. So expect Republicans to be distracted, Democrats to feel emboldened, Jeffries and Schumer to remain spineless cowards, and Elon Musk to struggle getting any attempt at a Tesla-SpaceX merger off the ground. That's probably something Elon's sad about, but for the rest of us, it can only be good news any time Elon's dreams go up in smoke.

Tech > Services & Software > AI As part of the company's post-midterms marketing campaign, data centers could be called “AI compute campuses.” Writer Writer  				Edited by Laura Michelle Davis  November 3, 2026, 7:22 pm ET OpenAI is shifting its marketing strategy after the US midterm elections conclude this week, proposing to rebrand its data centers as “AI compute campuses.” The creator of ChatGPT is preparing a public relations campaign that could include regulatory lobbying and efforts to rehabilitate AI’s image, according to Axios. The push coincides with a potential blue wave in Congress. OpenAI Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane is reportedly trying to steer the AI policy debate and to send a message that “AI should be built by and for people,” as Axios reports. The effort is a response to an increasingly enraged electorate, as backlash to AI data center construction becomes a unifying issue across party lines. A July Gallup poll found that as many as 70% of US adults are opposed to local data center construction, including Democrats, Republicans and independents. More from CNET Supporters of AI data centers often argue that the construction and operation of these massive AI server farms bring job growth to local communities. But studies show that employment is limited, and in some cases temporary. Residents continue to rally against the environmental impacts of water contamination, the burning of fossil fuels and noise pollution.  Lehane told Axios that OpenAI views the conversation as healthy and that “communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects.” The company is trying to reframe AI adoption as a means to access economic opportunities.  OpenAI’s new PR campaign aligns with Silicon Valley’s effort to repackage the controversial technology so it can move full speed ahead with building more data centers, which the White House has touted as vital engines for the US economy. President Donald Trump’s recent move to rename AI as “super intelligence” was another bid to dress up the capabilities of frontier labs, which have been under increased financial scrutiny by investors. A representative from OpenAI didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. (Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.) OpenAI’s post-midterms marketing package includes implementing speed limits and mandatory safeguards for AI model development, largely echoing Anthropic’s “pacing” talking points. The company is also trying to shape the international standards that dictate the technology’s development. Up to now, a lack of regulatory oversight has left top AI labs largely unchecked, leading to incidents where frontier models slipped past flimsy safety guardrails and caused real-world disruptions across the web. OpenAI’s lobbying strategy for an alleged “human-centered” path based on “trust” fits squarely in the company’s data center rebrand — all calculated to help deflect public criticism. If the company publicly advocates slowing its own AI development, it can be more effective in what critics call “regulatory capture,” a tactic that gives large AI companies significant advantages.  In other words, if OpenAI helps write the rules meant to govern the industry, it can shape regulations to protect its market dominance. If frontier labs are considered the experts in constraining the industry, they can create a legal moat around themselves, making it more difficult for smaller competitors to enter the AI industry, while protecting their bottom lines from any real damage. The Trump administration has been a major boon to the “Magnificent Seven,” the group of major tech companies that heavily influence the S&P 500 and global financial markets. After cozying up to the White House during the past two years, the most influential figures in Silicon Valley have been rewarded with a lax regulatory environment and expensive federal contracts. Many of the biggest tech and AI companies donated millions of dollars to the president’s inaugural fund and, more recently, to his $330 million White House ballroom project. (Apple and Nvidia were among the top contributors, at $25 million each.) As it stands, Trump is working directly with AI companies to define security threats and respond on their own terms. If the political tide turns in DC, however, it would make sense for Big Tech to make contingency plans for operating in a potentially less favorable environment. Democratic politicians have generally eyed the AI gold rush with greater outward skepticism and scrutiny, with some members of Congress even backing a resolution opposing AI company bailouts in the event of a financial bubble popping. Lehane told Axios he believes AI will be the primary issue voters care about in the next presidential election cycle, and that the midterms are a “bit of a movie trailer for what you’re going to see in 2028.” If nothing else, OpenAI is angling to make new political alliances before that time comes.      		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. The Honda Africa Twin is one of the best adventure bikes on the market, but Honda isn't resting on its laurels with its biggest ADV just yet. For EICMA, the company revealed a new generation for the Africa Twin line, bumping the bike from CRF1100L to CRF1150L with tech, styling, and comfort updates to match. The biggest change, though, is a new third sibling in the AT line: Africa Twin and Africa Twin Adventure Sports, meet the Africa Twin Enduro Sports. The new engine is a 1,131 cc parallel twin, presumably with the same 270-degree crank offset that's so in vogue right now. Honda claims 117 horsepower and 88 pounds-feet of torque from the new mill, though those are global numbers. If they're from the European-spec bike, expect some differences for our U.S. emissions and noise regulations. That engine's bolted to a new frame, one that tucks the fuel tank beneath the seat to lower the center of gravity. It's a trick that worked on my old F800GS, and it'll likely make the new Africa Twin feel smaller than its as-yet-unannounced weight. The big news out of the Africa Twin line is the new variant, the Africa Twin Enduro Sports. Honda is pitching this as a bigger brother to the CRF450, to which the company says the ES has "front suspension ... specifications" that are "equivalent." It's anyone's guess as to what that actually means on two bikes with different frames, dimensions, and riding styles, but Honda is certainly making it clear that the Enduro Sports is meant to be the most focused off-road member of the Africa Twin family — at least, as focused as any adventure bike can get. It's always been a bit comical to see people lugging farkled-out GSes through BDRs that would better suit a DR650, but now it seems Honda has made an Africa Twin for people who want to rip through dunes. Is a 500-plus-pound ADV the way to do that? No. Maybe the bike is targeted at Pol Tarres specifically.  While the Enduro Sports is a whole new variant in the lineup, Honda hasn't forgotten the standard AT and the AS. Both get what Honda is very concisely calling "Showa Electronically Equipped Ride Adjustment electronically controlled suspension with Honda Skyhook control," which I will simply be calling "Skyhook" from here on out because, Jesus Christ. Honda claims its Skyhook will adapt damping in near real time to insulate the rider from the texture of the road surface, a touring comfort feature that points toward these two models being more road-oriented than prior Africa Twins — even if the base bike keeps its 21-inch front wheel.  That electronic suspension is paired with the usual bevy of electronic rider aids: Lean-sensitive ABS, traction control, and stability control, all of which can be changed for six different rider modes. Honda of course also offers its dual-clutch transmission, long a staple of the Africa Twin lineup, likely across all three variants.  As usual, the Adventure Sports model remains the most road-touring oriented, with a larger 6.34-fuel tank (Honda didn't say the capacity of the tank on the base and ES models) and a unique fairing design. It retains the 19-inch front wheel of the outgoing model, cross-spoked for tubeless compatibility, and Honda has now given the bike some Gold Wing-tier software: Honda Sensing Ride, a system available on DCT bikes that uses dual front and rear radar units to monitor the area around the bike. The front radar enables adaptive cruise control, but Honda went one step further and gave its adaptive cruise the ability to come to a complete stop in traffic and resume moving when the car ahead of you does — a system I'm not sure I want on a bike. The radar also enables forward and rear collision warnings, brake assist, and a group ride mode for staggered riding.  The new Africa Twin promises to be a meaningful upgrade on the old model, with more power and a lighter frame, but it seems a more road-oriented bike than the CRF1100L — save of course for the hilariously Dakar-themed Africa Twin Enduro Sports. Sign me up for that variant. I love dumb fun.

Author of the CMO Insider newsletter Podcasting's growth story is facing a CMO reality check. Cluttered, repetitive ad breaks and a lack of consistent measurement standards are factors giving some marketers pause about continuing to pour budgets into podcasts. That's according to a new report from the podcasting ad agency Oxford Road, which was shared exclusively with CMO Insider. More than half (57%) of the marketers Oxford Road polled said measurement gaps were holding back their podcasting investments. For brands with annual media budgets of $100 million or more, 90% said measurement was a top concern. "The exposure side, the attribution side — they're both a bit of a mess, frankly," said Oxford Road EVP Giles Martin, referring to how marketers assess podcast audiences and measure the success of their campaigns. The podcast market operates across multiple platforms, from RSS feeds to Spotify, Apple, and increasingly YouTube. Each has its own audience metric: downloads, streams, or views, which are calculated differently. Attribution is just as fragmented, with marketers relying on an imperfect mix of promo codes, pixels, geo-testing, and media mix modeling to gauge what worked. "It makes it harder for advertisers to buy, it makes it harder for sellers to sell, and it can make it harder for creators to get the money they deserve," Martin said. That could go some of the way toward explaining why 40% of marketers in the report said other channels deliver a better return on investment than podcast ads. Growth in the podcast advertising market appears to be slowing. While 40% of the marketers surveyed by Oxford Road anticipated increasing their podcast and audio budgets in 2027, this was down from the 59% of brands that said they increased those budgets this year. That tracks with other industry spending forecasts. EMARKETER expects US advertisers to spend $3.76 billion on podcasts next year, up 10.4% year over year, but a slowdown from the 16.8% annual growth it estimates for 2026. "There's a significant disconnect between audience attention and advertising investment," said Patrick Dolan, head of display and audio at the media agency The7Stars. The pitch to advertisers is that podcasts offer highly engaged audiences who are selecting the shows they want to listen to, often around specific topics that align well with brands' business objectives. Host-read ads can offer an added degree of connection. "A good host read sounds like advice from a friend," said Byron Tassoni-Resch, CEO of the performance marketing agency WeDiscover. Yet for some marketers, podcast ad breaks have evolved to become too messy. More than 40% of the marketers polled by Oxford Road cited the "advertising environment" as a reason they were putting off podcast investments. Marketers said they were concerned about growing ad loads, ad repetition, and other quality-control issues, such as inauthentic, "ho-hum" host-read ads, or even ads that cut off mid-sentence. Oxford Road's report was based on a July survey that polled 41 marketers, a group it said represents $400 million to $500 million of podcast ad spend, including three of the top 10 podcast spenders. Media buyers said marketers need to adopt a more sophisticated approach to extract greater value from their podcast investments. Martin of Oxford Road said brands should consider treating podcasts as a deeper, multi-format partnership, combining host reads with creator social posts, short-form video, newsletters, and, where useful, lower-cost pre-recorded podcast ads that build reach and brand recall. The7Stars' Dolan said that bolder approaches to podcast plans create a "true value exchange" between the podcast creator and the advertiser and foster a more authentic partnership. "These more long-term approaches stop the short-term, high-frequency 'standard' read that lacks the passion we seek from our podcast creators," Dolan said. Media buyers made a similar case for measurement, where combining different methods is the best approach. "Brands buy podcasts like TV, but they measure them like search," said WeDiscover's Tassoni-Resch. Relying on promo codes alone, for example, is an imperfect science because it only counts the people who remember them. A podcast ad might have helped drive a sale, but it often doesn't get credit for it. Tassoni-Resch recommends brand-lift studies to show how awareness changes after a brand is mentioned on a podcast. Marketers should also combine methods such as holdout tests and media mix modeling to demonstrate how podcasts are additive to search and social ad spending, he said. "When CMOs can see this value, they invest more to improve the message and scale the channel," Tassoni-Resch said. "Good measurement turns a one-off podcast test into a long-term partnership." The podcast industry is pushing for unified standards to address fragmented metrics across audio and video platforms. Last year, Oxford Road convened the Alliance for Measurement in Podcasting, a group of industry executives across podcast platforms and media owners, advertisers, agencies, publishers, and talent and measurement firms. Author of the CMO Insider newsletter It's shopping season in the advertising industry, and I'm not just talking about the holidays. After a somewhat sleepy period, the M&A market is stirring back to life, with strategic buyers loading up their carts. In the past couple of weeks alone, Publicis Groupe completed its $2.2 billion acquisition of the data company LiveRamp; Salesforce announced a $5.7 billion deal for the customer-engagement platform Braze; India-based Affle said it's buying fellow adtech firm Perion for $420 million; and advertising holding company Stagwell picked up Freestar, a platform that helps publishers sell their ad space. Jay MacDonald, CEO of the investment bank Digital Capital Advisors, has a simple rule for predicting where M&A could strike next: follow the ad dollars. He pointed to areas including influencer marketing, retail media, and connected TV. He added that geography-focused acquisitions could help companies gain a larger share of wallet. The AI boom is also causing strategic players to rethink ad businesses they may have once overlooked, said Ana Milicevic, cofounder of Sparrow Advisers. "Adtech has been innovating with real-time decisioning, identity, and all these component parts that in a much more automated world are very relevant," Milicevic said. CMO Insider polled nine ad industry bankers, investors, executives, and consultants about which strategic buyers they thought could splash out on more acquisitions in the coming months. Their answers ranged from Accenture to Zeta. We've listed the highlights in alphabetical order. The consulting firm said last month it plans to spend around $5 billion on acquisitions in its 2027 financial year. Ad industry pros expect its highly acquisitive marketing services division, Accenture Song, to remain an active buyer. Karsten Weide, principal at W Media Research, said Accenture's recent purchases of the creator and social agency Whalar and the data firm Sagacity demonstrate its appetite for marketing technology, customer intelligence, and creative capabilities. "Additional acquisitions could help Accenture Song assemble a more integrated marketing offering spanning data, AI, creative production, commerce, and campaign execution," Weide said. Fresh off its $1.9 billion acquisition of the search engine optimization platform Semrush this year, Adobe, soon to be helmed by new CEO Anil Chakravarthy, could be on the hunt for more companies to help strengthen its marketing and creative stack. Sanja Partalo, general partner of S4S Ventures, said Adobe's competitive environment is getting more challenging by the day, with creative AI companies like Higgsfield, Runway, and Canva vying for its Creative Cloud customers. (Both Adobe and S4S invested in Runway's Series E round this year.) "As brands need to produce more content for more channels, I'd expect Adobe to keep looking for tools that connect creation to campaign execution and measurement, as well," Partalo said. "I believe M&A is a tool they will continue to deploy to strengthen their offering." Holding company Havas completed eight acquisitions in the first nine months of 2026, and its CFO François Laroze said last month that additional deals could close before year-end or in early 2027. "Publicis' acquisition of LiveRamp increases the incentive to strengthen Havas' data, identity, retail media, and AI capabilities, although its established strategy favors smaller, targeted acquisitions," W Media Research's Weide said. Digital Capital Advisors' MacDonald said Havas could pursue targeted acquisitions in the $50 million to $200 million range, compared with Publicis' billion-dollar-plus deals. On ad giant Omnicom's third-quarter earnings call last month, CFO Phil Angelastro said the company is getting back into acquisition mode, having completed its $9 billion mega-merger with IPG and some disposals across its portfolio. Industry insiders predicted retail media acquisitions could be high on Omnicom's list of potential targets. That would bolster its Acxiom data and Flywheel commerce assets. Nick MacShane, senior managing director at the investment bank Progress Partners, described Omnicom as a company that needs "to answer other people's M&A," pointing to the Publicis-LiveRamp deal. Omnicom "still lacks the commerce stack Publicis built with Epsilon, CitrusAd, and Profitero," said Andreas Roell, CEO of the advisory firm Evros Group. OpenAI is scaling its ad business at lightning speed. The company said last month that more than 100,000 advertisers had run ChatGPT ad campaigns over the eight months since its ad platform's debut. It's also launched a slew of adtech integrations, including with Criteo, Kargo, Pacvue, and StackAdapt. Industry insiders said partnerships can sometimes signal that buyers are road-testing a company's capabilities ahead of a potential acquisition. OpenAI could move to purchase an ad-buying platform that has baked-in advertiser and agency relationships, Sparrow Advisers' Milicevic said. "The biggest value is the advertising know-how," she said. "Hiring a larger team that already functions well with each other and knows how to speak to buyers, and knows what transactions are valued, can really accelerate their go-to-market." M&A will largely depend on what happens with OpenAI's forthcoming initial public offering, said Joshua Wepman, a managing director within Houlihan Lokey's technology group. "Anything they're working on, they'll slow roll it with the S-1 process," Wepman said. The highly acquisitive French agency group shows no signs of slowing down after buying LiveRamp, and said earlier this year it expected to resume incremental bolt-on acquisitions once that deal was completed. Abeed Janmohamed, a partner at the advisory firm Volando Partners, said those could include companies it can use to build additional data capabilities, such as European assets that can complement Epsilon, its biggest acquisition to date at $4.4 billion. Partalo of S4S Ventures anticipates Publicis could want to make an "agentic orchestration" play. She describes agentic orchestration as using AI agents to connect data and measurement to decisions made across advertising campaigns, from planning and audience selection through activation, optimization, and reporting. "A capability like that could help Publicis move from giving teams better insights to helping them act on those insights across campaigns," Partalo said. Stagwell has made more than 60 acquisitions since it was founded in 2015, and hot on the heels of its Freestar deal, it's still hungry for more. CEO Mark Penn told Adweek in a recent interview that he's looking at acquisitions to help the company expand further into Latin America and to "bolster our digital transformation companies and growth." Consultancies and agencies are increasingly competing on technical services as marketers shift budgets from campaigns into data and AI, Evros Group's Roell said. "I would expect midsize data engineering firms and AI implementation shops with real enterprise clients to see the most competition from buyers," Roell said. The Trade Desk has long been a large-M&A holdout, but as the adtech company faces a significant revenue deceleration amid fierce competition from the likes of Amazon and Google, could that change? Though The Trade Desk's share price has dropped dramatically since its peak, the company said in September it had about $1.5 billion in cash on its balance sheet. Industry insiders said the company, which operates a demand-side platform (DSP), could benefit from adding retail media infrastructure, unique connected-TV inventory or monetization technology, or a solution that gives it a leg up in the agentic media-buying space. "Any of the businesses that are workflow-oriented are going to have to do something to evolve their businesses in the agentic world," Wepman of Houlihan Lokey said. Digital Capital Advisors' MacDonald said that, given The Trade Desk's long-standing culture of "build it at home," he believes that if the company decides to go down the M&A path, the acquisition will be big, not a tuck-in. Zeta Global's share price has soared about 70% over the past year, as its acquisition-heavy strategy to build an all-in-one marketing platform gains momentum. Last November, it made its biggest-ever acquisition, acquiring martech company Marigold's enterprise software business for up to $325 million to expand Zeta's customer base and help it corner the loyalty market. Janmohamed said Zeta has a track record of making strategic acquisitions of companies where others may not have seen value, then quickly distributing their capabilities across its client network through the Zeta Marketing Platform and its AI agent, Athena. He expects that run to continue. "Zeta is one to watch," Janmohamed said. Zeta CEO David Steinberg said the company takes a disciplined approach to acquisitions, and every opportunity must meet five strategic pillars: "Be accretive from day one, create cross-selling opportunities, add differentiated technology or data, integrate into our platform within 12 months, and bring talent that strengthens our team." Principal Writer Principal Writer  				Edited by Jon Reed  November 4, 2026, 4:00 pm ET In the introduction to the essay published on X by Nothing CEO Carl Pei on Wednesday, it almost sounds like he’s arguing against the premise of standalone AI devices. In Pei’s post, he suggests AI’s “iPhone moment” is still several years away. This could read as though Nothing is holding its horses rather than diving into the fray right now. But that isn’t the case; in fact, it’s quite the opposite. “Our first AI-native product ships next month,” Pei says. “It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product. It has no new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app.” More from CNET Pei is playing it characteristically coy. He’s dropping clues, and you can bet there will be more to come in the ensuing days and weeks up until the official launch of this mystery product. Standalone AI devices are a burgeoning industry, even if they’re yet to result in a hugely compelling, must-have consumer product. Whether it be pins, pendants, glasses, headphones or tabletop devices, tech companies are flooding the market with new native AI devices. Some companies, such as OpenAI, are working on ideas behind closed doors, whereas others, such as AI note-taking experts Plaud, are already establishing a strong and loyal customer base. British startup Nothing is predominantly known for its retro-inspired audio products and cool smartphones, around which the company is building a cult following as an alternative to more mainstream, generic phone companies. It’s more closely aligned with lifestyle and fashion brands than most of its tech brethren. In spite of this, it sounds like its first AI device will be more work than play. Just like computers, AI will need to prove itself in the realm of productivity — the workplace — before it spills over into being truly useful and appreciated in our personal lives, writes Pei. And so, Nothing is building a tool for the workplace, albeit one with the company’s customary design-forward approach. “We were taught that seriousness and beauty could not share a room,” says Pei. But he wants you to know that work tools can be beautiful, and he promises Nothing’s will be. This is all very mysterious — perhaps more so because the image accompanying Pei’s post actually looks like it could be a snapshot of one of many different smartphones from the past decade or more. The simple black rectangle with one rounded corner looks distinctly unlike a Nothing device, and something a less imaginative tech company might produce. We shouldn’t be fooled by this, though. Nothing has yet to bore us with a design, and it seems unlikely to start now — especially after Pei’s treatise on the subject. No doubt there will be more hints forthcoming, as Nothing gears up to persuade you that its products belong just as much in your office as at a warehouse rave in Berlin, and that its approach to AI is essential to your workflow above and beyond the offerings of its strait-laced competitors.    		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. TOPICS                      on-prem                           Firms still want kit on-premises, but spike in revenue is as much about increased costs as higher sales       On-premises high-performance compute (HPC) is still in demand, according to Hyperion Research, which estimates the market is expanding at almost 20 percent year-on-year, often driven by requirements for AI processing. What Hyperion calls the "on-premises HPC and AI-for-Science" server market showed significant growth in the first half of 2026, with revenues hitting $16.5 billion, up 19.9 percent. However, the analyst says unit shipments over the same period grew only 4.4 percent, meaning that systems are carrying a higher price tag due to greater use of costly components such as GPUs and other accelerators, not to mention the effects of higher memory costs, which have tripled or quadrupled since last year. Its tracking of the HPC market is based on multiple surveys conducted of both buyers and suppliers, the firm says. The latest data shows a major change in the overall HPC market growth, heavily driven by a combination of the use of AI, large language models (LLMs), and purchases of large GPU/accelerator-based systems. This trend was noted a couple of years ago, with Omdia reporting in 2024 that revenue growth from server sales was racing ahead of actual units shipped, as customers prioritized investment in highly configured server clusters for AI. Much of that spending was by hyperscalers and cloud providers, seeking to profit from selling AI services to enterprise customers, but Hyperion’s figures focus on on-prem shipments, showing that many enterprises prefer to do their processing in-house. According to Hyperion, Dell has now surpassed HPE as the biggest HPC vendor, with server revenues of $4.2 billion for the first half of 2026. HPE, which picked up supercomputing specialist Cray for $1.3 billion in 2019, had long been pack leader in the global HPC arena in terms of market share and revenue. The figures put Dell on a 24 percent share, while HPE is not far behind on 21 percent. Lenovo and China-based Sugon trail behind at 4 percent share each, while 45 percent of the market is just labelled as "others" by Hyperion. This includes names such as Bull, which re-emerged from the shadows of Atos this year, plus Supermicro, Penguin Computing, and NEC.  The HPC infrastructure market is inherently cyclical. HPE recognized significant revenue in 2025 with sales of multiple exascale-class leadership machines, but procurement of that scale is intermittent and doesn't necessarily come along every year, Hyperion notes.  "Organizations and institutions are continuing to invest in their advanced computing infrastructure due to both replacing aging machines and the desire to adopt AI into their workflows to support their businesses and missions," said Hyperion Research CEO Earl Joseph.  "The growth reflects both a nominal increase in units being purchased and significant increases in system prices." When Raphael Lim, 23, and Jamison Teng, 24, met in 2022, their time together was filled with Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu training and playing video games. But now, their hangouts look different as they work through the twists and turns of running a year-old legal technology startup. Lim and Teng are the cofounders of Jam & Raph, a startup that provides AI consultancy services to law firms. Juggling the demands of the startup alongside their law and computer science degrees at two of Singapore's top colleges hasn't been easy, often putting their studies on the back seat. Lim, a second-year computer science student at the National University of Singapore, and Teng, a final-year law student at the Singapore Management University, competed in a collegiate legal tech hackathon in 2024 and placed second. This gave them the idea to start a business in the legal tech space. "I saw that there was a lot of money being invested in the big firms like Harvey and Legora, so that's when I realized there was actually a market for this," Teng said. Harvey, one of the most prominent legal AI startups, has conducted several funding rounds over the past year and announced a valuation of $15.5 billion in September. Legora announced a $550 million Series D round in March, at a $5.55 billion valuation. Lim and Teng launched the company in November — finals season for both of them — with 2,500 Singapore dollars, or about $1,950, from SMU's entrepreneurship incubation program. They brought on 10 team members, all college students, and kickstarted Jam & Raph. Their product: Running workshops for law firms to teach lawyers how to use AI tools effectively and token-efficiently. They also started offering consultations to the firms, helping them build AI products tailored to their needs. Their workshops, which are two to three hours long, cost SG$2,000 to SG$3,000, and they charge SG$120 per hour for consultations. They poured a little of their savings into the venture — less than $2,000 combined — but operating expenses are low, mainly their $150 monthly Claude subscriptions and email domain fees. They say they've stuck all their revenue in their company bank account for now, not paying themselves anything. Despite studying in Singapore, a country that is infamous for its rigorous and competitive academic culture, both Teng and Lim said that working on the business always takes precedence over their studies. "My GPA took a total hit, but I think that's just the cost of doing a startup when you are in university, so that is to be expected," Lim said. Teng said he's seen his grades improve in classes that blend tech and law. His core law classes have taken a hit, but that hasn't phased him. "I think Singapore still places a lot of emphasis on academics, but the more we talk to people and clients outside Singapore, like Americans or Europeans, they care more about your story," he said. But problems always seem to arise at the most inconvenient times, they said, like clients calling them about product failures during their final weeks, when they have to study for multiple exams. It's also taken a toll on their social lives. "We've had clients sending emails saying, 'Hey, your product is down,' while we're having drinks with friends, and we have to immediately deal with it," Lim said. Lim said that he's missed out on a large part of the freshman college experience. "Everyone was out partying and joining clubs, meeting new people, and I would be cooped up in my room, coding," he said. He added that his ex-partner got angry at him when he didn't answer the phone all day while he was solving a technical issue for their product, and then had to complete schoolwork. The duo doesn't meet to practice Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu or play video games anymore, either, and their hangouts are all about work. For Teng, it was an opportunity to test out entrepreneurship in a safe space before entering the workforce. "It's okay to fail because if you fail as a student startup founder, I think it's pretty expected; there's no real heat that you can get in terms of responsibilities," he said, adding that people are a lot warmer toward student entrepreneurs. Lim said running a business is a good window to the world outside the classroom. "My peers will be doing a lot of academics, research theory, but I get to see how these theories actually apply in the real world," he said. Neither of them sees this as a replacement for a postgrad job hunt, though, with both saying that they want to get corporate work experience. "It was more of a 'good to have,' something we built for the love of the game to bring something to the world," Lim said. Jump to

An issue Democratic and Republican voters can agree on: the rent — and the price of everything else — is too damn high. A "blunami" of Democratic wins swept the US as Americans cast their votes in the midterm elections, with affordability top of mind. Gas prices are high, inflation is exacerbated by the war in Iran, and cost-of-living concerns persist. And those wallet weights helped decide control of the House and Senate, with Democrats flipping key seats and gaining projected majorities in both chambers. "House Democrats are committed to fighting for an affordable America," Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who will likely become Speaker of the House in January, said in a Tuesday night speech. "We will fight hard to lower the high cost of housing and groceries and gas." NBC's early exit poll results highlighted voters' affordability concerns. Two percent of all voters thought the economy was in "excellent" condition; 59% of voters said they were "very concerned" about the cost of gas, and 88% said they were "very or somewhat concerned" about the cost of groceries. Those results are tentative and will be updated as vote tallies continue rolling in. Additionally, 89% of voters said the cost of living was a "crucial or major" factor when selecting a candidate. And when voters in those preliminary exit polls were asked to choose which issue was the most important facing the country, the largest share answered the economy. Economic worries were brewing ahead of the election: Half of voters said that the economy was "extremely important" to their vote this year, according to a pre-election Gallup poll of registered voters conducted October 1-19; 37% said it was "very important."  Jon Ossoff, who won his Senate reelection on Tuesday night, emphasized the economic challenges Americans face. He said in his victory speech that families are "working harder and harder while the treadmill just gets faster and steeper and the bills get higher and higher." He added that "for too many, homeownership's a fantasy" and that "health care has never cost more." James Talarico, the Democratic Senator-elect in Texas, said that his win was "for every teacher and every nurse, for every farmer and every rancher, for every young person who's trying to buy a home, for every parent who's trying to put food on the table." President Donald Trump himself ran heavily on prices and economic anxiety in the 2024 election. In speeches in the months leading up to the election, Trump targeted the "Biden inflation nightmare" and promised grocery prices would come down. In a September presidential debate with Kamala Harris, Trump said, "People can't go out and buy cereal or bacon or eggs or anything else. The people of our country are absolutely dying with what they've done. They've destroyed the economy." He echoed these comments a month later at an Atlanta campaign rally, arguing that "Starting on day one, I will quickly defeat inflation, and we're going to bring down the energy prices fast, fast." Candidates across the aisle took on voters' affordability concerns on the campaign trail. Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate candidate in Texas, had an economics-focused message before the election: "I believe every Texan should be able to buy a home, raise a family, and live a healthy life without struggling to make ends meet." Across swing state races, candidates have spoken about how gas, energy, electricity, and housing costs have weighed on their constituents. In Maine, both Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic opponent Troy Jackson have spoken about the impact of tariffs on costs for local products. That messaging makes sense: Heading into the midterms, inflation and affordability were top of mind across the aisle. Among voters surveyed by Harvard CAPS/Harris Poll before the election on October 24 through 26, 38% — the highest share among different issues — said that price increases, inflation, and affordability were the most important issues facing the country; 40% of likely midterm voters said it was the most important. Similarly, voters across all parties — and those who were likely to vote in the midterms — said inflation and affordability were personally important to them. Did high costs sway or impact your vote? Share your story with these reporters at jkaplan@businessinsider.com and asheffey@businessinsider.com. While Trump called the affordability crisis a "hoax" last year, he has since touted himself as the "affordability president" and said he is bringing prices down for Americans. But with the next inflation reading looming, and a relatively frozen labor market, high prices and jobs feel increasingly important to Americans — and the election might just show how important they are.
