It's free. seths.blog/subscribe  There’s an overlooked power tool right in front of us. Every individual and organization can use it well, but rarely does. I could write a book on this, but here’s the post instead: Synchronized work happens together, on a shared schedule, in real time. Asynchronized work (my spellchecker says this isn’t a real word) happens on our schedule. Phone calls are sync. Texts are async. Network TV was sync. Youtube and Netflix are async. Writing a screenplay is async. Making a movie from that screenplay is sync. Going to opening night is sync, watching it two months later online is async. Writing a book is async. Publishing a book is sync. Reading it is async. A staff meeting is sync. A memo is async. Commercial air travel is sync. A private jet is async. Each offers costs and advantages. When I go to a live concert, it’s happening. For me, for the audience, for the act. If any of us is having a bad day, it detracts from the experience. But when it’s right and it’s real, magic ensues. It’s largely unrelated from the experience of listening to the same song streamed (async) or on the radio (a blend of the two). I imagine that your energy levels and mood fluctuate during the day. When working on async projects, the smart path is to match your internal energy with the work to be done. Write blog posts when you’re on a post-swim high, pay bills when all you can manage is clerical work. Organizations that don’t account for the cost of sync-meetings waste not just billions of dollars but the insight and energy of the people who might be able to contribute if the timing and approach were different. Sync has three advantages: But it has costs and risks: The implications are everywhere we look, and the status quo works to maintain its sync or async status. Media companies that are in love with whatever sync/async built their organization often flounder when the media consumption axis flips. The only reason Amazon and Netflix exist is that their sync predecessors couldn’t figure out how to deal with an async relationship with the customer. And now that Netflix has a huge advantage, they’re timid about shifting some of the content to a sync model that would create more buzz… and Amazon has failed to capture the real-time shopping experience that’s so common online in China. When we were forced to work from home six years ago, offices freaked out. Some embraced the async magic it offered, while many bosses were at a loss on how to manage people they couldn’t see in real time. One reason is that employees had been indoctrinated in the idea that work was what you did when someone was watching. If you were ‘working’ from home, it was okay to also do errands and a workout, because without a hall monitor, you were off the clock. On the other hand, some used the freedom the way a productive writer does. Without the distractions of real-time sync, there was plenty of time to get some actual work done. Once you see it, all sorts of new insights come to mind: The handoffs. Much of the leverage and the friction in our modern world lives at the points where work switches modes. A deadline, for example, is a sync point imposed on async work. Who owns the clock? Sync is more than a scheduling choice, it’s also a display of power. The person who calls the meeting has already decided to spend everyone else’s time. Bosses call meetings; the employee sends a memo. Async moves power from the coordinator to the creator. Flips are opportunities. Why are college applications async, while job interviews are sync? Kickstarter turned product launches async, and Ted Turner turned news into something that broke. Fake async. Over time, async creeps toward sync. It’s ironic that Slack messages, texts and email which succeeded because they were async, now create an expectation of real-time response. These are async tools used with sync expectations, so you get the interruptions of sync without its energy. Name it. Protect your work style and the expectations for what you deliver. Organizations can be more mindful of the cost of sync, and creators can properly price their effort for each kind of work. There’s a reason it costs a million dollars to have Bob Dylan sing at your birthday party. Sync creates cultural side effects. When everyone at the watercooler is talking about the same thing, cultural cohesion follows. When Netflix moved to binge viewing, they used their capital advantage to make it very hard for others to keep up by producing enough shows. But by sticking with this moat, they’ve diminished word of mouth. Far more people talked about Nathan Fielder’s movie during launch week than ever talked about his streaming show. AI is currently async. An agent never needs a meeting and works at 3 a.m., so humans become the sync bottleneck. But as its power increases, expect AI to be a partner in most sync events. Trust is built in sync and spent in async. Async works better between people who already know each other. New teams, new hires, and new customer relationships may need sync at first. The alternative is to build systems that are async by nature, enabling new participants to earn trust in powerful new ways. Wireless			  One cornerstone of Elon Musk’s fraud-packed SpaceX IPO prospectus includes the claim that they’ll extremely quickly (as in a year or two) boost Starlink subscriber totals from 13 million to something closer to 300 million. Given the network’s congestion problems and physics constraints, that’s simply not realistic. Also: more users means even greater capacity problems and weird network restrictions. To try and goose growth, Starlink has recently been making it clear they’d like to try and get into the cellular and smartphone business. But the actual plan is, as with all things Musk, a misleading, hot mess. A key part of Starlink’s plan includes plunking down thousands of meshed femtocells installed on customer rooftops alongside existing LEO satellite dishes, something one telecom analyst recently stated was “one of the top three dumbest ideas in my four decades of being in this industry.”  In part because the femtocell installations are just logistically annoying and complicated, and will further will eat up capacity on the increasingly congested network (recall that Starlink customers in some areas already face “congestion fees” as high as $1500). To goose growth Starlink and SpaceX have been gobbling up valuable wireless spectrum (with the help of Trump FCC boss Brendan Carr). They are also apparently in conversations to buy Echostar’s Boost Mobile prepaid brand: “SpaceX has held talks with telecom firm EchoStar in recent months about launching its own signature wireless service through a deal with the company, the report said, citing ​people familiar with the negotiations. The move would support the Elon Musk-led ​company’s plans to build a hybrid satellite-terrestrial mobile network through Starlink ⁠Mobile, combining its satellite constellation with ground-based infrastructure to challenge US wireless ​giants AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile.” One problem? Boost mobile is just a mobile virtual network operator (MVNO). It’s primarily just customer-facing retail artifice that runs on the back of existing AT&T and T-Mobile networks; neither of which is keen to have their cozy regional telecom dominance disrupted. To actually compete, Musk and Starlink would still need to invest hundreds of billions of additional dollars in a high-powered 5G network over the next decade. And even then there’s no guarantee of success. You might recall that Boost Mobile was offloaded to Echostar as part of that doomed first-term Trump administration effort to approve the Sprint-T-Mobile merger, then hide its labor and competition impact by pretending that Dish Network would build a successful replacement 5G network. That of course never happened; the real impact was mass layoffs, higher prices and worse service for everybody.  I should note that the Trump FCC under Brendan Carr not only launched a fake “investigation” into Dish to try and force it to offload much of its spectrum to AT&T and Musk, but recent reporting suggests the Trump administration threatened Charlie Ergen with additional scrutiny if he didn’t ramp up his donations to Trump’s ballroom. So there’s entire layers of grift going on here.  Regardless: U.S. telecom is just generally a shitty market to try and disrupt. It’s extremely expensive and time consuming, and at every turn you’re likely to get creatively ratfucked by giants like AT&T and Verizon, whose political influence over Republicans historically rivals Musk’s. Again, even traditionally staid and bullish telecom trade mags have expressed concerns that Starlink’s smartphone push is doomed.  I think this mostly all exists as a way for Starlink to hoard valuable spectrum and goose stock valuations. There may be some people at Starlink who have convinced themselves this will actually work (the fact SpaceX has been lobbying for phone unlocking rules suggests some potential earnestness), but U.S. telecom history is littered with these sorts of half-assed disruption efforts that routinely go nowhere.  I’m not prone to believe things that come out of the mouths of Verizon executives, but in this case I think Verizon CEO Dan Schulman is correct when he states it would cost SpaceX something akin to $300-$500 billion and five years build a network capable of really competing with cellular giants.  And that’s just network infrastructure; you still need to convince users to sign up, provide a quality experience, and provide useful customer support (something Musk companies historically aren’t interested in). While fending off the political machinations of AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile, who all but own the legislature in most states after a generation of lobbying and campaign contribution.  The Musk cult and our shitty corporate press will spend the next few years enamored with the fiction that “Musk is disrupting smartphones,” but this mostly just reads as further stock-fluffing performance by a man with more money than sense. News › iPhone Apple released its first foldable iPhone a few weeks ago, dipping into an entirely new market. Apple has the potential to get about 30% of the foldable smartphone market globally next year as the share of shipments for the company rose from 24.8% this year to next year up at 29.8%. Samsung is anticipated to be keeping first place but forecasts tell their share could drop to 31.9% down from 35.1%. Huawei would be ranked third after its share has dropped to 21.3% from 24.8%. Shipments for the iPhone Duo are expected to be about 5 million units, while the overall shipments for other smartphones from manufacturers will grow by 0.5%. Trendforce states that the device and early feedback for it have been a mixed bag, where some individuals are dealing with issues such as a cracked inner display, certain apps displaying black borders, and they can’t use full-screen and with high cost estimates for repairs have gotten attention for costs in ownership. Some praise the device and its features like experience for viewing and the functionality of the split-screen for the iPhone Duo. The integration of chips, the ecosystem for developers, and Apple’s operating system is identified as a large advantage for the company against rivals in making the foldable experience even better for users. Reliability and compatibility for foldable devices are said to improve, and Trendforce is predicting that Apple with their iPhone Duo is expected to help with the competition in the market for the foldable smartphone to be more efficient with multitasking for foldable devices. The iPhone Duo is the first foldable iPhone offered by Apple, powered by the A20 chip and a dual-battery system. It features a 12MP Center Stage Front Camera, a 48MP Fusion Main, a Fusion Ultra Wide Camera, and Apple Intelligence and Siri AI.  iLounge is an independent resource for all things iPod, iPhone, iPad, and beyond. iPod, iPhone, iPad, iTunes, Apple TV, and the Apple logo are trademarks of Apple Inc. Four wheels have long been the standard for sports cars, but MTPEAK is exploring a different territory with its first vehicle, the One-All. Making its global debut at EICMA 2026 in Milan, the unconventional open-top machine combines a classic roadster-inspired design with a three-wheel configuration, a mid-mounted turbocharged engine and rear-wheel drive. The vehicle’s layout features two wheels at the front and a single driven wheel at the rear, placing it somewhere between a conventional sports car and a performance trike. The One-All takes visual inspiration from traditional sports cars, with a low-slung profile, sculpted bodywork and an exposed cockpit that puts the driver at the centre of the experience. Carbon-fiber body panels give the exterior a lightweight construction, while the overall silhouette recalls an earlier era of motoring, when compact proportions and mechanical character played a significant role in sports car design. Rather than adopting the increasingly technology-heavy appearance of modern performance vehicles, MTPEAK has opted for a more mechanical and driver-focused aesthetic. Designer: MTPEAK       At the core is a mid-mounted 2.0-litre turbocharged engine paired with a nine-speed automatic transmission featuring reverse gear. The powertrain sends power to the rear wheels and produces 165 kW (approximately 221 hp) and 385 Nm of torque. MTPEAK quotes a power-to-weight ratio of 370 hp per tonne, with a claimed top speed of 180 km/h. These figures put the emphasis on power delivery and a relatively lightweight construction rather than outright speed records. The mechanical package is supported by a chromoly steel tubular semi-cage chassis, designed to provide a rigid structural foundation. Carbon-fiber panels form the bodywork, while ventilated carbon-ceramic disc brakes are fitted across all three wheels. The manufacturer also specifies a 50:50 weight distribution, double-wishbone front suspension with twin dampers and electronic stability control (ESP). The front wheels use 205/45 R17 tyres, while the single rear wheel gets a wider 305/35 R18 tyre to handle the engine’s output.  Despite the compact proportions, One-All has a clearly defined roadster footprint. It measures 3,397 mm long, 1,496 mm wide and 1,148 mm high, with a wheelbase of 2,540 mm. The combination of a low body, wide rear tyre and exposed cockpit gives it a distinctive stance without relying on the conventional four-wheel sports car layout. MTPEAK also describes the front dual-wheel arrangement as race-tuned, with an emphasis on dynamic stability and handling. The vehicle is the first offering from MTPEAK, a new brand backed by Guangyu Industrial, a Chinese manufacturing company with around 30 years of precision engineering experience. Its capabilities include CNC machining, metal stamping, welding, and carbon-fiber fabrication. The company says research and development, vehicle calibration, assembly, and core manufacturing are integrated in-house, with the One-All developed to automotive-grade standards.       MTPEAK is positioning the vehicle as a limited-production offering, something more than a conventional mass-market sports car. Its official website announces a global limited launch of 100 units, with bespoke customisation intended to make each example individually specified. Production is scheduled to begin in 2027, although pricing and detailed market availability have not yet been announced. Watch CBS News  Updated on:  November 4, 2026 / 5:18 PM EST             / CBS News            The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared nearly 1,600 points, or 3%, on Wednesday, its biggest gain of the year, as investors digested the impact of the Democrats' sweeping victories in the midterm congressional elections. Other indexes also jumped, with the broader S&P 500 climbing 120 points, or 1.6%, to close at 7,689 and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index gaining 1.4%. "Investors are happy to have the midterms out of the way," market analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, told investors in a report. "This was a major source of uncertainty, and putting it in the rear-view mirror removes a key obstacle heading into a very favorable time of year seasonally." The shifting political winds could affect a range of issues that influence investment returns, from the pace of the data center buildout and cryptocurrency industry regulation to proposals to cap credit card interest rates.  At the same time, Wall Street analysts do not expect the outcome to derail a stock market being driven more by robust corporate profits and solid economic growth than by politics.  "The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation," Stephen Brown of Capital Economics said in a note to investors.  Stocks of solar power companies, dollar stores and hospital owners helped lead the way as Wall Street tried to sort the winners from losers following the widespread losses for Republicans.  Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Mr. Trump's social media company, the artificial intelligence sector and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans. Trump Media & Technology's stock price fell nearly 25% on Wednesday, while shares of Musk-owned SpaceX and Tesla sank 3.8% and 3.3%, respectively.  Investors also expect the election results to heighten gridlock in Congress, with Democratic lawmakers now in control of both the House and Senate, and Mr. Trump threatening to wield his veto power to block any legislation he opposes. Political gridlock has historically been good for markets because it limits Congress' ability to pass sweeping tax and spending legislation, reducing the risk of volatility, according to Wall Street analysts.  Meanwhile, stocks have generally performed well following midterm elections. The S&P 500 stock index rose an average of 15.5% in the six months after the last 14 midterm races, dating back to 1970, according to figures from investment firm Edward Jones. "Economic growth, inflation, interest rates and corporate earnings have historically mattered more to broad investment performance than the party composition of Congress, especially if the president and congressional leadership come from different parties," analysts with the Wells Fargo Investment Institute said in a report. "We do not expect sweeping policy changes," they added. "More likely, in our view, is a split-government alignment on affordability, energy policy and opportunities from artificial intelligence." Beyond the Beltway, the midterm electoral results could affect key issues for investors, such as the pace of data center construction, with enormous spending on artificial intelligence helping drive stocks to record highs this year while also raising concerns about a bubble in tech stocks.  "In divided government, the policy implications at the federal level may be limited, but data center policy decisions sit at the state and utility-commission level, making gubernatorial and utility races important alongside Congress, particularly Governor Abbott's loss in Texas," Jeff Buchbinder of LPL Research told investors.  "LPL Research continues to expect the buildout to occur, but strong performances by Democrats in key data center states (and pushback from the 'not in my backyard' folks) may slow it down some, potentially increasing regulatory pressure on AI infrastructure stocks including semiconductors, machinery and power generation," he added. These days, delivery platforms have to offer more than just delivery services to brands and retailers. DoorDash’s announced plans to acquire Instacart for $17 billion point to the constant need to gain market share by diversifying services and offerings. Over the years, both DoorDash and Instacart have invested heavily in new services like AI assistants, advertising programs and in-store B-to-B solutions. DoorDash, in particular, has been on an expansion streak, acquiring U.K.-based competitor Deliveroo and restaurant reservations platform SevenRooms in 2025. Last year, DoorDash also acquired search ad startup Symbiosys for $175 million to deepen its advertising capabilities. With the high cost of last-mile delivery, companies like DoorDash and Instacart have expanded well beyond delivering groceries and takeout. Leah Sallen, U.S. head of CPG and retail strategy at programmatic ad tech platform MiQ, said the growing services and tools DoorDash has come to provide have made it more than just a marketplace for delivery. “Between delivery, grocery shopping, restaurant reservations and advertising, DoorDash is gaining access to more consumer touchpoints and insights into when, where and how people shop,” she said. Over the past few years, DoorDash has aggressively built out its non-restaurant marketplace, partnering with major grocery, convenience and retail brands like Ulta, Skims and Macy’s. The company also introduced logistics features to solve pain points, like Dasher Returns. On the technology side, DoorDash has rolled out AI-powered tools, such as Ask DoorDash for shopping recommendations, DashBuddy for courier support and DashOS for restaurant customer management. These solutions are meant to create an all-in-one ecosystem for B-to-B infrastructure and logistics streamlining. Now, the Instacart consolidation will bring DoorDash grocery retailers that the platform currently does not offer its customers, notably Walmart and Sam’s Club. But with that market share also comes challenges in maintaining retail relationships by offering more than just delivery solutions.   Neil Saunders, managing director of GlobalData, said DoorDash’s latest hefty acquisition will require further streamlining to make sense as a long-term investment. Saunders said Instacart’s operations still largely rely on workers manually picking groceries. He said this is not only labor-intensive, but it’s also harder to scale efficiently as digital grocery orders continue to grow. “Either way, DoorDash should aim to position itself as a technology and infrastructure partner rather than simply a delivery provider,” Saunders said. Some experts believe DoorDash’s proactive strategy is to simply keep up with Amazon’s delivery offerings. However, retail media networks have also become an important revenue source for delivery platforms in recent years. At its surface, the DoorDash-Instacart deal is about two massive last-mile companies consolidating. But for advertisers, it could mean a broader disruption in retail loyalty, said Sallen, as the two platforms’ merger brings together deep data on restaurant, grocery and retail shopping. “We have already seen this play out with TikTok Shop, which fundamentally changed consumer shopping behavior by using sophisticated algorithms to deliver highly personalized product recommendations,” Sallen said. A similar shift can happen with this acquisition, Sallen said, thanks to the combination of DoorDash’s immediate-consumption insights and Instacart’s long-standing grocery data.   Sallen explained that, similar to how Amazon became a starting point for shopping, consumers may increasingly turn to platforms like DoorDash to find the best product, price or delivery option before deciding which retailer to purchase from. In turn, she said, “That shift from selecting the retailer first to selecting the retailer last could prompt CPG brands to reconsider how they allocate their retail media dollars.” Matt Gilbert, CEO of marketing platform Partnerize, agreed that the significance of a DoorDash and Instacart combination goes well beyond delivery.  “It’s about the growing concentration of consumer discovery, advertising, purchasing decisions and transaction data within a single commerce ecosystem,” Gilbert said. For consumers, that could mean greater convenience and fewer steps between discovering a product and buying it. “For advertisers, it creates an opportunity to connect marketing investment more directly to purchasing behavior across more categories and occasions.”  On the other hand, Gilbert said that when platforms increasingly control the consumer experience, the transaction and the reporting of advertising performance, advertisers need assurance that they’re measuring genuine incremental influence — “and not simply taking credit for purchases that would have happened anyway,” said Gilbert. Sallen added that, as platforms like DoorDash add capabilities and AI increasingly influences shopping decisions, “The consumer path to purchase is becoming more diluted and harder for advertisers to follow.”   That shift could become even more pronounced as AI agents increasingly help consumers weigh price, proximity and product availability before deciding what and where to buy. Sallen said this could mean delivery behemoths like DoorDash could have an advantage in shaping AI-driven recommendations to millions of consumers. “The more intelligence it [DoorDash] can bring together, the more personalized it can make the shopping experience,” Sallen said. “DoorDash’s growing portfolio of services could position it as a one-stop shop for retailers, with data becoming one of its biggest advantages,” Sallen added. Publishers are pushing back against Meta’s AI scraping terms, testing their leverage over a platform they still rely on. Political and news creators are relied on now more than ever, but what platforms are working for them? Which ones aren’t? People Inc. is moving toward custom APIs for AI systems, Forbes has adopted Markdown for agents, while the FT, Daily Mail are considering how agents could reach content for subscribers. TOPICS                      security                           Attackers reportedly set cold-room controls to 110°C, but safeguards prevented stock losses      Attackers tampered with cold-storage settings used by France's civilian blood service after compromising a refrigeration supplier, the organization said. The French Blood Establishment (EFS) confirmed the incident on Tuesday, saying its own systems had not been directly targeted. Safeguards prevented any loss of blood products. The affected equipment stored blood samples and frozen plasma, including plasma intended for transfusion. "The EFS' monitoring and alarm systems enabled the rapid identification of these anomalies and the implementation of necessary measures to ensure that no blood samples or products were compromised," it said. "Thus, depending on the circumstances, as soon as the incident occurred, the affected equipment was either brought under control without impacting the products and samples, or neutralized; the products stored in these cold rooms were preventively transferred to other facilities." The EFS did not name the supplier publicly.  According to reports, attackers changed cold-room temperature settings from -30°C to 110°C. That does not mean the equipment or its contents reached the higher temperature. The organization added that it notified the country's cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, and the Ministry of Health. News about cyberattacks targeting refrigeration devices across Europe emerged on Monday morning after retailers arrived to work, only to find puddles on the floor after cyber criminals activated defrost modes. Reports of the supermarket attacks describe remotely activated defrost cycles and temperatures as high as 50°C, forcing retailers to discard spoiled food. The attackers have not been identified. More retailers have reported disruption since the initial disclosures on Monday. Stores across Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden were the first to report issues, although cases from Estonia, Finland, Germany, Portugal, Romania, and the Netherlands have since been confirmed. Richard Horne, chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), told BBC Radio 4's Today program on Wednesday that he was aware of "a couple of impacts" in the UK's own food supply chain. No affected UK businesses have publicly identified themselves, although the British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC that some of its more than 300 members had become "collateral" in the attacks, with two reporting that their fridges had begun defrosting. The latest wave of cold-store attacks comes a month after the first, which affected French supermarket chains Carrefour, Coopérative U, Intermarché, Monoprix, and others. Both supermarket waves involved remote interference with refrigeration controls, causing stock losses. Whether the attack affecting EFS used the same access route remains unclear. Some affected chains identified Danfoss controllers in their systems; others said they did not use the company's equipment. CERT-FR published an advisory at the time of the attacks urging organizations to remediate vulnerabilities in Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers. War has left Sudanese workers jobless and consumers facing higher prices as factories struggle to reopen. Save Share Khartoum, Sudan – Mansour Gaily’s factory in Khartoum produced sweets for local consumers and provided employment for workers. But when fighting erupted between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in April 2023, production ground to a halt, like thousands of other businesses across the country. More than three years later, Gaily faces the challenge of bringing his business back to life. Production may have resumed, but the factory is only operating at 40 percent of its previous capacity. “Our losses are estimated at $1m,” Gaily told Al Jazeera. “We lost some machinery, spare parts, and needed to rebuild large parts of the factory.” Gaily’s troubles are typical of Sudan’s devastated manufacturing sector. Before the war, Khartoum was one of the country’s main industrial centres, home to factories producing food, textiles and other consumer goods. However, Khartoum became a major battleground between the SAF and the RSF during the war, and although there have only been sporadic attacks since the army fully recaptured it last year, the industrial sector has not been rebuilt. According to Sudan’s Ministry of Industry, approximately 1,800 industrial facilities have been damaged during the war, including 650 factories that were completely destroyed. The figures illustrate the scale of the challenge facing a sector that is essential to employment, domestic production and economic recovery. Abdulelah Mohamed owns a factory for plastic products and recycling in Khartoum. He describes the situation as catastrophic. “Damaging, destroying and looting the factories was systematic. We lost everything,” Mohamed said. “The industrial sector needs new planning and a new vision so Sudan can produce things again.” The damage extends beyond buildings and machinery. Raw materials, finished goods and equipment have been destroyed or looted, while electricity shortages, damaged transport networks and rising import costs have made reopening difficult even for businesses whose premises survived the fighting. Sara Elfatih Khalil, chief executive of Al Teital Advance Industries, is among the manufacturers confronting these challenges. Her company’s factory in Khartoum produced sesame oil and, before the war, provided employment for 300 workers. Its warehouses have been looted during the fighting, and with damaged buildings and a supply chain that remains broken, the factory continues to be shut down. “I believe industry will remain a cornerstone of any economic recovery and that it is capable of recovering rapidly if the basic conditions are met,” Khalil said. “Restoring our confidence as investors requires security and political stability, clear and consistent economic policies, legal protection for investment and property rights, and reliable financing and infrastructure,” Khalil said. “Our situation is not unique. Less than 10 percent of factories in the sector are currently operational, and those that remain open are operating intermittently, with costs that threaten their continued viability.” For Gaily, restoring production at his sweets factory requires a steady supply of ingredients, including sesame and sugar, as well as packaging, spare parts, electricity and workers. Disruption to any of these can bring production to a halt. “We are operating at 40 percent of our production capacity because the damage was severe and capital is limited,” he said. “Despite the lost spare parts and the lack of labourers, we chose to continue because we don’t have any other options.” Other manufacturers face similar obstacles. Some now must import materials that were previously available locally, increasing costs and making production vulnerable to further disruptions in transport and supply. The problems also extend to financing. Businesses that have lost machinery, stock and income during the war often lack the capital needed to replace equipment and pay for stock and employees before sales resume. The consequences have extended to workers who depend on factories for their livelihoods. Mohamed Haj is a worker who lost his job at a different sweets factory in Khartoum North and has struggled to find alternative employment. “I lost my job at the beginning of the war, and the factory owner is unable to restore it,” Haj said. “Reviving the industrial sector in general could provide jobs for thousands of workers who have been left without work.” At the other end of the supply chain, shopkeepers are struggling with the reduced availability of locally manufactured goods. Abdelgadir Mohamed, who sells sweets and other consumer products in Bahri Central Market, said the disappearance of many Sudanese-made products has made it harder for traders to source stock. “In some cases the imported products are cheaper for us and for the consumers,” the shopkeeper said, “but many of my customers prefer the Sudanese-made ones.” Imports have partly filled the gap, but for shopkeepers this can mean higher purchasing costs and uncertain supplies, and for consumers already facing a decline in purchasing power, that adds pressure on household budgets. “The prices are changing every day,” said Ahmed Mahmoud, a local consumer. “The local products’ prices are high and imported ones are also high, but for sweets like tahniya [a local sesame-based sweet], I prefer the Sudanese-made one.” Sudanese authorities are now seeking to fix some of the damage. In August, a Ministry of Industry committee was established to assess the condition of industrial facilities in Khartoum State and prepare incentives to encourage factory owners to reopen. The recovery plan also includes restoring essential services in industrial areas, including electricity, water, roads, sewage and waste management. The services are critical for manufacturers hoping to resume operations, but factory owners say reconstruction would require more than just restoring infrastructure. Many factory owners need capital, and representatives of the Sudanese Chamber of Commerce say businesses need real, practical assistance, rather than just promises from authorities.      Economist Mohamed Elnayer believes reconstruction offers an opportunity to address longstanding weaknesses in Sudan’s industrial economy. “Rebuilding the industrial sector will require a broader strategy that addresses the structural weaknesses that existed even before the war,” Elnayer said. Before the war, Khartoum was the industrial heart of Sudan, with the country’s factories largely concentrated inside it. That caused an inequality in opportunities between Khartoum and the rest of the country before the war, but a different problem arose during the conflict, when the capital became a major front line. Many factories were destroyed and looted as a result, and analysts like Elnayer believe that the industrial sector should be rebuilt across Sudan. This would serve the dual purpose of avoiding any future paralysis of the industrial sector if fighting were to break out in the capital again, and also spread economic benefits around the country. “Sudan needs to consider, before reconstruction, whether to simply restore the industrial sector that existed before the conflict, or provide an opportunity to develop a more competitive and productive economy in other Sudanese states,” he added. For Gaily, those broader economy questions are inseparable from the practical challenge of keeping his factory running. He hopes to repair the machinery, secure the ingredients needed to manufacture sweets and bring his former employees back. “We need stronger support from the authorities by facilitating production, rehabilitating infrastructure and adopting stronger policies to encourage factory owners,” Gaily said. “Above all, the industrial sector needs financial support and coordinated efforts by stakeholders to sustain economic recovery.”               Follow Al Jazeera English:

Foxconn is seeking to increase its share of artificial intelligence server manufacturing as demand for computing infrastructure continues expanding worldwide. The Taiwanese electronics manufacturer believes it could supply half of the market within the next couple of years. It currently controls about 40% of the AI server market, and its expansion plans include increasing manufacturing capacity, developing American operations and investing further across the artificial intelligence supply chain. The company expects its market share to reach approximately 45% next year before potentially climbing to 50%. Chairman Young Liu disclosed the projection during an interview with CNBC's Christine Tan, stating, “I think we can grow up to 50 percent." Artificial intelligence infrastructure is also expected to become an increasingly important source of revenue for the manufacturer. Foxconn anticipates that servers, racks and related infrastructure will contribute between 60% and 65% of revenue within three to five years. That projection excludes edge AI devices, which process artificial intelligence workloads directly on local hardware. Current orders mainly come from artificial intelligence developers and cloud computing providers, while government agencies and conventional businesses have yet to adopt the technology extensively. Manufacturing capacity is already fully booked for at least the next 18 months, indicating substantial demand for additional computing equipment. Foxconn also intends to increase its American manufacturing operations by taking on additional activities further upstream in the supply chain. A simultaneous reduction in spending across the artificial intelligence industry would create greater difficulties for manufacturers throughout the supply chain. Last week, news broke that hackers had stolen $6.3 billion from wallets on Binance, the most popular cryptocurrency exchange in the world. The company was able to freeze about nearly $3 billion of it, but the attack quickly made headlines, and rightfully so, as the largest financial heist in human history. At the time, I suspected, along with security researcher Christopher Lopez and plenty of others, that this could have very well started on a Mac. As Lopez pointed out, the $1.5 billion Bybit heist last year also began on a developer’s Mac. On top of that, Macs are hugely popular among DevOps engineers and crypto folks, and they’ve been on the receiving end of a steady stream of malware and social engineering campaigns over the past few years.  I can now say any suspicions that this heist originated on Mac were right. I’m still in a state of shock. Dazed not by the amount stolen, but how the said hackers did so using the same ol’ social engineering tricks they’ve been using for years. No sophisticated multi-milllion dollar underground zero-day here. Yesterday, Binance published a more detailed breakdown of the attack. The company never actually says “Mac,” but the malware it published targeted /opt/homebrew, which is where Homebrew lives on Apple silicon Macs. In other words, this was almost certainly an M-series MacBook. The attack basically transpired in two steps. According to Binance, in June this year, a DevOps engineer working on Wallet searched for an AI coding tool and downloaded a malicious clone of the Homebrew installer in Google Search. Binance claims it caught it early and stopped any damage. However, what it didn’t know was that it allowed the attackers to learn which employees worked on its wallets. This was phase 1. Fast forward a few months to September, a different engineer who, you guessed it, worked on wallets for Binance, was lured into a fake job interview. As these sort of social engineering attacks normally go, they told to run a coding “assignment” on their work computer. This was not caught by Binance security, and on October 29, the world learned that hackers (now widely speculated as North Korean hackers) walked off with billions. Of course, most of what we know so far comes directly from Binance, so if you’re looking for more details on exactly how this happened, you’ll likely be left empty-handed. It’s important to note here though, none of these two attack vectors are new. Back in early 2025, I wrote about fake Homebrew ads at the top of Google Search pushing Atomic Stealer to Mac users. Binance only says the engineer found his installer through “a search engine.” Of course, I can’t confirm it was a sponsored ad, but if history tells us anything… This is a rather uncomfortable situation for Apple to be in. The largest financial heist in history happen on Mac last week, though to be fair, there’s no security feature that can stop a developer from running a script he wants to run. Sure, the Terminal paste warnings introduced in macOS 26.4 could have helped here. But realistically, if someone’s convinced they’re doing a coding test for a job they really want, a warning pop-up probably isn’t going to stop them. Here’s what that warning looks like: I’m having Christopher Lopez (@L0Psec) a professional macOS reverse engineer back on the Security Bite Podcast this week to talk about the Binance situation with me. Tech > Computing > Laptops Two popular non-Apple brands still won awards for their affordability. Senior Consumer Insights Editor Senior Consumer Insights Editor  				Edited by Joshua Goldman  November 4, 2026, 8:00 am ET Of all of the laptop brands to choose from, CNET readers say Apple’s signature MacBooks really live up to the hype.  We recently surveyed CNET readers as part of our People’s Picks awards to find out what they think about their laptop and the brand behind it to help you make a more sound choice on the laptop you may be considering over the holidays. We listed several well-known names, including Dell, Lenovo — and Apple. We asked about everything that matters most on a daily basis, like battery life, durability and even its performance for handling tasks like gaming and graphics. Out of 10 categories, Apple swept up eight of the awards and claimed the overall winner for CNET’s People’s Picks award.  Here’s what readers say Apple gets right when it comes to its laptops, what the experts think about Apple’s landslide win and other brands worth considering. More from CNET Apple wins the overall award in CNET’s People’s Picks, and also takes home the overall satisfaction rating, with 74.2% of Apple users saying they’re extremely satisfied with their laptop. In comparison, 22.5% say they’re satisfied — bringing Apple to a near-perfect overall satisfaction score of 96.7%.  Apple’s overall impression also speaks to other awards it wins from CNET readers, including high ratings for its impressive battery life, display quality and high-quality build. All of those categories and more sum up Apple’s brand loyalty nod, with 68% of MacBook owners saying they would buy the same laptop and model from Apple again. How much are people paying for MacBooks? CNET found that 43.5% of Apple users paid at least $1,500. Until earlier in 2026, the MacBook Air was Apple’s entry-level laptop, priced at least $1,299. The introduction of the budget-friendly MacBook Neo brought that down to a more reasonable $699. However, despite Apple’s laptops being more expensive than those from other brands, they still ranked high for their value proposition. Part of the reason for that is that MacBooks received high marks for hardware reliability. “Apple’s MacBooks might cost more than the average laptop, but their premium build quality means they’re built for the long haul,” said Matt Elliott, CNET’s laptop editor. If you plan to have your laptop for a while, you may be impressed by other features that make work easier and faster, like its M-series central processing unit for task management and AI capabilities, great battery life and a one-of-a-kind operating system — currently MacOS 27. All of the features and specifications bundled together make Apple’s perception as a high-end laptop worth the investment for long-term satisfaction. Apple clinches a near-perfect score for its value perception. According to our survey results, 44% of Apple users said their MacBook has exceptional value. Others say their MacBook is worth what they paid for it (50.9%) — for a total positive score of 94.6%.  Digging deeper into Apple’s cost-to-value rating, 81.8% of Apple owners paid at least $1,000 for their laptops, which may seem costly, but Apple users seem OK with the price. That could be because, even though Apple has only three laptop models in a handful of sizes in its lineup, each one delivers solid performance and storage.  Take Apple’s proprietary processing chips, for example — each upgrade since the M1 release has improved the laptop’s speed, battery life and performance. Now the M6 can handle the MacBook’s AI capabilities, storage and high-resolution graphics. And for all of that power, most MacBooks are relatively thin and lightweight, making them easier for mobility — just a few of the reasons Apple users may be OK with paying more for what they’re getting. Battery life is a big deal for many laptop buyers, and that’s another area where Apple delivers. Over a quarter of those surveyed (25.7%) said their MacBook’s battery life exceeds 10 hours — which is more than enough for a full day of work in most cases. And 18.7% say their MacBook’s battery lasts between 8 and 10 hours — totaling 44.4% of MacBook users saying their battery lasts 8 hours or more.  Comparatively, non-Apple laptop brands fall short in this category. Only 16.4% of Lenovo users say their laptop’s battery lasts at least 8 hours, and even fewer for Dell (12.7%) and HP (11.8%). If you’re leaning toward a MacBook for its battery life, CNET’s lab test shows that the MacBook Neo lasts 13 hours and 26 minutes for online streaming, whereas the Apple MacBook Air 13-inch M5 (2026 model) lasts 17 hours and 2 minutes. Apple sweeps the brightness, color accuracy and clarity category with 99.2% of its users either satisfied or extremely satisfied with their laptop’s screen performance. No Apple users reported dissatisfaction.  “Apple has long been a favorite for creative professionals and content creators for good reason: Its MacBook displays are some of the best you’ll find on any laptop,” said Josh Goldman, CNET’s managing editor for computers. “While Apple may use marketing names like Retina and Liquid Retina to describe display features, they do translate into sharp and clear text and images, with excellent brightness, contrast, color gamut coverage and color accuracy.” The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR even goes beyond what MacBook users have come to expect. It’s Apple’s first OLED touchscreen laptop and features next-level brightness, color and contrast.  Apple receives high ratings: 80% of MacBook owners say it has premium build quality, 18.2% say it’s solid, and those results don’t surprise us.  And MacBooks seem durable and reliable, with 87% of Apple users reporting no hardware failures on their MacBooks, while 8% say minor software fixes resolved their issues. Only 3% needed minor hardware repairs, and 2.2% needed major repairs — which could be fixes such as a battery or screen replacement.  Our editors say the M5 MacBook Air is thin and lightweight, but still has a well-built aluminum design. And the M5 Pro MacBook Pro is sturdy, too. What sets Apple’s laptop hardware apart could be its aluminum chassis — the casing that holds all of the components together.  “Apple makes three lines of MacBooks — the Neo, Air and Pro — and focuses on making those the best they can possibly be. They are all built to deliver a premium experience using high-quality materials, and that even includes the entry-level MacBook Neo,” said Goldman.  Lastly, Apple uses durable materials, such as the 100% recycled aluminum alloy it says encloses the 14-inch MacBook Pro. And the tech giant has several testing facilities to test MacBook durability. When it comes to getting your daily tasks done, most CNET readers with MacBooks (70.9%) say Apple’s laptops handle workloads flawlessly. It’s worth noting that 45% use their MacBook for work tasks, but no Apple users reported poor performance.  Here’s why that might be: Apple’s laptops are packed with top-notch performance specs and features, like their powerful processors, unified memory and fast storage. Better processor performance means enhanced graphics, on-device AI capabilities and faster task speeds, all of which add up to being able to finish work, play games or stream videos without issues or lags caused by your laptop’s hardware.  On the software side, MacOS 27 Golden Gate gives you built-in AI features, like Siri AI and Visual Intelligence. And you can organize your Safari tabs by topic and use the Notify Me tool to be notified of website changes, like price drops or breaking news. Plus, you can create shortcuts to automate tasks. Coupling all of these features and specifications explains why Apple users rate MacBooks so highly for getting the job done. Apple leads the way on brand retention with 68% of Apple users planning to buy the same MacBook model again, while 29.1% would buy another model from Apple’s lineup. Only 3% would switch to another brand that’s not Apple.  Usually, when you buy one Apple product, you’re likely to stick to the brand’s ecosystem, especially since Apple has its own operating systems to access its unique features and work seamlessly with other Apple products with Apple’s Continuity feature. For example, you can start an email on your iPhone, but finish typing it on your MacBook. Or you can call or send a text from your laptop without reaching for your iPhone. Other features work across Apple devices, including iCloud, Universal Clipboard and AirDrop. Asus wins as a midtier laptop choice with 67% of Asus owners paying between $500 and $1,499. There’s a sweet spot in this range with 38% spending between $500 and $999, and 28% paying between $1,000 and $1,499.  If you’re planning to spend that amount on a new laptop, you may also be pleased to know that Asus earns a higher satisfaction rating compared with other non-Apple laptop brands — 48% of Asus users say they’re extremely satisfied.  Asus laptops have a few features and specifications that may speak to that rating, regardless of budget. For example, the Zenbook A14 has a thin, lightweight design that’s rigid, with long battery life and an OLED display with strong contrast and color performance. This Copilot Plus PC sells for $1,600 (but retailers like Best Buy regularly have it on sale for less). Comparatively, these premium features from other brands could cost more or sacrifice important must-have features for the price.  Asus has other laptops worth exploring depending on your needs, like the budget-friendly Asus ZenBook S 14 or the premium Asus ROG Zephyrus G14 that could be good for gamers and creators. Over one-third of Acer laptop owners (38%) paid less than $500 for their laptop — which is greater than other laptop brands in this price range. Yet, 44% of Acer users say their laptop has exceptional value, while 50% say the value is fair — bringing a total positive cost-to-value score of over 94%. Acer also has an overall satisfaction score of 92.6% — the highest of non-Apple laptop brands.  If you’re impressed by Acer’s value and satisfaction scores, there are a few budget-friendly Acer options to consider. The Acer Aspire 16 AI wins CNET’s Editors’ Choice award. It has a big 16-inch screen but is still lightweight (3.5 pounds). And it has good battery life (over 21 hours on CNET’s battery drain test). There are a few other pluses, like the 1440p web camera that may be good for video conferencing and a sizable touchpad. All of those features and more add up to $700, which could make it a good computer for work or casual browsing. If you’re looking to spend slightly less, its predecessor, the Aspire 14 AI, is originally $639, but you may be able to score deals on both models during holiday sales. Even though Apple is highly recommended by CNET readers, there are plenty of other laptop models and brands worth considering depending on your needs. Here are a few non-Apple laptop brands that are runner-ups to CNET’s People’s Picks winners that you shouldn’t count out of your laptop search.  Lenovo is best known for packing a powerful laptop into a compact design with tablet functionality, like its Yoga line, and its durable ThinkPad business models. But CNET readers with Lenovo laptops say the brand’s battery life stands out most compared with other non-MacBook laptops.  Survey findings show that 16% of Lenovo owners say their laptops can run for 8 hours or more. And 10.5% say their laptop battery lasts between 8 and 10 hours, while 6% say their Lenovo laptops can withstand at least 10 hours before needing a charge. That’s more than what readers say about other non-Apple brands. The Yoga 9i 2-in-1 Aura Edition lasts 25 hours and 45 minutes — making it one of the best laptop batteries CNET experts have tested.  Goldman said Lenovo has such a large and varied PC selection using the latest chips from Intel, AMD, Qualcomm and Nvidia that there is something for everyone and every budget. Even those who spend less on a Lenovo laptop can expect solid performance, including battery life. For instance, the Lenovo Legion 5i Gen 10 has an open M.2 slot for a second storage drive and an OLED screen for crisp, colorful images — making it perfect for gaming. And its new designs don’t sacrifice the must-have needs like long battery life, durability and chip efficiency that lend to strong performance. Asus wins over nearly half of its laptop owners, with 47.5% giving it an exceptional value rating  — exceeding expectations for its price. Take our Editors’ Choice pick, the Asus Zenbook A14. It’s super thin and lightweight, but it’s still sturdy thanks to its Ceralumnium body. Plus, it has supreme 24-hour battery life, 1TB of storage and an OLED display — all for $1,200. While that’s more expensive than some laptops, it’s what’s included in that price that makes it worthwhile compared with other non-Apple laptop brands.  Asus is the top non-Apple laptop option to consider for tasks, with 47.7% of CNET readers giving it high ratings. That’s followed by 40.4% of Asus laptop owners who say it has very good task performance. When it comes to tasks, 37% primarily use their Asus laptops for work, while 5% use theirs for gaming.  Asus is well known for having lightweight laptops with all-day-and-night battery life and stunning display quality. Asus laptops like the Asus ROG Zephyrus G16 have a good port selection, which could be good for gaming, work or simply connecting different devices without the need for additional adapters. And the Asus Zenbook S 14 has a strong neural processing unit that contributes to its high-speed AI performance.  Asus scores highest for its screen brightness and clarity, with over half (51%) extremely satisfied with its screen quality and brightness, while 38.6% say they’re satisfied, giving Asus an overall satisfaction rate of 90%. One common thread we noticed in Asus laptops is their OLED screens, which deliver high-resolution video and graphics. Asus laptops also combine stunning display quality with excellent performance and at surprisingly low prices for all of their features.  For example, the Asus Zenbook 14 isn’t the highest-quality OLED we’ve seen, but it still produces clear text and graphics on a 14-inch screen, along with exceptional black levels, Elliott said. That’s still better than LCDs that many other non-MacBooks have, and could be the reason Asus owners rate it so highly in this category.  Dell wins our readers over as a top choice for high-end laptops. One-third (33.3%) of Dell owners spent over $1,500, and of that percentage, 15.2% spent over $2,000.  Dell’s premium laptops largely cater to business and gaming with their standout features and performance. The Alienware 16X Aurora is Dell’s midrange gaming laptop with user-replaceable RAM, a bright display and strong performance for $2,280. And if you’re looking for a non-Mac alternative that comes close to MacBook quality and performance, the higher-end Dell XPS 14 is the one to choose. It seems fair to say that semiconductor technology has been one of the most influential inventions in human history. Practically overnight it turned human technology from being large, cumbersome and power-hungry into an increasingly sleeker, more power-efficient and much more capable form. It has become practically impossible at this point to imagine modern society without semiconductor technology. That said, we didn’t always use today’s silicon-based semiconductor technology, and although silicon-based semiconductors are exceedingly versatile and adaptable, they do have their limitations. The past years we have seen for example gallium-nitride semiconductors make big inroads in power switching technology, and more exotic forms like diamond-based semiconductors keep making their tantalizing appearances. In this article we’ll take a look at how we ended up at silicon as the default for semiconductor technology, as well as why we may want to consider moving to other materials.  Although semiconductor technology works on very different principles than vacuum tubes and relay-based electromechanical systems, ultimately the goal is the same. This being to make electrons go to certain place when and where you want them to go there. In the case of semiconductors this is achieved through n-type and p-type materials, which are areas in the semiconductor material which display different electron mobility behavior. The base material is – as the name suggests – a material that falls in between a conductor and an isolator. This conductivity can further be altered by embedding other elements into its crystal matrix, which is generally called ‘doping’. This creates an extrinsic semiconductor, as opposed to the pure, undoped intrinsic semiconductor. This doping process create two distinct types of semiconductor, being the aforementioned n- and p-types. These letters refer to whether they hold a negative or positive charge, effectively whether this semiconductor material is an acceptor (p-type) or a donor (n-type) of electrons. It’s not required to dope the base material to create both n- and p-type areas, which led to many variations just within the metal-oxide-semiconductor (MOS) family, including the n-type MOSFET-based NMOS, p-type MOSFET-based PMOS and the complementary CMOS that uses both types. CMOS became the dominant technology by the 1980s to create field-effect transistors (FETs), although the ‘MOS’ part isn’t necessarily technically correct any more as the original aluminium layer can be replaced with polysilicon. Of course, semiconductor technology didn’t start right off the bat with today’s silicon, dopants and construction methods. The first functional transistor and diode designs are good examples here of where the revolution began, and how things evolved from there. Although the invention of the point-contact transistor in 1947 is pretty well-known at this point, semiconductor diodes came onto the scene first. The first crucial discovery here was made by German physicist Karl Ferdinand Braun in 1874, when he discovered the asymmetric conduction of electricity in a range of materials involving a metal-semiconductor junction between a metal and types of minerals. The discovery of this type of junction laid the groundwork first for a practical point-contact diode by the 1930s, using semiconductors ranging from selenium and silicon carbide to germanium and silicon. These were found to be much superior to the thermionic diodes that were first put into commercial use. Especially the push to develop radar and radio technologies during World War 2 drove the development of better semiconductor diodes. With increased understanding of doping the intrinsic semiconductor material to affect its behavior, it was thus only a matter of time before the point-contact transistor was developed. From there both practical experimentation and a deeper understanding of the underlying electron mobility principles drove innovation forward. The primary reason why silicon is the most-used semiconductor material today has less to do with it being a good base material and more with it being both plentiful, cheap and easy to process. The silicon dioxide (SiO2) that forms the pure silicon crystals is the main constituent of sand where it’s called quartz. It will readily melt and can be drawn into very large crystals that can subsequently be cut up into the silicon wafer on which semiconductor circuits can be etched. Silicon’s band gap is however rather small at 1.14 eV, which means that the correct functioning of circuits created with this semiconductor will cease much sooner with higher temperatures including those generated by the device itself. So-called wide-bandgap semiconductors have a bandgap of >2 eV, which includes the gallium-nitride (GaN) semiconductor which the past years has become a frequent sighting in compact power electronics where being able to run hotter without issues and higher efficiency is considered a big selling point. GaN’s bandgap is 3.4 eV, which puts it pretty high up in the bandgap rating. In addition to a higher bandgap number, its thermal conductivity is also pretty good at about 230 W·m−1·K−1. These advantages makes it economically feasible to produce GaN components despite the material being harder to process. Which is also the crux of why diamond semiconductors haven’t yet cornered the market. Before moving on, an interesting note is that germanium has one advantage over silicon despite having an even smaller bandgap. This being that it doesn’t have to be as extremely pure as silicon to work well, which was a benefit especially during the early days of semiconductor technology. Although diamond isn’t necessarily the ultimate semiconductor material, its properties makes it look very good indeed. With a bandgap of about 5.6 eV and a thermal conductivity of 900–2,320 W·m−1·K−1 it pretty much destroys both silicon and GaN. The only problem we are facing here is that diamond is an absolute pain in the backside to create large wafers from, not to mention dope the crystal lattice without using the easy ion implantation used for silicon wafers. Creating diamond wafers requires growing them from seed crystals, rather than just drawing a massive crystal from a vat of molten goo as in the case of silicon. This alone is highly problematic for any large-scale commercialization. The issue of doping and similar typical semiconductor circuit things being rather hard with diamond is not unique to silicon semiconductor alternatives, which is one reason why the MESFET  field-effect transistor was developed. This drops the insulating oxide layer under the gate, instead using a metal-semiconductor (Schottky) junction. Such a MESFET design allows for other exotic semiconductor materials like gallium arsenide and silicon carbide, the latter being rather comparable to GaN in terms of bandgap and thermal conductivity, while allowing for very high switching speeds. Despite the occasional bouts of doom-and-gloom stories about the semiconductor industry and issues with scaling and cooling, semiconductor materials like diamond show that there’s still a lot of potential to look forward to. Diamond-based semiconductors could potentially outperform all currently used commercial semiconductor materials, while rapidly moving any waste heat away to whatever cooling solution exists. Even before said Diamond Age commences, the rise of silicon alternatives like GaN are already showing that despite many decades of breakneck innovation we are hardly at the pinnacle of what is possible. Although making predictions about the future is a fool’s errand at the best of times, it’s good to remain optimistic about such potentially world-changing events like the death of silicon semiconductors in favor of something much better. The big advantage of silicon for integrated circuits is that the oxide is an insulator and is relatively easy to form in place. High thermal conductivity is nice, but when heat removal is a problem it’s more important that the heatsink have high thermal conductivity than that the device have high thermal conductivity. It’s better to call the opposite of a conductor an insulator than an isolator. Even in electronics, isolator has multiple meanings. Happy Wednesday! It's November 4, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift — your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around. In this morning's edition we're looking at last night's election and its fallout on the auto industry, as well as its effects on Elon Musk's companies. We'll also look at U.S. buyers dialing back their automotive luxury spending, and Honda looking at European production.  If you'd like a recap of the latest auto news sent to your inbox each weekday, you can sign up for Jalopnik's free Morning Shift newsletter here. Midterm elections were last night, and voters overwhelmingly went blue. Not just in battlegrounds like Ohio and Michigan, but in reach states like Texas. Votes are still being tallied, but Mississippi and Alaska may well go blue too. Kansas has its first Democratic senator in nearly a century! Voters have soundly rejected Trump and the Republicans, which could spell some real complications for the party and the automakers that allied with it. From NBC: President Donald Trump told voters to pretend he was on the ballot in this year's midterm elections. They did. And they resoundingly rejected both his policies and his Republican Party. Democrats have captured full control of Congress, NBC News projects, with voters delivering a forceful repudiation of Trump's agenda, coupled with a clear-cut message that Congress has not done enough to provide checks on his administration and needs to do more to address affordability and corruption. The Trump administration of the last couple years has spent its time rolling back emissions regulations, destroying EV incentives, and generally cordoning off the U.S. automotive market as a little piece of history — somewhere automakers need not innovate to compete. With the legislative branch going blue, though, we may well see new environmental regulations. What will that mean for automakers that cozied up to the MAGA camp? Will we start to match European regulations and resume our EV push? Only time will tell, but all those automakers that returned to V8s may well regret their investments.  Elon Musk was the single largest donor in the 2026 election cycle, having spent nearly half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates across the country. Not only were his efforts for naught, but his adoptive home state of Texas has gone entirely blue — governor, senate, attorney general, even the railroad commissioner. He's likely to see some complications in his business plans, and the markets are recognizing that. From the Wall Street Journal: Shares in Elon Musk-led SpaceX and Tesla fell sharply premarket after Democratic candidates swept the midterm elections, handing a defeat to Republicans backed by Musk to the tune of hundreds of millions of dollars. ... Democratic control of Congress could derail a potential merger between SpaceX and Tesla, XTB's Kathleen Brooks said. "While Congress cannot stop a merger between SpaceX and Tesla, they could slow it down via extra scrutiny," Brooks said. "There is now a political risk premium attached to both Tesla and SpaceX that could weigh on their share prices." Shares have trended upward since market open, but they're still down from yesterday's close. Nathan Johnson, former composer for "Dragon Ball Z" and incoming attorney general of the state of Texas, has already promised to investigate Musk and his companies for corruption. With pressure on both the federal and state levels, 2027 could be a rough year for the world's richest man.  U.S. consumers are getting ever broker, and when you've got less money to spend you're unlikely to go RV or boat shopping. Yet, while automotive toy sales are down, Harley-Davidson is still up. In fact, the company is doing better than it has in years. From the Wall Street Journal: His purchase helps explain why Harley is bucking a downturn in sales of leisure products: High interest rates, punishing gas prices and broad economic anxiety have dented sales of everything from RVs to boats. But that downturn hasn't come for Harley. In its primary market of North America, the bike maker has recorded year-over-year retail-sales growth in each of the last four quarters, and is on track for the first full-year increase since 2021. Globally, sales are up 4% so far this year. The WSJ credits some of this increase to Harley revamping its Tri-Glide line, giving the trikes more power and comfort. Moving those trikes is good for Harley's bottom line, but it's not addressing the fundamental problem of the company: It carved out a market in the '60s, '70s, and '80s, and has largely sold to those same people ever since — buyers too old to keep a million-pound Harley upright. If the company wants new buyers, bikes like its new Sprint are the way it'll get them.  Europe is looking to bring automotive production home to the continent, tariffing car imports to encourage automakers to build in local factories. Plenty of Chinese automakers have already bought in, but one company is still wary to dip its feet into EU production: Honda, which is still just thinking about what it'll do. From Automotive News: Honda's European chief said the automaker may rebuild a manufacturing presence in the region, depending on the final outcome of new rules in the European Union that will favor locally made cars. The company has "certainly no intention of leaving Europe," Hans de Jaeger, president of Honda's European unit, said Nov. 4 in an interview at the EICMA motorcycle show in Milan. ... Honda registrations across Europe were almost 59,000 in the first nine months of 2026. That's too few to justify building a factory, De Jaeger said, though higher volumes could eventually change the calculation. It's an unenviable position: Honda doesn't sell enough cars in Europe to justify building new factories there, but it sells enough that it likely doesn't want to leave the bloc entirely. It could share space in a factory owned by another automaker, or eat the tariff costs, but none of those options are perfect. I'm certainly glad I'm not in charge of making that call.    This is how we'll look back on Washington's passage last night of a bill mandating genital inspections for participants in girls' sports. Just, what the hell?  Will we see prices crater after last night's election? Rise based on deadlock within the government, with no veto-proof majorities in the House or Senate? Stay the same?  Libbing out is permitted through today. After that, the work resumes.

By Jill Goldsmith  Co-Business Editor  AMC Entertainment swung to the black for the three months ended in September on higher revenue, noting market share gains in both domestic and international markets, with CEO Adam Aron saying the chain’s second consecutive record quarter means the company has “recovered” from its post-Covid struggles.  	The world’s largest exhibitor swung to a profit of $109.3 million from a year-earlier loss of $298.2 million. Revenue rose 31% to $1.7 billion and surpassed a previous all-time high achieved in Q2 2026.  	During the quarter, the company completed a $3.97 billion refinancing covering approximately 97% of its debt, extending maturities to late 2031 and 2033, simplifying its capital structure and reducing cost of capital. Aron said that allows the company to “move forward from a position of significantly increased balance sheet strength.”   	           	On a call after the earnings report, he also said AMC would be cash-flow positive for full-year 2026.      			Watch on Deadline		       	Strengthening the balance sheet has been his key priority since after the dark days of the pandemic pummeled theaters and was particularly devastating to chains like AMC, which already carried significant debt after years of expansion. Rumors of imminent bankruptcy have dogged the company for years since. On the call, Aron insisted AMC has outrun the crisis after paying down several billion dollars in debt over time and with the help of a newly healthy box office.  	“On this webcast, I declare that AMC has finally emerged from the storm clouds created by Covid,” he said.  	The current fourth quarter continues strong with the October domestic box office up some 35% year on year, he said, anticipating upcoming films I Play Rocky, Wild Horse Nine, Ebenezer, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, Dune: Part Three, Avengers: Doomsday, Mr. Irrelevant and Jumanji: Open World, which Aron called “an impressive and promising film slate that is a fitting close to a wonderful year for moviegoers.  	           	He said he sees the remaining film slate propelling both the domestic and global box office to their highest full-year levels in seven years, with domestic box office easily hitting $10 billion or more.  	“Today, we can finally say that AMC has recovered. To our studio partners, lenders, business partners, employees and our millions of passionate shareholders, thank you for standing with us as we traveled through a long, and at times brutal, road,” he said. “Mere survival was never the goal. Our goal ultimately was to thrive, and that is exactly and precisely where our focus now lies. Okay, so I'll admit it; Microsoft has been doing better with the Windows 11 Start menu lately. The company has fixed most (if not all) of the pain points I had with it, and I have to give it credit for that. However, I do also love what Start11 is doing, which was my go-to app when I wanted something different. Now, Stardock has announced that a new version of Start11 has hit preview, and it contains widgets. As announced on the Stardock blog (via Neowin), Start11 v3 has now hit release preview. One of the highlights for this version are widgets, which you can place directly inside the Start menu for a quick digest. Here's how Stardock describes the new feature: "Users can now add interactive widgets that display important information and provide quick access to everyday tools without opening another application. With more than 20 widgets available, including calendars, system monitoring, notes, clocks, and more, Start11 v3 makes the Start menu a more useful destination for getting things done." Given how Microsoft is slowly adding customization options to Windows 11's native Start menu, Stardock needs to pull ahead to keep its position as one of the better ways to use it. Fortunately, it seems the company knows this, as Start11 v3 introduces new features that keep it ahead of the official offering. Taskbar Islands gives the UI a sleek, modern look, while the new taskbar grouping feature lets you put applications into little niches for an easier time navigating them.  To top it off, Stardock is reducing the price of Start11 from $10 to $8 during the release preview phase, so now's the perfect time to hop in if you're curious. In the fall of 1621, members of the Wampanoag tribe and several English colonists gathered for a feast in Plymouth, then part of the Plymouth Colony in Massachusetts.Â  Neither Native Americans nor the Pilgrims could have predicted that this one-off meal, celebrating an abundant harvest and a brief alliance, would be printed in history books as the first Thanksgiving. Yet, the occasion was much more historically significant than a spread of food and a side of gratitude.Â  In 2026, Thanksgiving is a federal holiday: a time to reflect, give thanks, and gather with family over turkey, stuffing, pumpkin pie, and other holiday confections. But what was the first Thanksgiving really like? And what did they eat? According to the National Archives, the Pilgrims survived the Mayflowerâs journey from England and "came ashore on Wampanoag land." The Wampanoag, having already had contact with Europeans before the Pilgrims arrived (contact that resulted in diseases and the enslavement of some tribe members like Squanto), spoke English by the time of the feast. To give thanks for a bountiful harvest and their first peace treaty, signed earlier that year (despite hesitation from tribal leaders), both groups sat down for a meal together, made possible by the hunting and planting techniques the Wampanoag shared with the Pilgrims, which greatly alleviated food shortages.Â  According to historical records cited by Smithsonian Magazine, the feast lasted for three days. "Many of the Indians coming amongst us, and among the rest their greatest king Massasoit, with some 90 men, whom for three days we entertained and feasted," English leader Edward Winslow wrote of the occasion.Â  Although the gathering itself was friendly, the alliance did not last. Just 54 years after the first Thanksgiving, the treaty dissolved, sparking King Philip's War (led by Massasoit's son), in which the English defeated the Native Americans. The battle resulted in mass casualties, and the Wampanoag lost their land and freedoms. Both settlers and Native American tribes held feasts to commemorate significant events, but this Thanksgiving feast did not become an annual tradition. In fact, it all but faded from memory until Abraham Lincoln proclaimed it a national holiday during the Civil War in 1863. While the treaty and the feast werenât enough to sustain civility and respect between the groups, the food provided moments of connection and respite, as shared meals do. Today, our plates (and growling stomachs) are filled with turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, green bean casserole, cranberry sauce, dinner rolls, and, of course, pumpkin pie. In 1621, however, the menu looked very different.Â  Winslow wrote: "Our governor sent four men on fowling, that so we might after a special manner rejoice together after we had gathered the fruit of our labors. They four in one day killed as much fowl as, with a little help beside, served the company almost a week."
