The Commerce Department reported that U.S. economic growth rose to 3.4% in the latest quarter, up from 2.2% in the previous quarter. The report underscored the strength of the economy even as market volatility has increased in recent weeks, according to the department. Strategists said the combination of historical midterm patterns, AI-related spending concerns and interest rate uncertainty has created a complex backdrop for investors. "Typically speaking, after midterms, markets do pretty well, actually," Mark LoPresti, CEO and chief market strategist at Market Rebellion, told NewsNation. "If one thing markets hate, it's uncertainty."Historical Gains After Midterm Elections BNY Investment Strategy & Research Group found that since 1950, the S&P 500 has gained an average of 16.6% in the year after a midterm election, the firm said. MarketWatch reported that the S&P 500 delivered an average return of 15.5% in the nine months between Election Day and June 30, going back to 1950. A Ned Davis Research study cited by Ed Clissold and Thanh Nguyen found that since 1930, the S&P 500 or its predecessors rose an average of 14% in the year after midterms; when the president's party lost control of the House, the average gain was 8.8%, the firm said. The Trends Journal previously reported that after each of the last 40 midterm elections, the S&P 500 has gained an average of 15% in the following 12 months on a sense of clarity about short-term tax, fiscal, and economic policy [1]. BlackRock noted that midterm election years have historically been among the weakest performing years for the U.S. stock market, compared to presidential election years, but that markets have typically recovered and moved higher afterward [2]. Russell Investments said that once election results are known, clarity often gives investors the confidence to step back into markets, driving a rally irrespective of which party wins [3].Recent Market Turbulence and Economic Data Stocks have been rocky this month, with technology shares under pressure as investors assessed AI-related valuations and spending, according to market data. The Commerce Department's 3.4% growth figure compared with 2.2% in the previous quarter, the report stated. The Federal Reserve held rates steady this week and does not meet in November, he said. He said another rate increase is likely at the December meeting, and most traders expect at least another 50 basis points of increases in the first half of 2027. Higher borrowing costs could weigh on AI spending, LoPresti said. Investing.com reported that quarterly results intensified concerns about financing and financial returns needed to support the AI investment theme at the heart of the market [7]. The report noted that investors are focused on whether companies can sustain high levels of AI-related capital expenditures amid rising financing costs.Election Outcome and Data Center Opposition Prediction market Kalshi showed Democrats with better than a 90% chance of winning the House and a 63% chance of taking the Senate, LoPresti said. The Kubly House, a midcentury modern residence in Pasadena, has returned to the property market 61 years after its completion.  Designed by Craig Ellwood Associates in 1965 for Don and Sally Kubly, the house was built for $45,000 and is now listed for $3,250,000 through Suarez + Benz.  Located at 215 La Vereda Road, the approximately 2,280-square-foot residence occupies a 0.6-acre site among eucalyptus and oak trees. The scheme’s single-story design takes the form of an elevated wood-and-glass pavilion, with extensive glazing providing views of the surrounding landscape.    Unlike Ellwood's better-known steel-framed buildings, the house uses post-and-beam timber construction. The change is likely due to an original construction budget of less than $45,000.   Don Kubly also subsequently helped select Ellwood's practice to design ArtCenter's Hillside Campus, completed in 1976. The architect's firm was responsible for the landmark steel-and-glass complex, with associate James Tyler recognized as its principal designer.  The Kubly family retained the residence until 2022, when it was sold for the first time in approximately 57 years. The subsequent owners commissioned a restoration with Carl Bronson of Bronstruction, guided by a stated principle of doing no harm. The work included updating building systems, removing an interior partition to enlarge the primary suite, and undertaking surface repairs, while retaining the house's defining structure, glazing, and material palette. Any takers? Craig Ellwood (born Join Nelson Burke) was what in California was called a Registered Building Designer. He only became licensed beginning in 1986 when his license was converted from registered building designer to architect. He was a building designer. One of the benefits of the registered building designer registration was it allowed building designers to design houses in other materials than conventional  wood framed construction. In California, a building designer who wasn't registered (just as they are today) was limited to conventional wood framed construction and some other basic limits. A registered building designer was a registration that expanded the scope of practice but still limited compared to architect license. Under current California law, as a building designer, I would have to approach things similarly to Craig Ellwood by partnering with licensed architects/engineers for certain technical submissions. This registered building designer program was one of the original source material and principles used by AIBD in formulating the CPBD certification. It was modeled somewhat from the California's RBD program. Technically, the "registered building designer" title still exists on California's law books as a protected title although the actual registration program had ended in 1985. Craig Ellwood had already largely retired from practice in 1977 but kept his registration going even after retiring just in case he wanted to design something in California.  Refreshing to see that the owners did not fancy-up and upscale the interior beyond recognition as was done a few years back at Ellwood's Moore house in LA.  Hope the next owners have the same mindset. If there’s one category among those we see here at Hackaday that has something for everyone, it’s retrocomputing. Spanning everything from relay-based machines that fill a wall through to modern machines with a retro twist, there must be few of us who haven’t seen such a project as been impressed. Our most recent contest challenged you to come out with your best retrocomputing projects, and we’re extremely pleased to say that you didn’t disappoint us. Here are the results, both the outright winners, and the honourable mentions. First up, our top three. For these, we are happy to award the prize of a  $150 DigiKey gift certificate. It’s difficult not to be impressed with [Mike]’s  Vacuum Tube Computer, a behemoth of a machine composed of wall-mounted panels studded with 460 Russian 6N3P dual-triodes. These along with 1840 1N33 point-contact diodes form the physical implementation of a fairly conventional 8-bit computer. It uses a NOR gate architecture, and there are only 16 instructions. It comes with a flip-digit 7-segment display, using modules salvaged from redundant British railway platform clocks, and runs a simple airship simulator as its demonstration program. We wish we had the dedication to see a project like this one to its conclusion. When we think of a 1980s computer our minds are immediately drawn to the 8-bit home computers of the period, a desktop console case with a keyboard and a TV used as a monitor. But these were far from the only machines in town at the bottom end of the market, they were joined by a range of much more bare-metal educational designs. The Busch Microtronic was one of them, made in then-West Germany, it was unusual in having a 4-bit TMS1600 processor. A group of hackers has come together and recreated the device as an emulator using an Atmel microcontrolloer, with the big difference from other Microtronic emulators being that theirs runs the original firmware. It’s called the Microtronic Phoenix, and the difficult task of retrieving the mask-programmed firmware was achieved using a logic analyser. Making a PCB with a microcontroller and associated peripherals may not be a task in itself worthy of attention, however the board itself is only the carrier here. The attention to detail and skill required to make it do its job so accurately by persuading a 1970s microcontroller to reveal its secrets is what makes this project special, and you can count us impressed by it. We deal with all manner of computing devices here at Hackaday  so it’s very rare indeed for a Hackaday writer to be presented with an entirely new one. Yet that’s the case with A Tiny Sieve, it’s a Lehmer number sieve, machine for very quickly factoring very large numbers. A mechanised version of modulo arithmetic, it’s a real-world implementation of sieve theory. The first Lehmer sieve used bicycle chains of varying lengths, while later versions progressed through gears, film strips, and mercury delay lines before eventually becoming fully electronic. They were only surpassed by computers in the mid-1990s, which provides some indication of how fast they could be. The Tiny Sieve implements a Lehmer sieve with 30 ATtiny412 microcontrollers replacing those bicycle chains or delay lines, with an RP2040 performing the task of controller. This reflects in a curious way the delay line sieve of the 1960s, where the controller task was performed by an IBM minicomputer passing a paper tape to the machine. Its results are comparable to those in the paper describing the bicycle chain sieve so perhaps it’s not the fastest, but  it works. This project is special on many levels, impressing the judges because of its unusual subjkect, and its explanation of this niche in mathematical and computing history. We may never need one, but now at least we’ve seen one and know how it works. The quality and breadth of the entries to this contest was a joy to read through, and it’s sad that we had only three prizes to award. We came up with a set of categories for the competition, and here follows just a small selection of the ones which caught our eye. This category was for old hardware doing something much newer. Can your 8-bit micro compete in 2026? Here was its time to shine! We’re used to air traffic displays, usually based around a single board computer or a microcontroller. What we’ve not seen before is NES Radar, the venerable game console doing the honours. It uses a small server on another computer squirting the data down a controller cable, a novel interface method. Continuing the fresh take on an old idea, replacing a cassette storage or a floppy drive with modern high capacity alternatives has been a thing for years now. Meatloaf takes it a step further, using an ESP32 to allow your Commodore 64 to run code from any network resource it can see, up to and including an Internet URL. The Commodore SID is a staple of the chiptune scene, and there have been many emulators and standalone SID players. USBSID-Pico does it with a pair of real SID chips, and a Pi Pico to control them. This category turns the previous one on its head. Let’s take the hardware we have, and make it act like the hardware we used to have. Microcontrollers are now powerful enough to run emulators for machines of the 16-bit era, so emulated hardware is starting to look almost powerful. Among these is the original Mac 128k on the RO2040, but Pico-mac-nano takes the basic idea to a new level. The emulated Mac sits in a miniature version of the famous all-in-one Mac case that’s perfect to the n’th degree. If only an accompanying keyboard and mouse could be made this small. The Cheap Yellow Display has lowered the barrier to entry for projects with a touchscreen, and we’ve seen it in all manner of projects. A weather display on a CYD isn’t that special in itself, but Win95 Retro Weather Display caught our attention for its retro attention to detail. In a lovingly crafted mini CRT monitor case, it uses a Windows 95 display aesthetic to perfection. We could almost be in a diminutive version of the ’90s. David Rumball made a single board computer back in the 1980s called the Microbox. Here in the 2020s he’s recreated it, but not in the way many other emulators do the job. In Microbox 2K2 he’s used an Xmos XU216 SoC, an unusual highly parallel multicore architecture, allowing him to devote an individual core to emulating each component of the system. We think this emulation technique deserves a lot more attention, and could deliver emulated versions of some of the more difficult or powerful retro platforms. This category is for the retro hardware itself. Repairing it, upgrading it with contemporary parts, or getting it to do things which might have been done when it was new. Old hardware can be fragile, especially so when someone tries to repair it. It’s easy to damage a PCB, and in the Lazarus Daughter Board for the Lazer (Vtech) Vz200 we see a practical way to recover from this. It’s a CPU daughter board that puts the device’s memory on a new PCB alongside the processor, allowing the damaged board to be ignored. This technoique could save other machines aplenty. It’s a welcome sight to have several entries using obscure educational computers, of which the Philips MC6400 with its National Semiconductor INS8070 was one. With the aid of a resistor ladder DAC, we’re seening Oscillocope vector graphics  on a machine from 1984. Another educational computer of that era was the Kosmos CP1, which reatured a very unusual emulated decimal architecture. Here it is running Towers of Hanoi on an LED matrix. The experience of writing software has changed immeasurably since the days when your computer booted into a BASIC interpreter. This category is for those who prefer to write software the old way. Getting DOOM running on a machine is now no real novelty, as we’ve seen it on all manner of unexpected devices. Getting it to run on a TRS-80 CoCo is impossible, but that doesn’t mean you can’t  try to code something that looks a bit like it. The daddy of all video games is Spacewar! written in 1962 for a DEC PDP-1. Later games passed the early DEC minicomputer by, but never fear. Here’s Lunar Lander for the (emulated) PDP-1. AI is all the rage these days, and we’re told that to be a player you need a huge data centre stuffed with expensive NVIDIA GPUs. Not at all, it seems, for here’s A Transformer Trained in HyperCard. We’d like to thank you all for participating i this contest, for submitting entries, or for reading about them here. Judging it has been fun, and we look forward to what you produce in our next contest. And special thanks again to DigiKey for sponsoring! Congratulations to all the winners and honorable mentions! US editor                 Photography by         Eric Mueller  A set of speakers with flesh-like exteriors was among the conceptual design work shown at the first Walker Design Triennial in Minneapolis, USA, which curator Joseph Grima said reflected on the meaning of design in a world fixated on optimisation. Filling a series of galleries at the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis, Minnesota, the exhibition was called Beyond Materialism and featured numerous examples of conceptual design.  The pieces ranged from the historical works such as Italian radical designer Alessandro Mendini’s 1970s Lassù – paired with depictions of the performance of the chair on fire – to an international set of design studios representing the field today. Grima, who has served as a curator and educator for several high-profile institutions including Design Academy Eindhoven and international exhibition series Alcova, said the show was meant to challenge mainstream conceptions of design. “We live in an age that is conditioned to think that anything and everything can be designed, and often what is that everything can be optimised,” said Grima. “And it’s precisely this association between design and optimisation that this exhibition intends to question.” With objects of various scales on display, the Walker Design Triennial featured a room with large-scale conceptual installations. Many of the participants were international, with a cohort of contemporary US designers, including Germane Barnes and Theaster Gates. Terracotta plinths were included as part of the exhibition design, supporting many of the small and large objects.  Some of the pieces were commissioned directly for the event, mainly in the large-scale section.  Among these was Spanish designer Lucas Muñoz Muñoz’s All Ears, a set of latex-covered speakers that were programmed to play sounds recorded in the months before in Minneapolis. A sleek soundboard allowed users to play the tracks, with multiple tracks routed through the amorphous, fleshy speakers all at once to cacophonic effect. Muñoz told Dezeen that the installation was designed to be a “microphone” for the city itself and “make visible the act of listening”.  The broadcast from the soundboard was also projected out of the gallery as a radio sequence. Also commissioned for the event was a work by Vessel, featuring two massive rolls of fabric spooled over a kiosk. The fabric was based on Vessel cofounder Navine G Dossos’s paintings of her and her partner James Bridle’s self-built home. Also in the large-scale room was a series of post-apocalyptic appliances made from found objects by Brussels-based Espace Aygo, derived from the studio’s 2022 transformation of a derelict apartment building into a home and art space. The themes of fleshy objects, post-apocalypticism, and reuse continued into the rooms with smaller objects. Here, London-based studio Superflux showcased objects from its Relics of Abundance series, showing objects created by a future civilisation that may someday use our objects today in a time of scarcity, including a chair made from straw and rebar.              Read:            Austro-Canadian designer Christoph Wimmer Ruelland created a series of furniture pieces with found objects that are extraordinarily colour-matched, while Korean designer Jonghoo Jeong utilised jerrycans to create a fountain, a reference to his past practice of dumping the objects in his process. Athens-based studio Astronauts showcased inflated metal works informed by the autobody shops, creating love seats, chairs and even a seesaw that are iridescent while still familiar. Italian-German designer Maximilian Marchesani created a structural piece made of smartphone glass that refracts metal-coated leaves as well as a chandelier that combined LEDs with branches. South Korean studio Wknd Lab created a series of stools made from discarded shells. Dozens of other designers took part in the installation, including Moon Seop Seo, Studio Ker, Objects of Common Interest, Stef Fusani, Kevin Quale and Kostas Lambridis, representing a who’s who of avant-garde design, refracted through the lens of Grima and the event’s artistic director, Asli Altay. It was an “opportunity to stop, take stock for a moment, and reflect on what design is today,” said Grima.  Other recent design showcases include a show of wood furniture by Armadillo and furniture made from fragments of New York buildings by Rafael Prieto. Beyond Materialism is on show at the Walker Art Center from 17 October 2026 to 14 February 2027. Consumers commonly rev up to potentially buy high-ticket items on Black Friday, when prices are often traditionally slashed to start the holiday shopping season. TVs are a staple purchase consumers rush for while Black Friday deals are available, and some OLED models may appear the best options on the market for their bright, vivid displays. Not everyone can tell the difference between cheap and expensive OLED TVs, though, or even how they compare to other display types. Understanding those distinctions could very well determine whether you're wasting your money or getting the most bang for your buck. Thus, regardless of how good a deal you can nab one for, it's crucial to know what slip-ups you should avoid while shopping for your next OLED display. The best television choice for you hinges on how bright its viewing space can get. Bright, sunny spaces often require extra-luminous TVs. Thus, opting for an OLED model can be risky, as they aren't always brighter than LCD-powered peers unless you choose to splurge on a costlier option. Some shoppers would be better off considering certain LED options, which may perform better in highly-lit settings. Prospective OLED buyers should also be mindful of their intended viewing space's size, and choose the right model accordingly. The Big Screen Store suggests that 65-inch options are a happy medium for most rooms, while 55-inch OLEDS are better for bedrooms and smaller spaces. Those reaching 77 inches or higher are recommended only for in-depth home theaters and for viewers whose highest priority is picture quality. Understanding size differentials beforehand can prevent future TV owners from overpaying on devices too large for the area in which they're being installed, while also making the most out of a viewing space with the largest, best-quality picture it can support. It's no secret that excited Black Friday shoppers are prone to making several common mistakes when buying TVs, and that's particularly true with OLED models. Avid deal hunters in particular may fall victim to the wrong choices, especially if they value price over quality and don't double-check their specs. One area many budget devices fall short is with processing power, which manufacturers sacrifice to maintain a lower price. The end result can be garbled images due to less advanced image processing. Underpowered processors can also introduce noise and other artifacts into the picture. Whether you decide on a cheap OLED over premium options should ultimately hinge on how you intend to use it. Those who are willing to embrace cheaper models, warts and all, should also know that they are intended for consuming media with lower frame rates and resolution, like movies. Avid gamers, meanwhile, may want to consider more expensive options designed with support for standards like G-Sync and FreeSync, and other technologies meant to support variable and higher frame rates while avoiding annoying visual flaws.

November 4, 2026 7 min read As SpaceX sunsets Falcon 9, a launch crunch is looming What happens when the most successful rocket in history stops flying? The world is about to find out By Ramin Skibba edited by Lee Billings SpaceX’s ubiquitous Falcon 9 rocket has lofted astronauts, NASA’s Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer spacecraft, the European Space Agency’s Euclid space telescope, the Space Force’s GPS satellites and thousands of the company’s Starlink Internet satellites into orbit over the past few years. By most any measure, the rocket is the most successful launch vehicle ever flown. But if SpaceX has its way, the Falcon 9 era will soon come to an end. Since SpaceX engineers developed the innovative rocket and its reusable first stage in the 2000s and 2010s, it has become a mainstay for space access, accounting for 85 percent of U.S. launches in 2025. Now SpaceX plans to wind down the Falcon 9 within the next few years to better accommodate the company’s sprint toward using Starship, its fully reusable megarocket meant to spark another even greater spaceflight revolution. But unless and until Starship demonstrates Falcon 9–like reliability, SpaceX’s shift away from its current mainstay seems destined to produce major ripple effects across the space industry, affecting numerous customers. From NASA and the Pentagon to start-ups, universities and international organizations, many entities depend on SpaceX’s Falcon 9. “Whenever you rely on one launch provider, especially one that’s commercial, you’re kind of at their whims,” says Kathleen Curlee, a senior research analyst at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today. The U.S. Department of Defense’s Space Force contracts using the Falcon 9 run through 2028, so those launches continue through that year, but Politico has reported that SpaceX has so far rebuffed Space Force efforts to secure further launches. Similarly, some companies have been unable to book future Falcon 9 flights as well, according to the Wall Street Journal. That means more uncertainties, and potential delays and cost increases for U.S. space launches. Curlee expected such a decision by SpaceX. “I’m more surprised that people are so shocked this is happening,” she says. The company needs to pivot to its Starship program, she argues, and that may require retiring the Falcon family of rockets—not just the Falcon 9 but also the Falcon Heavy, a much beefier vehicle that also has partial reusability. Though Falcon 9 has been profitable, SpaceX’s business interests have been especially buoyed by Starlink, and the company is banking on the uncertain prospect of data centers in orbit, which would create yet more demand for Starship launches. In SpaceX’s early years, major launch contracts from NASA helped prop up the company, which at the time was struggling to attract customers while developing and deploying Falcon 9’s precursor, the Falcon 1. SpaceX ultimately became the biggest success story of NASA’s commercial crew and cargo programs, allowing the space agency to send astronauts to the International Space Station without relying on Russia’s Soyuz rocket. In this relationship, NASA now seems the one more in need of favors: the space agency books most of its orbital trips and deep-space launches through SpaceX but represents only a fraction of the company’s total launch business. Joshua Finch, a NASA spokesperson, told Scientific American in a statement that “NASA and SpaceX are in regular communication and continue to work together on contract to launch cargo and crew for the safe operations of the International Space Station, as well as launch science, exploration, and research/technology missions through our launch services contracts.” Finch also highlighted the agency’s collaboration with Boeing for astronauts’ trips to and from the space station. NASA had seen the company’s Starliner as a backup to SpaceX’s Crew Dragon, which flies atop the Falcon 9. Starliner has proven to be the much more expensive and less reliable option, however, with its development suffering numerous costly delays and its test flights going so poorly that one in 2024 stranded NASA astronauts at the space station for months. A Crew Dragon eventually brought that crew back home. NASA and Boeing plan for another uncrewed Starliner test flight as early as this December, followed by more crewed flights in 2028. The Space Force has come to rely on SpaceX’s Falcon 9 (or its heftier cousin, the Falcon Heavy) for launches of sensitive national-security-related spacecraft, including those for the Golden Dome missile defense program. “I hope we don’t just lose this technology. It seems like a tremendous waste, if there isn’t some way for someone to pick up this program and keep it running,” says Matthew Weinzierl, a Harvard Business School researcher who studies the private space sector. He suggests it’s conceivable that the Space Force or other parts of the U.S. government could pay SpaceX to license the Falcon 9 technology, effectively taking control of the program and freeing the company to pursue other priorities. “There’s so much value. It seems strange to let it go,” he says. SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment. A Space Force spokesperson, Rose Riley, tells Scientific American that the agency has Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy launches planned through fiscal year 2032, and that as many as six other companies will soon be in a position to provide national security launch services as well. “We have an inherent duty to plan for possible contingencies,” Riley says. “While we don’t expect to have to use them, we are talking through all scenarios and what options we can leverage should we need to.” The prospects for Starship remain uncertain; its goal of full reusability would be a historic first for any orbital spacecraft—let alone the largest launch vehicle ever built. But many of its test flights so far have ended in fiery explosions; its next test, Flight 15, is slated for mid-November. Even if SpaceX’s wildest dreams come true, with Starship soon entering routine service and ramping up to launch at an even higher cadence than Falcon 9, it’s unclear whether the huge rocket will have correspondingly huge demand. One glaring issue is that Starship presently lacks a payload fairing door of the sort most satellite customers currently need; instead it has a narrower aperture custom-made for ejecting batches of Starlink satellites. Another concern is the shifting landscape around artificial-intelligence-powering orbital data centers. On October 25 SpaceX continued its push into AI with a $40-billion debt-financing deal for data center GPUs, but the AI industry’s accumulation of debt now makes such deals more difficult. Despite that, Anthropic has reportedly become one of SpaceX’s biggest customers. “Is this too big a risk? [SpaceX] takes big swings,” says Carissa Bryce Christensen, founder and CEO of BryceTech, an analytics and engineering contractor with NASA and the Space Force. Falcon 9 was once seen as unduly risky, too, she notes, when the rocket suffered high-visibility failures on its long path to routine flight and, eventually, industry dominance. As SpaceX sunsets Falcon 9, some commercial customers are already scrambling to find new launch providers, Curlee says. The closest competitor to Starship, at least in the Earth-orbit launch market, is Blue Origin’s New Glenn, but that rocket exploded on its Cape Canaveral launchpad during a May 28 hotfire test and remains grounded. Blue Origin aims to have the pad and other infrastructure rebuilt by December. United Launch Alliance (ULA), a joint venture of Boeing and Lockheed Martin, has its new Vulcan Centaur rocket, which first flew in 2024 but is now grounded as well after problems with its solid rocket booster during a launch in February. ULA announced on October 28 that it’s resuming Vulcan spaceflights in mid-November. Other competitors include Rocket Lab, which has mostly cornered the small-launch market, as well as rising companies such as Firefly Aerospace, Stoke Space and Relativity Space. “When there’s a big profit opportunity, there’s nothing more powerful for getting competition going than a lot of money sitting on the table, and this is probably one of those situations where there’s a lot of business to be had,” Weinzierl says. Nevertheless, he points out, thanks to Falcon 9 helping to lower the bar for launch access in recent years, space start-ups have been able to scrape together money from investors to try new spacecraft designs. If that bar rises again and costs go up in the absence of SpaceX’s tried-and-true workhorse, those nascent companies might never get off the ground. International competition has emerged on the horizon as well, especially from China’s expanding space sector, which is seeking to develop homegrown reusable rocketry to rival SpaceX. China has begun launching satellites for customers in countries such as Oman and Thailand over the past couple of years. But some potential customers may be hesitant to go that route because current U.S. law restricts contractors working with China or Chinese-owned companies. That means anyone that launches a spacecraft aboard a Chinese rocket may have trouble subsequently contracting with NASA or the Space Force. Europe’s space industry remains behind the U.S. and China, though it is attempting to catch up. France’s Arianespace has a heavy-lift rocket called Ariane 6, and its partially reusable successor is in development for the 2030s. On October 5 European Space Agency chief Josef Aschbacher proposed investing €10 billion (about 11 billion USD) over the next decade to develop a new launch system to deliver astronauts to orbit. European governments will weigh the idea at a mid-December meeting in Rome. “ESA’s priority is to ensure reliable, resilient and autonomous European access to space. Our baseline approach is therefore clear: for ESA missions, we look first to European launch services and seek to maximize their use,” said Kathryn Fleet, an ESA spokesperson, in a statement to Scientific American. Fleet points to the Ariane 6 rocket and Vega-C, a medium-lift rocket, while looking forward to emerging options. These include German start-up Isar Aerospace’s Spectrum rocket, which achieved its inaugural spaceflight in September, a milestone for the European commercial space sector. Fleet also said that working with Soyuz again is “not on the table,” because Soyuz launches from Europe’s spaceport in French Guiana were suspended in 2022 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. SpaceX is, of course, led by CEO and almost-trillionaire Elon Musk, a mercurial figure active in far-right extremist politics in the U.S. and abroad. SpaceX has also swayed foreign policy, notably in Ukraine, such as by restricting Starlink Internet access. So far, however, such incidents haven’t significantly affected SpaceX’s ability to ink lucrative government launch contracts, and federal agencies have found SpaceX to be the best option in terms of capability and price, Weinzierl says. He adds, “At the same time, no government wants to be reliant on a single company, so I imagine there will be substantial and sustained interest in supporting competitors to SpaceX.” Ramin Skibba is a science writer based in San Diego, Calif. campaign Looking for an Airtable alternative? See how Grist compares. Here is a formula many of us wrote early on. Put transactions in a traditional spreadsheet, like Excel or Google Sheets, one per row, and keep a running balance: Copy the formula down, and it works. Each balance is the balance above it plus the amount on its own row. Now you find a receipt from January 11 and insert a row for it, between rows 3 and 4. The new row has no formula, so you type one in, or copy it from above. But the balance below it now says =C3+B5. When the rows shifted, the reference was adjusted to keep pointing at the same cell, and that cell is no longer the row above. The new transaction is skipped without showing an error of any kind. The balance is just wrong from that row on. Delete a row instead, and the formula below it becomes #REF!, and so does every balance after it. None of this is a bug. To a traditional spreadsheet, “the previous transaction” means “the cell above”. The two agree only as long as nobody rearranges anything. There is, if you know the tricks. Vertex42 suggests OFFSET(), or a relative named range, to point at “the cell above” in a way that survives edits. Exceljet suggests a single SCAN() formula for the whole column in Excel 365. What about the spreadsheet-like tools with database foundations? In Airtable and Baserow, a formula can only see the record it’s in, and the same goes for NocoDB and Notion databases. People asking on their forums how to do a running total in Airtable or Baserow get pointed to scripts, or to linking each record to the previous one by hand. So these tools avoid the problem by not having a “row above” at all. But the need is there: a running balance, the days since a patient’s last visit, the stock left after each shipment. SQL has an answer: window functions. There’s LAG and LEAD for the previous and next row, or SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account ORDER BY date) for a running total. They also work, but they’re an advanced tool for developers writing queries, not for people working in a table. What we really mean by “the previous row” is “the previous transaction, by date”. So let’s say exactly that. In Grist, a running balance, or any cumulative total, looks like this: PREVIOUS(rec, order_by="Date") sorts the table by ‘Date’, finds the current record (rec), and returns the previous record. It’s a whole record (not just a cell), so .Running_Balance gets that record’s balance. The very first transaction has no previous one, so its balance comes out empty, and or 0 takes care of that. The ordering is in the formula, not in the view. Insert a transaction anywhere, and it falls into place by its date. Delete one, and the balances close up around it. Sort the table by ‘Amount’ or filter it, and each record still holds its balance by date, because that’s what we asked for. Now, a credit card account may have several cardholders, and each might want their own balance. You might be tempted to split the data into a table per person. Please don’t do that. Keep one table, and be specific: PREVIOUS() now finds the previous transaction by date among those of the same card member. And since the order lives in the formula (order_by), nothing stops you from having several running totals side by side: one for the whole account, one per card member, one that starts over each month. Each column keeps its own count. Add a view linked to card members and sorted by date, and you can pick a card member and see their transactions, with their balance adding up row by row. PREVIOUS() has two siblings. NEXT() looks the other way, and RANK() gives each record its position in the order, so RANK(rec, order_by="-Amount") <= 10 marks the ten largest transactions. The help article covers all three in more detail. Once a lookup knows about order, “previous” is just one thing you can ask of it. Say people’s pay rates change over time, and you keep the history: Bertha earns $110 an hour starting August 30, 2019, and $125 starting March 24, 2020. A payroll entry from February 2020 needs the rate in effect on its date, which is the latest rate that started on or before that date: lookupRecords() gets Bertha’s rates, sorted by start date. find.le() finds the last one that’s less than or equal to (that’s the le) the payroll date. Nothing about this is specific to dates. Commission tiers work the same way: sell $5,000 and earn 7%, sell $10,000 and earn 10%, and so on. Excel and Google Sheets users know this as an approximate match: VLOOKUP() with TRUE as the last argument. Microsoft’s own docs say the first column then needs to be sorted, and if it isn’t, “the return value might be something you don’t expect.” No error, just a different answer. In Grist, the order is part of the formula: it sorts the tiers itself, no matter how you choose to present them on the screen. The same two lines answer a whole family of everyday nearest-match (sometimes called “approximate match”) questions: And for the simplest question of all (the first or last record in a group) you don’t even need find(). Here’s a customer’s most recent order: The minus sign means descending, so the first match is the latest. Grist formulas are Python, so you could always write all of this by hand: get the records, loop over them, pick the right one. We should check what that costs. A running total done by scanning, SUM(r.Amount for r in Transactions.all if r.Date <= $Date), looks at the whole table for every record. With 1,000 transactions, that’s a million steps. With 20,000, it’s 400 million. On a test table of 20,000 transactions, PREVIOUS() computed the whole column of running balances in seconds. The scanning version was still running after five minutes. The ordered lookups don’t scan. They keep the records sorted, and find what you ask for with a binary search, which is the fast way to do it. Remember when we added the receipt from January 11 and it broke the running total? In Grist, you can add it anywhere. It takes its place by date, and every balance after it recalculates. The new row’s balance is right, and so is each card member’s. Nobody has to copy a formula down, check an adjacent row, or fix an error. That’s what you get from formulas that say what they mean: they update on their own, and they’re right every time. Markets     Hot Stocks     Fear & Greed Index                  Latest Market News                  Hot Stocks                  For decades, it was all the bells and whistles that was the selling point for a fancy coffee machine. Now, consumers are looking for what it lacks.               Growing concern over microplastics and sustainability is sparking a wave of plastic-free coffee pods and machines.                   Coffee companies and appliance makers have released new machines and redesigned capsules in recent months. Keurig and Lavazza’s new pods ditch the traditional plastic cups for compostable coffee tablets. Caraway’s new machine uses traditional coffee grounds, but unlike a conventional drip machine, the stainless steel and glass machine doesn’t have plastic in its brew path.                   More research is needed to determine the actual harm microplastics cause. But nine in 10 Americans are concerned about the effect of the minuscule plastic pieces on the planet and their bodies, according to a 2025 poll conducted by environmental group 5 Gyres; and studies have shown that pods shed microplastics.                   The growth in pricey equipment and plastic-free pods fits a broader pattern of consumers trading up on home coffee equipment since the pandemic, said Peter Giuliano, senior adviser for research at Specialty Coffee Association.                   The appeal and growth combine three things: health worries about microplastics, concern about plastic in the environment and the “feeling that metal and glass are more ‘luxury’ than plastic,” he told CNN.                   In June, Lavazza introduced Tablì in the US, a $129 machine that uses only single-serve espresso tablets made with compressed ground coffee — a shift from its capsules made from plastic and aluminum.                   The tablets are made by a custom technology that “compresses precisely dosed, ground, and tamped coffee into a solid, ready-to-use tab,” Lavazza said in a press release.                   The Italian company says the new machine is its “largest investment yet” in the United States as it looks to double revenue to $1 billion by 2029, unlocking the stranglehold Keurig Dr. Pepper has on the coffee market.                   Tablì is aimed at customers who want a sustainable alternative to the traditional pod, according to Daniele Foti, vice president of marketing for Lavazza North America.                   “Consumers want to enjoy their coffee without the waste that usually comes with single-serve,” he told CNN.                   Keurig, which ushered in the boom of plastics with their K-Cups back in the 1990s, launched in October a new line of compostable pods with a specially designed machine called the Alta. (The new pods don’t fit in the old machines.)                   Called AltaRounds, the pods have been in development since 2020 in response to consumers’ shifting sustainability and health preferences.                   The new pods represent a “significant reduction in plastic compared to our K-Cup pods,” said Phil Drapeau, senior vice president for Keurig’s Future Coffee Systems unit.                   “We’ve heard clearly from customers that they want more sustainable products and specifically less plastic and plastic waste,” Drapeau told CNN. “Our data shows that drink variety, quality, and less plastic waste are high priorities across almost every group.”                   Keurig has come under fire in the past over its pods, agreeing in 2022 to pay $10 million to settle a class-action lawsuit alleging it misled consumers by marketing its plastic K-Cups as recyclable, though it denied any wrongdoing.                   But while the pods and the machine contain less plastic, they are considerably more expensive than a traditional Keurig machine. The Alta bundle that includes glassware and pods costs $499.                   Melissa Valliant, director of communications for 5 Gyres, said that both the Lavazza and Keurig products still use plastic packaging, which “ends up in a landfill, incinerator, or our environment after use, contributing to the planet’s growing plastic pollution crisis.”                   Caraway has focused on developing a $495 coffee machine, released last month, that’s created entirely of stainless steel and glass, ensuring that no plastic touches the ground coffee. (Lavazza’s and Keurig’s machines contain some amounts of plastic.)                   Developing a coffee machine with plastic-free brew path was challenging, according to Caraway CEO Jordan Nathan. That’s because the pricey glass and steel parts all need to be custom-made.                   “We had to make the best coffee possible with no plastic on the interior with a full metal body, but also in a small (counter) footprint that had a single dial,” he told CNN.                   Concern over plastic in the kitchen and its affects on the endocrine system has been growing for the past few years, Nathan said, referencing a viral article that linked black plastics in the kitchen to alarming levels of toxic flame retardants.                   Social media, influencers and various scientific studies have all fueled the conversation, with parents and other health-conscious shoppers avoiding plastic where they can, including in makeup, food and bedding. Caraway’s other plastic-free products, like cutting boards, have soared in sales over the past three years.                   Coffee is a natural next step, Nathan added, because “you never want to heat plastic.”                   Demand for Caraway’s new 10-cup coffee maker has been so strong that it’s sold out until January, forcing the company to ramp up production. Meanwhile, Keurig and Lavazza reported similar interest with both company’s product selling out quickly after their initial release.                   That appetite for these pods and machines signals the industry will move toward more plastic-free alternatives, Nathan said.                   “If you’re not doing it, you’re behind where the puck is moving,” he concluded. ROME, Italy — The 12th edition of MIA (Mercato Internazionale Audiovisivo, or International Audiovisual Market) came to a close over the weekend with a strong presence from the international filmmaking community. Over 100 projects from 43 countries were presented across the various programs in Rome, reaffirming MIA as an essential market in the European landscape. This year, animation was more prominent than ever, with MIA introducing a new gap-financing market for animated series that provided projects from around the world with significant financing and the opportunity to complete their funding with the help of distributors, co-producers, and other financiers. Projects from 24 countries were submitted, with 19 projects representing 15 countries selected for the first edition of the gap-financing market. Though there was a palpable excitement at the market this year, there was also one recurring feeling — that of uncertainty in changing times. Between mergers, big firings at Netflix, and shrinking budgets, it’s hard to know what the future holds for the industry. Even the question of AI felt like an unspoken specter that virtually everyone refused to acknowledge, while still being very much felt as a concern. Here are a few takeaways from the 2026 edition of the Rome MIA Market. With the big studios undergoing mergers, there was a palpable sense of concern about the shrinking landscape of places to go to help produce new animated projects. But there was also a clear sense that international co-productions are and will continue to be an important way to make sure new and established voices in the industry get their foot in the door. Going smaller but with more players on board seems to be one workaround to the shrinking of the industry. Of the projects presented at both the series and feature markets, most titles were international co-productions. Not only was there a sense that going international would help projects get financing faster, but it would also help a project reach new audiences more easily. One notable example was Storie in Viaggio (Stories on the Run), based on a series of books and produced by La Sarraz Pictures. The series was pitched as Love, Death + Robots for kids, an animated journey through Italian myths, traditions, and folklore, with each episode being done by a different animator in a different visual style — from cutout paper to 2D to stop motion. The producers were seeking international partners and talked about the possibilities of going beyond just Italian stories to also explore the local folklore of other countries involved in the production. When Cartoon Brew had a chance to speak with MIA director Gaia Tridente after the end of the market, she pressed the issue of financing. “With commissioners becoming more selective and financing structures increasingly complex, producers need to explore new sources of investment and international partnerships,” Tridente told us. “This is also why we launched the European Investment Hub at MIA 2026, bringing together public institutions, private investors, funds and financial institutions to explore new financing models and improve access to capital across the audiovisual industry. This is particularly relevant to animation, where long production cycles and the development of original IP require substantial investment.” During a children’s pubcaster meeting panel, a report was shared from a closed-door discussion between representatives of various broadcasters in Europe. One of the big topics discussed was that of the increasingly blurred definition of children’s target audiences. The conclusion was that traditional age categories are no longer accurate representations of what children are consuming. It’s always been true that kids will be interested in media aimed at older audiences, but now more than ever, kids are not really responding to the specific targets broadcasters are focusing on. The problem is that if the industry can no longer define its audience accurately, then how can it develop stories that will find the right audience? This becomes especially tricky when it comes to slightly older audiences, around the 10–14 demographic, where competition for audiences’ attention becomes harder and the offerings slimmer. That same report made it a point to highlight the challenges of reaching the 10–14 audience, mostly due to a lack of European animation for preteens and teenagers. During a panel about the challenges facing animation distribution, Monica Levy from Federation Studios (Ollie & Moon, Kung Fu Wa) talked about the difficulty of producing and selling animation aimed at those ages because broadcasters rely more on live-action titles to cater to teenagers. Not only are audiences growing out of traditional children’s programming and instead discovering projects aimed at older audiences, but public broadcasters in Europe are also struggling to offer enough alternatives to live-action programming or anime. This last bit is important because teens are very much still consuming animation; it’s just not necessarily programming made in Europe. Seeing the different projects presented at MIA, particularly at the gap-financing market and a presentation about Italian animation, it was clear that the vast majority of projects were aimed at very young audiences, with only a couple meant for older kids or teens. It’s part of why Wildwood feels so special, even if it very much isn’t the first PG-13 animated film. There just aren’t enough. It probably isn’t surprising, but IP remains crucial in ensuring a project gets made. Having some established property to adapt means having data showing that the property has already found success in another medium, and fans who would check out an adaptation. Most of the pitches at the gap-financing market were projects based on books, and considering they already have most of their financing in order, it’s easy to see how having established IP helped. From adaptations of the Juniper Mae and DragoXP books to news of Barry Loser getting an Italian partner right before the show’s presentation at MIA, it’s clear that in these turbulent times, IP is a way to help a project get made. At the distributors’ panel, Diego Ibáñez Belaustegui from DeAPlaneta Entertainment (Milo) talked about the importance of not only having established IP but also brand-building. For distributors and producers, knowing how to build and expand a brand is important beyond just the initial TV show or film. Belaustegui highlighted the success of Milo in Europe and Bluey in Australia as examples of brands expanding exponentially beyond how they originated to become global phenomena through licensing and international exposure. Sign up for Executive Dysfunction, a weekly newsletter that highlights one under-the-radar story about how Trump is changing the law—or how the law is pushing back—and keeps you posted on the latest from Slate’s Jurisprudence team. The American abortion debate had gone relatively quiet before the midterms, even if that calm seems unlikely to last. A number of federal cases seek to impose new national limits on telemedicine abortion or take abortion pills off the market together. Other suits seek to establish that an obscure 19th-century law is actually a national ban on mailing or receiving any item intended or adapted for abortion. And a federal court is set to decide whether even after the end of Roe, the Constitution doesn’t offer women a right to an abortion even if they are going to die or suffer severe and permanent health damage if they continue a pregnancy. And with a historic blue wave reshaping Congress and potentially marking the end of the Trump era, new policy opportunities involving federal protection of reproductive rights may open up.  Because of all that’s coming, it’s especially important to make sense of what the midterms can tell us about what Americans are thinking about abortion and reproductive health more broadly—and what the Trump administration is likely to make of those results. While measures protecting reproductive rights passed in three states—most strikingly, in Missouri—Idaho voters comfortably rejected a proposal to legalize abortion. Expect conservatives to point to that outcome in pushing the Trump administration to crack down on abortion in the president’s last two years in office. On a night when Republicans got shellacked in congressional elections, the Idaho result will embolden conservatives convinced that the president can use executive power to restrict abortion without future electoral fallout for the GOP, even as Democrats in Congress could take steps toward federal protection for reproductive rights. The Idaho result does not change the general trajectory of ballot-measure disputes since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022. All but a handful of these proposals have passed, with the exception of measures on the ballot in Idaho, Nebraska, and South Dakota. Only Idaho and South Dakota voted to preserve strict bans that criminalize virtually all abortions from the moment of fertilization. Tonight’s results crystallized that Americans still tend to favor reproductive rights when the issue is on the ballot. That was clear in exit polls showing a national electorate that said abortion should be legal in “most” or “all” cases by a whopping 63 percent. That view translated into tangible electoral results. Nevada passed Question 6, which establishes a right to abortion until fetal viability (and allows abortion thereafter subject to certain exceptions). While abortion was already broadly legal in the state, the measure will provide insurance that policy will not change should Republicans gain control of the state Legislature (a Republican—who lost on Tuesday—already serves as the state’s governor, even if he signed an executive order shielding doctors and other Nevadans from out-of-state criminal and civil consequences). The same is true of Virginia’s ballot measure, which protects reproductive rights. As recently as 2020, Republicans controlled the Virginia Legislature and governor’s mansion, and the state imposed a number of abortion regulations. Since then, Democrats have repealed those restrictions. The state’s new ballot measure will still make a difference, not only allowing plaintiffs to challenge the state’s remaining restrictions, such as limits on Medicaid reimbursement for abortion, but also ensuring that abortion remains legal in the state if Republicans regain control of state politics. Missouri’s Amendment 3 will be the most devastating for abortion foes. That state had voted to protect reproductive rights just two years ago, narrowly passing another ballot measure annoyingly also named Amendment 3. The state’s Republican Legislature, dissatisfied with this result, put a ballot measure of its own before voters. Champions of Amendment 3 first sought to confuse voters, making it sound as if Amendment 3 primarily permitted access to abortion in cases of severe threats to health or rape and incest if a patient reported her harm early in pregnancy. In reality, Amendment 3 constitutionally banned all other abortions from the moment an egg is fertilized—going further than many of the sweeping bans already on the books. Then, Republicans tried to strike a bargain with voters: accept an unpopular abortion proposal in order to entrench in law opposition to gender-affirming care for minors. Amendment 3 would also have constitutionalized such a prohibition, even though Missouri law already prohibited such care. None of this was enough. Missouri voters comfortably rejected Amendment 3. These results reflect the reality that abortion rights remain a winning issue for Democrats. And now that Democrats control both chambers of Congress, the party is in position to pass protections for reproductive rights and dare Trump to veto a popular bill. But the result in a fourth state could give conservatives a boost when lobbying the Trump administration and the 2028 candidates who are waiting in the wings. Idaho’s Proposition 1 would have established reproductive rights in a state with one of the nation’s harshest bans. Idaho’s exceptions are so narrow that the state’s ban has drawn multiple federal challenges, one under the federal Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act and a second under the federal Constitution, with Dr. Stacy Seyb, the plaintiff, arguing that even after Dobbs, the Constitution protects a right to life- or health-saving care. Idahoans seemed supportive of the measure until Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador issued an opinion last summer establishing that churches could legally fund ballot-measure campaigns without disclosing their donors as long as they used their general funds to do so. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, to which a significant number of Idahoans belong, responded by issuing a letter read in individual congregations condemning Proposition 1. The church then contributed $1 million to a super PAC opposed to Proposition 1. The move seems to have worked: Approximately 55 percent of Idahoans are on track to reject the ballot measure. The midterm results are hardly a windfall for the anti-abortion movement. Idaho is one of the nation’s most conservative states. Ballot measures in general have been a bloodbath for abortion opponents. On top of it all, the elections of Democrats to surprise governorship and attorney general positions in red states where those positions had been on the front line of enforcing abortion bans—including in Texas—will have potentially significant effects on the future of those bans in those states. Nevertheless, the result in Idaho will prove to be a powerful talking point for abortion opponents pressuring the Trump administration to use executive power to limit abortion access in the president’s remaining time in office. Given what has happened since the fall of Roe, it is all but impossible to argue that focusing on abortion helps conservative candidates. But conservatives have begun to argue that voters simply are not concerned about abortion. The midterm results could be read to support this hypothesis: Abortion was not front and center in midterm races. A blue tsunami swept the House and Senate, but in the same election, voters in a major contest in Idaho rejected protections for reproductive rights. Abortion foes will point to this result in convincing the president that he can deliver for his base with no consequences for his legacy or the future of his party. Reading the results in this way is a mistake. Voters were not focused on abortion because there has been no major news on the subject in months—and all by design. Republicans chose to postpone action on the issue until after the midterms concluded. And Idaho, one of the nation’s reddest states, is hardly a bellwether for attitudes about reproductive rights nationwide. All of this means that Idaho’s ballot result is likely an outlier in a ruby-red state. For Republicans, however, Tuesday’s result may be the perfect excuse for an abortion crackdown they had planned all along. And even with Democrats in control of both houses of Congress, there is plenty of damage Donald Trump and the judges he has put in place could do to reproductive rights. See the full analysis here: By Georgie Hewson The elections could give some countries in Asia more reason to slow-walk investment pledges they made to stave off tariffs, and hand economic rival China a perceived upper hand in ongoing trade talks, analysts told Reuters.  However, broad US-China economic relations will likely maintain a state of "fragile stability", said Chim Lee, industrial policy analyst at the Economist Intelligence Unit in Beijing. Trump's midterm losses could spell relief for India's negotiations for a trade deal with the United States, which has faced delays as New Delhi strives to protect its farmers. "After the US midterm losses, President Donald Trump's capacity to impose arbitrary tariffs will certainly face a challenge. At some point he needs the Congress's approval for trade actions and, to that extent, he's weakened," said Anup Wadhawan, a former trade secretary to India's federal government. Congress has the right to regulate commerce and set import duties, but Trump has taken advantage of laws to impose tariffs on grounds of national security or unfair trade practices. Democratic Party efforts to limit that power would be likely to face a presidential veto. Another question is whether Trump will follow through on more immediate threats, such as a 100% tariff on European countries that impose a digital services tax on American tech giants, or whether a €3 billion ($3.37 billion) loan to Airbus AIR.PA from the European Investment Bank will undermine what has been largely a transatlantic trade truce since 2025. European Parliament Vice-President Christel Schaldemose:  "Not because everything now changes for the better, but because it could benefit the support for Ukraine, the green transition, and relations with the rest of the world," she wrote on X. In Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom has led an insurgency against Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith and now leads her by 0.1 of a percentage point. Approximately 38 per cent of Mississippi's population is black or African American according to a 2020 census and, if elected, Colom would be the first African American the state sent to the Senate since the years following the Civil War. By Elissa Fitzgerald We've been talking a fair bit in the last day about whether a redistricting arms race that occurred ahead of the midterms would backfire on the Republicans as some had tipped. If you're not familiar with this, states across the country began redrawing their electorates to try and give certain parties more of an advantage in House races at this election after US President Donald Trump encouraged Republican states to try and shore up seats. This is a strategy known as "gerrymandering". Essentially, a party rejigs electoral boundaries to shave down its majority in comfortable seats to boost numbers elsewhere. But it comes with a risk: If you lose support in those comfortable seats, you could suddenly find competitive races where there were none before. You might hear this outcome called a "dummymander". Design and interiors reporter                 Photography courtesy of         Alter  The second edition of young designers’ exhibition Alter has opened in central Tokyo, featuring a glowing lung-like lamp and Japanese cedar stools made from every part of the log. Alter is being held at Nihonbashi Mitsu Hall during the 10th iteration of Designart Tokyo, which is ongoing across the Japanese capital. The show brings together work from 75 international creators, mostly in their 20s or 30s, united by a desire to “re-examine the value of product design” in an industry that the exhibitors say is growing increasingly rigid in its output. Among the offerings on display is a group show of texture-heavy design pieces curated by Dutch designer Tim Teven.  Under the title At First Contact, it includes a bright green vessel by French designer Audrey Large. Complete with protruding, tentacle-like embellishments, the vase is typical of Large’s otherworldly style. Nearby, Dutch creative Teun Zwets presents a wall-mounted, mirrored cabinet made of his recognisably glossy lacquered split wood, while Paris studio LS Gomma contributed a polyurethane rubber scone lamp with a glowing ribbed body that loosely resembles a pair of lungs. “The pieces’ attention to surface resonates with traditions within Japanese craft, where the effects of making, material behaviour and use remain visible in the finished object,” said Teven, who selected pieces that draw attention to “reflection, gloss and wear”. Elsewhere, Alter presents a “tea ceremony with no host” by Tariki Research Institute, created to invert traditional Japanese tea ceremonies. Instead of a tea master choosing the right cup for the occasion, environmental data picked up by sensors at various locations around the world is translated into organic shapes by an AI algorithm and blow-moulded into unique vessels, from which visitors were encouraged to drink. Bole is a project by London architecture studio Pan Projects, completed in collaboration with local forestry company Morisho and Nara-based wood specialist Morisuke Mei Tree Industry. Working with the knowledge that a typical Japanese cedar tree yields five logs, each four metres long, the collaborators made eight stools from each of these logs, cut into simple discs to use every part of the log. For Alter, the stools are presented as a large totemic column to highlight the process. “Today in the mountains of Japan, the market value of logs is below the value of the labour of the people who grow and care for them,” explained the show organisers. “Even though wood continues to flow through construction and manufacturing sites, most of its value never goes back to the forest. Bole was born as a response to this imbalance.” Also on display is Capillary Drift, a project by Japanese designer Yuma Kano, washi paper specialist Gen Taniguchi of Nao Tesuki Washi, and artisan Kurara Omichi, who works at Uchida Dyeing Factory in Tokyo. The trio is presenting a selection of stools, vessels and other material experiments made out of delicately dyed washi paper. “Rather than seeing washi simply as a flat surface, we approach it as a complex network of interwoven fibres, seeking to reveal expressions hidden within the material itself,” said Taniguchi.              Read:            The inaugural Alter exhibition was shown during last year’s Designart Tokyo. At the time, the exhibition team spoke to Dezeen about their desire to revive the city’s “increasingly homogenous” design scene. Designart Tokyo 2026 takes place from 30 October to 8 November 2026 at various locations across Tokyo, Japan. So what has prompted Beijing to step in, how will the new measures work - and can they stop the sell-off? The measures aimed at making more money available for stock purchases and encouraging companies to buy back their own shares. First, the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) is making it easier for major financial institutions to raise funds to invest in stocks. Under a mechanism known as a swap facility, securities firms, fund managers and insurance companies can exchange assets they already hold, such as government and corporate bonds, for more liquid assets from the central bank. These can then be used to obtain funding to buy stocks, without the institutions having to sell their existing investments. The PBOC said it would conduct a fresh round of swap operations on Tuesday (Nov 3) - potentially channelling more than 100 billion yuan (US$15 billion) into the stock market. Thirty-one securities and fund companies have applied for swaps worth more than 100 billion yuan, the central bank said. Gary Ng, senior economist at investment banking firm Natixis, said the facility would make it easier for large financial institutions to access funding, encouraging them to invest in shares. The latest move also sends a strong signal of Beijing's determination to stabilise its stock market and shore up investor confidence, Hao Zhou, a Hong Kong-based analyst at Guotai Haitong Securities, told Reuters. However, he cautioned that global market volatility and external uncertainties continued to weigh heavily on investor sentiment. Beijing is also making it cheaper for listed companies to buy back their own shares. The PBOC has cut the interest rate on a special lending facility for share buybacks and stake increases from 1.25 per cent to 1 per cent. The scheme, introduced in 2024, will also become a permanent arrangement rather than a temporary measure. Under the programme, banks can obtain cheaper funding from the central bank and lend it to listed companies to repurchase their shares. Such buybacks can help support share prices by reducing the number of shares available in the market, observers said. But Ng cautioned that buybacks do not guarantee higher share prices. Companies could end up taking on more debt to finance the purchases, even as their stock prices continue to fall. Regulators are also encouraging major companies and investment funds to buy more stocks. The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) has urged major companies in key stock indices, as well as leading tech firms, to repurchase shares to help stabilise their market value, Reuters reported. It is also encouraging newly established exchange-traded funds (ETFs) to speed up stock purchases, while urging fund managers to invest during market downturns. ETFs are investment funds that typically track a basket of stocks, allowing investors to invest in multiple companies through a single fund. Together, the measures are intended to increase demand for shares and cushion the market against further sharp declines. Chinese stocks have been under pressure for months, with the sell-off intensifying in October as tech and artificial intelligence-related shares suffered sharp declines. But the downturn goes beyond technology stocks. Ng from Natixis said that the broader decline reflects weak investor sentiment and persistent problems in China’s economy. Sluggish domestic consumption, a prolonged property downturn and persistently low inflation have heavily weighed on corporate earnings and investor confidence. Weak demand and low inflation would make it harder for companies to raise prices and increase profits, Ng said - particularly when competition is intense. China's consumer inflation stood at just 0.9 per cent in September, according to official data released in October. With corporate earnings under pressure, investors may be less inclined to buy Chinese shares, particularly when they see opportunities for better returns elsewhere. Beijing's latest intervention also reflects growing concerns about financial stability. Ng noted that state-backed funds had already stepped in to support the market around a major Communist Party meeting held in October. According to a Bloomberg report on Oct 16, regulators urged state-backed investment funds to accelerate stock purchases, while Bloomberg Intelligence estimated that such investors bought about US$15 billion worth of shares through exchange-traded funds between Oct 9 and Oct 20. “It's all about stability,” said Ng, adding that authorities appeared concerned that a prolonged market slide could pose wider risks to the financial system. The latest measures could help put a floor under share prices, but some analysts cautioned that they may not be enough to drive a lasting recovery. CNA Correspondent explores China’s big push for a tech-fuelled market boom, tracing key developments since early 2024 and examining why this time, the rally might be different. Kenneth Goh, director of private wealth management at financial services firm UOB Kay Hian, said Beijing’s immediate priority was to stop the market from falling further, rather than spark a major rally. The measures are designed “more to steady market sentiment”, he said - by making it easier for financial institutions and companies to obtain funding to buy shares. Ng from Natixis added that making the share buyback lending facility permanent could also help reassure investors. Unlike a temporary scheme that may expire, a permanent arrangement gives banks and companies greater certainty that funding will remain available, potentially encouraging them to plan share purchases over a longer period. But cheaper and more readily available funding does not guarantee that investors will buy more stocks. Ng cautioned that financial institutions and companies would still need to weigh the risks of investing, particularly in volatile sectors such as technology and AI. Ultimately, while Beijing's measures may help cushion further losses and restore some confidence in the short term, a sustained recovery would depend on stronger economic growth and an improvement in corporate earnings. Analysts expect the measures to provide some relief in the short term - but cautioned that the rebound could be short-lived unless China’s broader economic outlook improves. Chinese stocks rallied on Monday following the announcement of the support measures, offering an early sign that Beijing's intervention had helped steady investor sentiment. The Shanghai Composite Index climbed 1.1 per cent, its biggest one-day percentage gain since Aug 27, according to Reuters. The Shenzhen Component Index rose 1.6 per cent, while Hong Kong's benchmark Hang Seng Index gained 0.4 per cent. Associate Professor Qu Feng from Nanyang Technological University's (NTU) economics division said that the measures “should help stabilise market sentiment by signalling that policymakers are prepared to intervene to prevent a further stock market decline”. However, he warned that the initial gains were unlikely to last without stronger economic growth, fresh investment into the stock market and an easing of concerns over a potential AI bubble. Feng also pointed to the high valuations of AI-related stocks, which cannot be addressed simply by pumping more money into the market. A sustained recovery “would require stronger corporate earnings and greater clarity about the future profitability of AI investments”, he said. Ng from Natixis similarly pointed to China's persistently low inflation and sluggish corporate profit growth as major obstacles to a lasting rebound. Goh at UOB Kay Hian said that a sustained recovery would depend on stronger domestic demand and improved corporate profitability. If market conditions fail to improve, Beijing could introduce further support measures before the end of the year, Goh said. These could include additional cuts to borrowing costs, expanded liquidity facilities or more incentives for institutional investors to buy shares. Ng also raised the possibility of further stock purchases by state-backed funds through ETFs if the sell-off continues. But China's previous attempts to shore up its stock market offer a cautionary tale. Beijing introduced similar liquidity support measures in October 2024 and January 2025, with the central bank providing a combined 105 billion yuan through earlier swap operations, according to Reuters. Ng said such interventions had helped stabilise share prices temporarily in the past, but their effects often faded when underlying economic conditions failed to improve. Ultimately, the latest measures offer more immediate relief than a foundation for lasting growth, Qu said. “Their effectiveness in supporting a longer-term market recovery will ultimately depend on whether they are accompanied by improvements in economic fundamentals and investor confidence,” he added.
