Every camera owner has their own list of things they wish their camera could do—features that seem easily achievable with a simple software update. Normally, that list dies quietly the moment a camera leaves the manufacturer's support cycle. Take the Nikon D3 as an example: unless you take matters into your own hands, nobody at Nikon is going to allocate resources to add new features to a flagship body from 2007. This is where I stumbled upon Marcus Low's firmware experimentation. He was kind enough to document and share his thoughts and the technical process of how he got there. He was completely upfront about his methodology: he didn't write this patch by hand. What he did have was a strong understanding of what current AI coding agents can actually achieve, utilizing them to reverse-engineer the Nikon D3's firmware and change what he needed. The division of labor went roughly like this. The AI (Claude Code, in this case) did the heavy lifting: disassembling the firmware, tracing how the shutter release and focus logic operate, and writing the patch. His role was acting as the director—picking what to build, determining acceptable risk levels, flashing test builds to the camera, and reporting back on the real-world results. As he noted, that final testing phase mattered far more than he expected. Early builds were based on incorrect assumptions and simply didn't work. Testing on the actual camera was crucial to sorting out these bugs, ultimately resulting in a patched sub-CPU firmware that added a feature he had wanted for a long time, running natively on his own Nikon D3. The idea of altering camera firmware didn't start with Nikon for him. His initial experiment was with the Sigma DP2x, a compact camera with a large sensor and a lens that extends every time it is switched on and retracts when switched off. To him, that essentially meant unnecessary trips for the lens motor and gear train per power cycle, regardless of whether a picture was taken. On compacts with extending lenses, that mechanical sequence can be a point of failure. The dreaded "lens error" is one way these cameras can meet their end. That was his first AI-assisted project: modifying the DP2x firmware to keep the lens extended when the camera turns off. If the lens is already out at power-on, it simply doesn't need to extend again. The logic is straightforward: fewer trips mean less physical wear on the mechanism that could potentially fail. Although he couldn't objectively prove the longevity gain on a single camera, reducing the number of extension and retraction cycles could potentially reduce wear over time. The firmware doesn't eliminate all lens movement, however; the focus motor still initializes at startup, and the lens can retract under certain conditions. Along the way, he also added a shot counter and a handful of other modernizing tweaks, publishing the project as the DP2X Longevity Firmware Update.  This led me to think about the obvious next candidate: the Ricoh GR series. My own previous resurrection plan for my GR II failed miserably, so this hits close to home. For context, the Ricoh GR series features a retracting lens that can suffer from mechanical failures after years of use. Yet, anyone who has seriously shot with one understands that it occupies an irreplaceable spot in a photographer's heart—fostering a true love-hate relationship among its cult following. I genuinely hope Marcus gets his hands on one to test some experimental firmware. Following the DP2x project, he noticed that the camera runs on a Fujitsu FR-family processor, an architecture also used by the Nikon D3's sub-CPU. This meant that some of the disassembly tools, annotation scripts, and AI-assisted mapping techniques from the DP2x project could potentially be carried over to the Nikon. Since he owned a Nikon D3, the next logical step was Project "Trap Focus." Project "Trap Focus" was named after the feature built to catch focus automatically for manual lenses. The idea is to make the experience of shooting manual-focus glass on a DSLR significantly more intuitive. Once the firmware is installed and configured, all you need to do is hold the shutter release down completely, turn the focusing barrel, and when the in-focus indicator lights up in the viewfinder, the camera triggers the shutter without requiring another button press. The patch requires effective manual-focus mode, Custom Setting a2 (AF-S priority selection) set to Focus, and release mode S, CL, or CH. Setting a2 to Release disables the feature. He clarified that this isn't a groundbreaking new concept, nor does he claim it to be. Pentax has shipped essentially this exact feature for years as "Catch-in Focus," a custom-menu option on many of its K-mount DSLRs. The frustration lies in the fact that it is an established, proven feature that one manufacturer deemed worthy of inclusion, while others didn't offer the same dedicated functionality for manual lenses despite having much of the hardware capability. That is exactly the kind of operational gap that firmware modding can fill.  Without trap focus, the mechanical sequence is: you fiddle with the focusing ring until the dot lights up, you visually process it, you make the decision, and your finger moves to depress the shutter. Simple visual reaction time is commonly measured at around 200 to 250 milliseconds—and that is before the finger has even traveled. Is a quarter of a second really a problem? At shallow depths of field, absolutely. A 50mm lens at f/1.4, focused at 1.5 meters on a full frame camera, yields a total depth of field of roughly 7 to 8 centimeters under conventional depth-of-field assumptions. A subject breathing, or your own bodily sway, can shift the focal plane a meaningful fraction of that in a quarter of a second. With trap focus, the camera reacts directly to its own focus-confirmation signal, triggering the shutter when the sensor reports focus without waiting for the photographer's reaction. Disclaimer: The camera isn't instantaneous either. The focus sensor has to measure, the firmware has to see the result, and the D3's normal shutter lag still applies. So the actual gain is really to eliminate the delay in the human part, not everything. And if your subject and camera are both perfectly still, there's little to gain here at all. Actual test images shot with Nikon D3 (loaded with Focus Trap) and 50mm f/1.4  With trap focus, the release is already fully depressed when focus arrives, removing the need for a final, physical button press at the exact moment of exposure. That downward jab can be a source of camera shake at slower shutter speeds, which is precisely why cable releases and self-timers exist. This is particularly relevant for this generation of DSLRs. The D3 lacks in-body image stabilization (IBIS), and many of the vintage manual-focus primes you would typically adapt to it have no optical stabilization. With nothing in those lenses or the camera body to correct for motion, anything that removes a source of micro-jitter is highly welcome. Bright DSLR focusing screens are optimized for a bright viewing experience with autofocus lenses, not necessarily to display accurate depth of field with very fast glass. A well-known optical side effect is that they can fail to show the true, razor-thin depth of field of very fast lenses. At apertures wider than roughly f/2.8, what you see in the optical viewfinder can look sharper than what is actually rendered onto the sensor. Combine that with dim lighting or less-than-perfect eyesight, and judging critical focus by eye becomes considerably harder. This firmware utilizes the D3's existing phase-detection AF module and its viewfinder focus-confirmation dot to determine when to release the shutter. It is worth noting that the AF dot has a tolerance window—at f/1.2 or f/1.4, that window can actually be wider than your true depth of field, and it inherits any calibration errors your specific AF module might have. Trap focus simply hands the decision-making over to the dot; it doesn't fundamentally make the dot more accurate. The Nikon F-mount boasts one of the deepest manual-focus lens catalogs in existence: AI and AI-S Nikkors, Series E glass, and premium manual lenses from Zeiss and Voigtländer. Much of this optical catalog is now relatively affordable on the used market. The D3 is a rugged, full frame body that can also be found for reasonable money. This Trap Focus firmware makes pairing the two more user-friendly, potentially increasing the practical value of both. At the same time, this is just one feature—it doesn't alter the D3's 12-megapixel sensor, its hefty weight, or its focusing screen. Flashing unofficial firmware also carries genuine risk. While the patch includes a software kill switch (Custom Setting a2 = Release) and Nikon's stock firmware files are provided for reverting, a bad flash can still leave a camera unusable. Reverting is only possible if the camera can still boot and run its firmware updater. It is important to note that everything in this section is pure speculation. Marcus has no inside knowledge of how Nikon or Canon plan their firmware roadmaps, and anyone claiming absolute certainty probably doesn't either. These are educated guesses informed by his dive into the camera's code. One thing the experiment demonstrates is that the D3 has the hardware and existing firmware functionality needed to implement this feature. The D3 can already achieve a form of trap focus with autofocus lenses using the classic back-button AF setup (AF-ON only, single-servo AF, focus priority). The patch builds on existing focus-confirmation and shutter-release logic already inside Nikon's firmware, extending that behavior to manual-focus operation. And, as Pentax has proven, a manufacturer can offer this as a supported feature. With that in mind, here are a few plausible reasons why the industry giants didn't offer the same dedicated functionality: Any of these theories could be wrong. The reality is likely a mix of them, or something as mundane as the feature simply never making it onto a product manager's to-do list. Either way, the result was the same: the underlying capability was already present in the camera's hardware and firmware, waiting to be put to another use. Trap focus is merely the first feature, not the final destination. Once you have the ability to read and rewrite the firmware, the "I wish it could…" list transitions from a grievance into a tangible to-do list. Marcus has already developed an experimental main-CPU patch that displays the shutter count on the firmware version screen and builds Nikon's D2X Mode 1, 2, and 3 Picture Controls directly into the D3. Be warned that this specific patch hasn't been flashed to a physical camera yet and should be treated as untested on actual hardware. At the time of writing, he was also working on custom color profiles. Beyond the D3, he is looking into porting these firmware mods to the D3X and the D700. Both cameras share aspects of the D3's generational architecture, potentially providing a head start, though he does not intend to publish those modifications until they have been verified on physical units. Whether any of this is worth the effort depends entirely on how much you value breathing new technical life into vintage digital cameras, weighed against the very real risk of bricking your gear with unofficial code. If nothing else, it shows that "the manufacturer won't add it" no longer has to be the end of the conversation. Disclaimer: These files are unofficial, modified firmware. They are not affiliated with or endorsed by Nikon or Sigma, and flashing modified firmware can brick your camera. Use at your own risk. The authors take no responsibility for any damage. Trap focus was tested on a Nikon D3 with patched sub-CPU firmware A 2.05 and stock B 2.03. The experimental main-CPU patch has not been tested on a physical camera. Tech stocks were particularly under pressure on Tuesday night. Investors appear to be wary that Democrat victories could advance policies aimed at stymying super-intelligence investment and data center build-outs. Government bonds rallied, often a sign that investors are becoming more concerned about the possibility of an economic downturn. The 10-year Treasury yield fell 0.05 percentage points to 4.90 percent. Yields on two-year Treasuries fell 0.064 percentage points to 4.55 percent. RocketNews24 Japanese  The site with a goal of “Adding muscles to everyday life” has released a new gallery collecting its most viral muscly moments up to the present.   Fukuoka-based Smile Academy’s Muscle Plus free stock image site has been around for a while now and it hasn’t stopped causing a stir. We can only thank the muscular geniuses who decided to gift the world with free-to-use, professional-quality shots of themselves posing in situations that make you think, “Heck, I can’t use that for anything!” before immediately downloading it anyway. Their purpose is not only making viewers’ smile muscles move but also promoting local people, cultural artifacts, events, and places in rural Fukuoka Prefecture in an effort to revitalize the area. Much of their work is seasonally appropriate as well, as seen in the epic Halloween photo story collection a few years back. ▼ Logo for the Muscle Plus free stock image site  Thanks to the positive public response, Muscle Plus has just released a new page that collects the photos and some quantitative data behind its most trending photos on Twitter. Thanks to this new system, you can simply check out which photos are getting the most hits when you’re in need of an image with impact. Below, we’ve compiled five of the top trending photos along with the date when they were uploaded to Twitter and their cumulative likes and views. All numbers are accurate as of October 21, 2026, so many have likely gained more hits since then. 1. Uploaded to Twitter on September 26, 2026 123,553 likes / 9,337,570 views There’s nothing quite as refreshing as two buff dudes frolicking in a field of vibrantly pink cosmos in Nokonoshima Park. This would be a peak tourism campaign if we ever saw one.  2. Uploaded October 1, 2026 52,535 likes / 2,170,577 views Two guys demonstrate how to harvest tea leaves at Yame Central Tea Plantation. It’s not a technique that we’ve ever seen before, but they seem to know what they’re doing.  3. Uploaded July 18, 2025 94,684 likes / 3,594,236 views This quintessential summertime shot in the sunflower field at Fukufuku no Sato farmers’ market reminds us that it’s OK to stop and sniff the flowers–sans shirts–sometimes.  4. Uploaded September 29, 2024 109,505 likes / 6,548,394 views Have you ever been sitting there eating some delicious yakiimo on a crisp autumn day with your weightlifting buddies when a cat suddenly decides to crash the photoshoot? No, it’s never happened to us, but we’re very thankful it happened to them.  5. Uploaded December 25, 2022 14,419 likes / 846,854 views We just hate it when we’re baking in the kitchen at Patisserie Serenite and someone comes along and sneakily adds liquid protein to the freshly whipped cream we were making. Thank goodness there’s a stock image to capture that situation.  The dudes at Muscle Plus have almost gotten us excited enough to start our own library of free stock images–though in our case, there would be much less of the buff and more of the puff. By  James Hercher Criteo has weathered considerable storms in its day, including a painful moment in March 2020 when its market cap bottomed out below $500 million. But for a month now, Criteo’s market cap has hovered between $700 million and $750 million. So, can it pull off yet another turnaround? The numbers from the company’s earnings report on Wednesday are … not great. Criteo’s revenue decreased 12% year over year to $416 million. Its profit shrank from $40 million a year ago to $6 million in Q3 2026. “This has been a challenging year,” Criteo CEO Michael Komasinski began the company’s investor call. “Our performance is not yet where I want it to be. The strength of our capabilities and the progress we’re making give me confidence in our direction.” For Criteo, that “progress” mostly comes in the form of monetizing new media channels and formats. Criteo introduced CTV support last year. It’s also pursuing more LLM chatbot integrations after being the first ad tech vendor partner for ChatGPT. And it’s striking social media ecommerce integrations with the likes of TikTok Shop and Meta.  Old dog, new tricks Criteo underwent a similar evolution many years ago, when it shifted from a retargeting business to retail media, which was one of the high-growth, high-optimism channels at the time (and also now). But during its earnings call, investors pressed on whether retail media was a mature channel. They wondered if retail media growth slowing down is a result of Criteo customers requiring fewer client services. Or maybe it speaks to a general dearth of new retail media business opportunities to tap. There could be something to those concerns, since Criteo seems to have more room for growth in nonretail channels. CTV, AI platform advertising and social media integrations now represent 13% of spend for Criteo Commerce Growth, the company’s AI-based optimization product. That’s up from 6% a year ago. CTV, LLM and social ads are also outpacing Criteo’s legacy display ad web targeting business, which is down year over year. Can Criteo turn those emerging channels into real revenue pillars for years to come? That proposition remains unproven. Always-on chatbot ads On the LLM front, “ChatGPT has been our fastest-growing partnership and channel for some time,” Komasinski said. But “fastest growing” comes with caveats. Percentage growth can be through the roof even if the line item went from a smidge above zero to a number that’s still quite small. We can’t really say either way. Criteo did not provide a hard revenue number for its LLM business. Still, one important proof point for ChatGPT Ads growth is its market spread, Komasinski said. Criteo was in seven countries with ChatGPT a few months ago. Now it’s in 89 countries. Plus, ChatGPT Ads traffic spends 15% more per visit on average, he said, which could help secure bigger budgets from brands who’ve seen success in early tests. Thus far, Criteo has had “3,600 clients on and off the platform,” Komasinski said. He explained the specific and strange wording of “on and off the platform,” which he said is because brands are mostly not “always-on” advertisers with ChatGPT (and other AI platforms). Looking ahead to Q4, Komasinski expects brands to run test campaigns over the holidays and deconstruct the results. Then they’ll probably come back and test again. How long it’ll take for those budgets to grow and become sticky is anyone’s guess, but Komasinski said he expects to see revenue growth ramping next year. Meanwhile, third-party ad tech can’t complain about getting access to a trendy new platform. “We’ve got a great position with a fast-growing channel, fast-growing partner who is introducing functionality at a rapid pace,” Komasinski said of the ChatGPT Ads partnership. Social and CTV Of the three new channels Criteo is prioritizing, social is the most mature. In the past year, social media spend on its platform and total social campaigns were up 20%. But Criteo is still very early in working its way into CTV. “It took us a little time to tune our bidder, build the right campaign structure (and) the right workflow” for streaming TV ads, Komasinski said. Getting advertisers to approach TV as a performance or direct response-caliber media also requires a change in education and industry thinking, he said. But performance CTV is “a great fit for what we do,” he said, and the required mindset shift around CTV as a performance channel is “now coming to fruition.” Becoming Apple-proof For Criteo, there are other reasons to pursue these new media channels, even if it means starting from zero with whole new types of ad formats and workflow software. Apple’s crackdown on ID infrastructure is a great motivator for moving beyond display and retail media, which require extensive cross-site tracking. “We’re not currently seeing an impact from the Safari changes in iOS 27, supported by our longstanding investments in privacy-safe technology and durable addressability,” Komasinski said multiple times when addressing questions about Apple’s recent changes to WebKit and iOS. Of course, iOS 27 gained little adoption during Criteo’s Q3, one investor pointed out. So the effects naturally haven’t arrived yet, right? Komasinski declined to weigh in any further on WebKit specifics. However, he added, “our channel diversification with social, OpenAI and CTV just puts us in a fundamentally different position today than where Criteo was a couple of years ago.” Disaffection and outright anger toward US sports institutions run deeper than logo-cluttered fields. Leagues and teams are sacrificing player safety and fan enjoyment for marketing dollars. People Inc.’s referral traffic from Google search is down 70% over the past two years, and by 26% in Q3 alone. But its digital revenue is still growing, albeit slowly. On Tuesday, Chord, a six-year-old commerce tech startup, acquired Zenlytic, an AI startup with an anthropomorphized data analyst agent named “Zoë,” for $5 million. If you ask the executive leadership of Affle and Perion why the two companies are merging, the answer you’ll get is “synergies.” A combo of Tubi, sports and political ads powered Fox’s growth this last quarter, even as Fox News lost viewers and the Roku deal awaits DOJ clearance. It’s fall, and M&A is in the air. Two acquisitions happened this week: Stagwell bought Freestar, and DoorDash bought Instacart. If you’ve ever lived through a heat wave or drought, you know there’s a sound when the rain finally breaks. The atmospheric shifts as the first, fat drops fall, yes—but then as it all cuts loose, whoops from the streets. It is the sound of relief. This is the sound of America’s blue tsunami from a Southwest Ohio pizza parlor. First, a trickle of positive results: With a fraction of the vote in, gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton was way ahead, as was Sherrod Brown in Ohio’s Senate race. People cheer, then wait. Later in the night, a deluge: A group of Democrats, ostensibly gathered to support three candidates at a different Montgomery, Ohio, tavern, cheered over the Georgia governor’s race, called for Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms. Then Annie Andrews took South Carolina’s Senate seat. Dems secured control of the House—a wave of screams.  Though MS NOW was still waiting, a voice across the tavern shouted that Bloomberg and NBC had called it: Amy Acton had won the governor’s seat. A statehouse rep in the room won reelection, so did a judge. Within a minute, another shouted message: Dems were on track to win multiple new seats in the Ohio House, breaking the supermajority. It started to be hard to hear why everyone was bursting into elated cheers. Talarico won in Texas! On the TVs in the tavern, Acton’s image filled the screen, final confirmation she had won. Thunder. Relief. Vivek Ramaswamy spent $79 million (including $41.3 million of his own money) to lose a governor’s race in which the billionaire showed himself to be so out of touch, he thought it would help his campaign to dig Acton’s estranged mother out of the cobwebs for an unconscionable attack ad that drew resounding disgust from across parties (with the notable exception of Donald Trump and JD Vance). The grossest campaign in America lost last night. Ohio, which hasn’t swung left in a governor’s race since 2006, just did. I suspect, though, that the result, while certainly part of a national referendum on Trump and Republicans who’ve kowtowed to him at every level, is also a reflection of Democratic candidates who activated an impressive grassroots campaign. Every time Ramaswamy skipped across the state (or out of state) in his private jet or invested millions in cartoonishly evil attack ads, Acton was on a family farm, or on a union picket line, or at a diner, leaning in to talk to voters regardless of party. And down-ticket candidates did the same. Ohio was won by making the race not about party but about Ohioans, writ large, winning.  Ohio used to be a key swing state, but highly effective gerrymandering has carved us into right-locked districts that have produced increasingly extreme candidates and a Republican supermajority in the statehouse. Ohio has had a Republican trifecta (governor’s office and both chambers of the statehouse) for 28 years since 1992, and in that time, Ohio’s schools have suffered (now forty-fifth in the nation for our state share of public school funding). Ohio’s economy ranks thirty-ninth, and we’re thirty-fourth for health care. Our infrastructure and water scores low too. The relative security of Republican seats surely contributed to our dark money–fueled FirstEnergy bribery scandal, which landed former Ohio speaker of the House Republican Larry Householder in prison for racketeering. Sizable sums wash in and out of the state, but not often to benefit the common good. Tens of millions in PAC money was donated from outside billionaires, such as Elon Musk and Jeffrey Yass, to sway votes for Ramaswamy. (Over 95 percent of Acton’s donations totaled $100 or less.) A projected $11.6 billion was spent on Ohio’s midterm election this year, with more than half a billion on the U.S. Senate race alone.  Our gerrymandered maps and millions of dollars have been invested in chopping up Ohio to ensure Republican power. And in some parts of the state, the partisan divide still strains.  In rural Shelby County, Democratic Party Chair Christopher R. Gibbs has been busy trying to help Democratic candidates understand rural voters who regularly feel ignored, sidelined, and taken for granted. I met him on a family farm whistle-stop for the Acton campaign. Gibbs, who used to be the county’s Republican chair, left the party in 2019. It “no longer shared my core values.”  Anecdotally, Gibbs says in Shelby, one of the reddest counties in Ohio, there is a visceral hate for Democrats, based on locals’ perception of national Dems. But data centers, a significant rural issue, isn’t yet partisan. Over 200 data center projects are planned or under construction, and 21 initiatives were on the ballot yesterday (the most nationally). Both Acton and Ramaswamy campaigned on tighter rules around data centers after, in May, current Governor Mike DeWine ordered a pause on tax exemptions on the centers—which had already surpassed $2 billion in 2025. Across the state last night, a number of data center bans passed.  Electoral maps and MAGA aside, Ohioans may have been united by practical realities. I passed a gas sign that read “$4.17/gallon” for regular unleaded, yesterday driving between polls. Big Tech has planted data centers that slurp up our energy, land, and water. About one in eight Ohio families lives under the poverty line and, according to the United Way, another 23 percent live above the poverty line but can’t afford basic expenses. We are, collectively, done. And the billionaires could not buy this election. Acton often talks about how people in Youngstown who didn’t have much would share with those who had less. Desperation communicates across boundaries, if we can really see each other. Maybe the current state of the country and Ohio has finally made enough of us too tired to hate each other. At my own polling location, in Wyoming, Ohio, hometown of the Democrats’ incoming lieutenant governor, David Pepper, two middle-aged women stood side by side just off the lawn outside our community Civic Center. One held blue handouts of the Democrats’ slate; the other held the pink Republicans’. Voters swept in and out. It was nice to see the two chatting volunteers, holding opposing slates, getting along so well. I said so. The woman holding the Republican slate said of course they were friendly, they live in the same neighborhood. But the stakes were still obvious. I ran across voter Michael Robinson on my way to grab a bagel. His hair is dappled with grey, and his hoodie was adorned with an “Ohio Voted” sticker. The sticker is important. His mother-in-law insists upon photographic evidence, though Robinson wouldn’t miss a vote. His parents and grandparents lived in Washington, D.C., before the majority-Black city was allowed to vote in presidential elections. His paternal grandfather grew up in South Carolina as a sharecropper who could not afford the poll tax. Robinson, an Ohio resident for 26 years now, was born in the Nation’s Capital, and at 18, voted in the District’s first home rule election in 1974. He tells me his grandmother drilled into him that education and the vote were the two things no one could take away, “That’s how you have power … that’s what they wanna take away.” (A voter ID requirement passed today in Ohio too.) In the Cincy suburb of Montgomery, Ohio, two men, each holding slates of opposing parties, chatted in a friendly way at a church entryway, a polling site. A father and young daughter come out, and the Republican asks, “Is it her first time voting?” It was indeed her first time tagging along. She got a sticker. Everyone cheered. At the other entrance, though, from the Democrats, I hear the police were called earlier because a man was berated by a volunteer for a Republican candidate after voting. A Republican volunteer tells me it’s been a beautiful day. She says, “It’s up to how God turns the hearts and minds of men. But I do hope they choose his values over their own desires.” I know it’s not what she meant, but I kind of suspect many would say they did. Outside Norwood Community Center, shortly before polls closed, I open my car door to Rihanna. There was no line, but the music was pumping. The DJ, Bizzy Bizz (Rodney Hayes), is part of DJ at the Polls, a good-vibes-only, nonpartisan get-out-the-vote effort. Under the thump of “This Is What You Came For,” Bizzy Bizz tells me that it has been an incredible day. After the past few years, the positivity he’s seen at the polls, people coming together to vote, “honestly, it’s restored my faith in humanity.” As the music plays, this, he says, “this is what this nation needs.” People who are stressed over how they are going to stock their kitchen cabinets have been subjected to a dizzying demonstration of disqualifying behavior from candidates who seem to have lost the plot on human decency. Congressman Max Miller, who represents a Northeast Ohio district, has been accused of domestic abuse. Despite a delay in speaking out, our other senator, Bernie Moreno, whose daughter happens to be Miller’s estranged wife, finally did pipe up, saying Miller needs “psychological help,” that he holds his breath whenever Miller has custody of his granddaughter, and calling for Miller’s resignation from Congress. Miller’s opponent, Brian Poindexter, a union organizer and ironworker, was named the presumptive winner overnight. Longtime U.S. Senator Sherrod Brown lost his seat in 2024, after $251 million in attack ads that largely weaponized trans rights and lied about Brown’s positions. This time, as he ran against Jon Husted, a widely debunked attack ad claimed that “Sherrod Brown supports sex change surgery for minors.” However, the woman in the ad who claimed she got surgery without her parents’ consent as a minor is actually from Texas (not Ohio) and was 19 when she had her double mastectomy. This time, many Democrats, including Brown, have strategically pivoted from getting bogged down in a culture war over trans rights, either pointing out the inaccuracies in such ads or redirecting away from the vanishingly small handful of trans youth in Ohio school sports. (It’s debatable whether it’s better to have your identity weaponized or ignored, both for political ends.) Instead, Democrats’ energy has largely focused on pocketbook issues, which affect almost all of us (yes, including trans Ohioans). At 11 p.m., CNN called it for Ohio’s Senate race: Mr. Brown is going back to Washington. The tavern where I was watching results erupted. The local TV news happened to cut away and fill the screen with an image of Amy Acton. More cheers. A chant of “O-H, I-O.” Acton took the stage in Columbus behind a “Governor-Elect Acton” sign, saying the state had chosen “unity and decency over division and hate. The healing begins today.” As Acton took the stage for her acceptance speech, for a moment, I had the heart-pounding sensation of witnessing a local girl done good.  I grew up a couple miles down a long cross-county road from where Acton grew up, once she and her brother settled in with their father. This was after she spent time hungry and homeless, living in a tent over winter in Youngstown, after escaping her sexually abusive stepfather and a mother who skipped town with him after his indictment for Acton’s abuse. We come from this place, where steel still runs in people’s veins, generations since the mills closed, decades since opportunity was anything people could count on. A place where those who could were often coached to go away to school, get out. Acton, with Brown, held her last campaign stop in her old high school. “I’m a scrappy kid from Youngstown,” she said before hundreds as the high school gym erupted in applause. Her reprise, this entire campaign, has been a stubborn fixation on the issues “99 percent of Ohioans can agree on.” She talks like she was aiming for, not a blue wave, but enough to drink for everyone. As we were each growing up, our corner of the state was a Democratic stronghold, but give a place a couple generations of broken promises of change, grown kids moving away, and those who stayed staking a sad, fierce loyalty to a place of want, and the region was ready for a new promise-peddler when Donald Trump ran in 2016. Youngstown’s Mahoning County switched from reliably blue to red.  But Acton and Brown both won there last night. When people vote, they choose a person to represent them in government, but they also approve the person who publicly represents their interests, their values. They represent us as a people. When Acton started campaigning, she was bothered that on the internet, young people used phrases like “That’s so Ohio” as a catchphrase for things that were bad or cringe. Acton suffered as a child in Ohio, but her ambition and effort were also rewarded in Ohio. She learned in the great public schools that have been quietly underfunded and now are being siphoned of over $1 billion per year for private school vouchers. She served the state over Covid, and even after enduring the brunt of blowback, she put her hand up for more service as governor.  She had the cruel indignity of campaigning to serve this state and getting sideswiped by her mother, a woman who has failed her over and again. As the nation has looked to Ramaswamy with a collective “WTF,” Acton told me recently that since the attack ad, she has been stopped at event after event by survivors whose worst moments were dredged up by Ramaswamy’s disgusting campaign ploy. The swipe could have derailed most people. Others might have become overwhelmed by the disclosures of abuse, but what Acton took from it was that there are more survivors of sexual assault in the state than most people realize.  Ramaswamy’s campaign tried to destroy her; Acton’s empathetic heart found an additional policy front. When I was young, people called Ohio purple, a reliable mix of red and blue. As went Ohio, so went the nation. For a long time, we’ve been painted red by state and congressional maps, and a lot of us got used to officials who extracted their power and influence from the state but failed to see us, on rural farms now in the shadow of data centers, or striving for more in the three C’s (Cleveland, Columbus, and Cincinnati), or for kids growing up in towns where almost everyone struggles. If they saw our dreams, it was just to exploit them. A lot of pundits may tell the story of 2026 as a blue wave, but from here in Ohio, it looks more like the first gulp of an enormous storm, skies cracking open after a long, hard drought.
